def: Gel strength measured after the mud has rested 10 minutes.
Gel strength measured after the mud has rested 10 seconds.
A seismic survey recorded along separate lines, giving vertical sections rather than a full volume.
The lowest standard viscometer reading, used to judge sag and low-shear viscosity.
Gel strength measured after 30 minutes of rest, used to check progressive gels.
The rotational viscometer dial reading at 300 rpm, used with the 600-rpm reading to compute yield point.
A survey recorded on a dense grid that produces a full volume of the subsurface rather than individual lines.
A VSP recorded with many sources to image a volume around the well.
Four-component seismic recorded with a hydrophone and three geophones, usually on the seabed.
Repeated 3D surveys over the same field at different times, used to see how fluids and pressure in the reservoir change with production. Also called time-lapse seismic.
Filling missing traces using inline, crossline, offset and azimuth together.
The low-speed viscometer reading that indicates hole-cleaning ability.
The rotational viscometer dial reading at 600 rpm, used to compute plastic viscosity and apparent viscosity.
Plugging a well permanently and removing equipment at surface.
A guide saying bridging particles should be at least one third of the median pore size.
Cutting pipe with a high-pressure jet carrying abrasive particles.
The theoretical rate a gas well would deliver with zero flowing bottomhole pressure, used to compare wells. Abbreviated AOF.
Pressure measured from a perfect vacuum, in psia. Gas-law calculations always use absolute pressure.
Conversion of seismic energy into heat as waves pass through rock, which removes high frequencies first.
The flat, deep ocean floor beyond the continental rise, covered by fine sediment.
A tool run above a jar that stores energy and increases the jarring blow.
The space available for sediment to fill, controlled by sea level change and subsidence.
Cuttings sticking to the BHA and building up, often with sticky shale.
A wedge of sediment scraped off a sinking plate at a subduction zone.
A weak organic acid used for carbonate treatments and iron control.
A breaker that uses acid to dissolve calcium carbonate in filter cake.
The strength of an acid, usually in weight percent.
An additive that protects tubulars from attack during acid treatments.
Producing spent acid back after a treatment.
Fracturing a carbonate with acid instead of proppant. The acid etches the fracture faces unevenly, so it stays open after closure.
A treatment that pumps acid into a well.
Getting acid to the zones that need it.
A thick deposit formed when acid reacts with some crude oils.
Leaving acid across an interval to dissolve filter cake or scale.
Pumping acid into a well to dissolve damage or rock and improve flow.
Circulating acid past perforations or screens to clean them without pumping into the rock.
Lost circulation material that dissolves in acid, so it can be removed from the reservoir later.
Pumping acid into a well to dissolve damage or rock and improve flow, for example hydrochloric acid in carbonates or mud acid in sandstones.
The deepest surface that gives coherent seismic reflections, below which the data shows little structure.
Finding the fluid level by sending a sound pulse down the annulus and timing the echo.
The product of a rock's density and its seismic velocity. Changes in it from layer to layer create seismic reflections.
A log of velocity times density, used to make synthetic seismograms.
Sending data up the pipe as sound waves.
A pressure wave that travels through a fluid or solid.
Regular stripes or patterns in seismic data caused by the survey geometry rather than geology.
The layout of sources and receivers in a survey.
A synthetic polymer built partly from acrylamide, used for fluid-loss control or shale encapsulation.
The mud pit connected to the circulating system.
The mud pits that are connected to the circulating system at any given time. Their volume is watched closely for gains and losses.
In an interference test, the well whose rate is changed.
Matching the water activity of an oil-base mud to that of the shale so water doesn't move between them.
Any material added to a drilling fluid to change its properties.
A bent housing whose angle can be set at surface.
A choke whose opening can be changed while flowing.
Gas held on the internal surfaces of organic matter and clay in shale rather than as free gas in the pores.
Mud gas measured with a constant-volume trap and fast chromatograph for fluid typing.
Relating to wind. Aeolian sandstones form from desert dunes and are usually well sorted and porous.
Sediment carried and laid down by wind, such as dune sand.
Drilling fluid with air or nitrogen injected into it to lower its density.
A magnetic survey flown by aircraft to map basement depth, faults and volcanic rocks over large areas.
Analysis of pressure after fracture closure to estimate permeability and reservoir pressure.
Fluid that keeps flowing into the wellbore after it is shut in at surface, as the well contents compress.
A time function that lets build-up data be analyzed like drawdown data.
Vertical stacking of sediment when supply and accommodation are roughly balanced.
A pressure-rated steel cell in which mud samples are heated for hot-roll or static ageing tests.
A tool that vibrates the drillstring axially to reduce friction while sliding.
Drilling with compressed air or gas instead of liquid mud. It gives fast penetration in hard, dry rock.
The usual marine seismic source. It suddenly releases a bubble of high-pressure air to make a sound pulse.
A percussion drilling tool driven by compressed air.
Injecting air to support in-situ combustion or low-temperature oxidation.
Sound traveling through the air from a land seismic source, which appears as noise on the records.
Mud with entrained air bubbles, which lowers its density and can mislead pit readings.
Several air guns of different sizes fired together to make a strong, clean source pulse.
Air injected per barrel of oil produced in combustion projects.
Gravity measured from aircraft.
A linear approximation of the Zoeppritz equations for small contrasts, the basis of most AVO analysis.
Designing and handling alarms so operators see what matters.
Distortion that occurs when a signal is sampled too coarsely in time or space, so high frequencies appear as false low frequencies.
Loss of alkali to reactions with rock and brine during alkaline flooding.
Injecting an alkali, such as sodium carbonate, which reacts with acids in the oil to form surfactants in place.
The ability of a mud's water phase to neutralize acid. It is measured by titration and reported as values such as Pf and Mf.
The amount of acid needed to neutralize the bases in mud filtrate, reported as Pf and Mf.
An oil-base mud with little or no water phase.
A fault-plane map showing which layers on each side meet, used to analyze juxtaposition and seal.
The ratio used to adjust well test rates so they add up to measured totals.
A fan-shaped body of coarse sediment deposited where a steep stream spreads out at a mountain front.
The first gravel deposition wave moving along the low side in a horizontal gravel pack.
The two-stage way gravel fills a horizontal openhole annulus: the alpha wave packs the low side first, then the beta wave fills the top back.
An additive that precipitates in shale pores to slow pressure transmission and stabilize shale.
A metallic soap added in small amounts to break foam in water-base muds.
Background vibration from wind, waves and human activity, which can be noise or a passive-seismic signal.
The main US oil and gas trade association, which publishes many of the industry's equipment standards and recommended practices. Abbreviated API.
The radioactive neutron source used in many neutron tools.
An amine compound that sticks to clay surfaces and stops water entering them, giving water-base mud some of the shale stability of oil-base mud.
A gas sweetening process in which an amine solution absorbs H<sub>2</sub>S and CO<sub>2</sub> from the gas and is then regenerated by heat.
A plant that removes acid gases from gas with an amine solution.
Another name for organophilic lignite.
A liquid oxygen scavenger used in muds, brines and packer fluids.
A salt used in low-density brines and to stabilize clays.
A wettability test using spontaneous and forced fluid displacement.
An area of unusually high or low reflection amplitude.
A map of seismic amplitude along a horizon, often used to outline reservoirs or hydrocarbons.
Processing that keeps relative reflection amplitudes true so they can be used for AVO and reservoir work.
The strength of each frequency in a signal.
The change in reflection strength as the source–receiver distance increases. It is used to predict lithology and fluid content. Abbreviated AVO.
AVO analysis done with incidence angle instead of offset. Abbreviated AVA.
A polymer containing acrylamido-methyl-propane sulfonate, used for fluid-loss control at high temperature and salinity.
The scheme linking normal, strike-slip and thrust faults to which principal stress is vertical.
Prestack traces sorted by angle of incidence, used for AVO analysis and inversion.
A stack of traces from a range of incidence angles, such as near or far.
An unconformity where older tilted layers are cut and covered by flatter younger ones.
Calcium sulfate without water (CaSO<sub>4</sub>), a dense evaporite that often acts as a seal. It reads about 2.98 g/cm³ on a density log.
The lowest temperature at which an oil fully mixes with an equal volume of aniline. A low value means more aromatics, which attack rubber seals.
A polymer whose chains carry negative charges, such as PAC or PHPA. Most water-base mud polymers are anionic.
Variation of a property with direction, for example horizontal permeability being much higher than vertical permeability.
A flow regime with gas in the center and a liquid film along the pipe wall.
Pumping waste slurry down a casing annulus into a disposal formation.
The pressure in the annulus between drillstring and hole or casing.
The friction pressure lost as mud flows up the annulus. It is what makes ECD higher than static mud weight.
A downhole measurement of annular pressure from an MWD/LWD tool, used to monitor ECD and hole cleaning in real time.
A blowout preventer with a doughnut-shaped rubber packing element. It can seal around pipe of almost any size, or close on an open hole.
The average upward speed of drilling fluid in the annulus, found by dividing the pump rate by the annular cross-sectional area. It has to be high enough to lift cuttings out of the hole.
Watching annular pressures to detect leaks.
Describes test tools opened or closed by applying set pressures to the annulus.
A valve on the wellhead or tree that controls access to the annulus.
Automatically flagging data that departs from normal behavior, for example to catch equipment problems early.
An algorithm that follows edge-attribute lines to pick fault surfaces automatically.
The highest rank of coal, hard and high in carbon.
Carbon dioxide captured from industrial sources.
A filter applied before sampling to remove frequencies above Nyquist.
Planning and surveying wells so they don't hit nearby wells.
An additive that prevents sludge forming when acid contacts crude.
A trap formed by an upward fold.
An arch-shaped fold of rock layers with the oldest rocks in its core. It is the classic structural trap.
The API specification for casing and tubing.
The API grades of well cement, A through H, set by depth and temperature use.
The standard cell for measuring mud fluid loss: filtrate is collected through filter paper for 30 minutes at 100 psi and room temperature.
Filtrate volume in 30 minutes at 100 psi and room temperature in the API filter press.
The unit of gamma ray logs, defined by a calibration pit at the University of Houston.
A scale of oil density: °API = 141.5 / SG − 131.5, where SG is specific gravity at 60 °F. Higher values mean lighter oil.
A glass float that measures the API gravity of oil.
The API recommended practices for field testing water-base (13B-1) and oil-base (13B-2) drilling fluids.
The recommended practice for testing and labeling shaker screens.
The API recommended practice for testing and reporting how perforating charges perform.
The API RP 13C label for shaker screens based on their tested cut point, such as API 140.
The API specification for drilling fluid materials such as barite and bentonite.
The dip seen in a section not perpendicular to strike, smaller than true dip.
Neutron or density porosity read on a limestone scale before lithology correction.
The resistivity of a uniform earth that would give the measured response.
The speed at which a wavefront appears to move across the receivers, which depends on its angle of arrival.
For drilling mud, half the 600-rpm viscometer reading, in centipoise. It is a single-number summary of how thick the mud is at high shear.
A value calculated from Archie's equation assuming a zone is fully water-bearing. Written R<sub>wa</sub>. Readings well above R<sub>w</sub> point to hydrocarbons.
A defined way for programs to exchange data.
A well drilled after a discovery to find its size and properties.
A water-bearing rock connected to a reservoir. When the reservoir is produced, water from the aquifer can flow in and support the pressure.
Water flowing into a reservoir from a connected aquifer as pressure falls.
An empirical equation linking resistivity to water saturation in clean rock: S<sub>w</sub><sup>n</sup> = a·R<sub>w</sub> / (φ<sup>m</sup>·R<sub>t</sub>).
The fraction of the reservoir's plan area that the injected fluid has contacted.
A sandstone with more than about 25% feldspar.
The fraction of aromatic hydrocarbons in a base oil. Low-aromatic oils are less toxic and kinder to elastomers.
A solvent rich in aromatic compounds, effective on asphaltenes.
The family of empirical equations (exponential, hyperbolic and harmonic) used to fit and forecast declining production rates.
A formula for converting fluid resistivity from one temperature to another, since resistivity falls as temperature rises.
An induction logging tool with several receiver spacings that gives resistivity at several depths of investigation.
A laterolog with several current patterns that gives resistivity at several depths in conductive mud.
Using several sensors spread across the pipe to measure segregated flow in deviated wells.
A production logging tool with several small spinners spread across the pipe, used in deviated wells where phases separate.
Computer systems that perform tasks that normally need human judgment.
Any method that adds energy to bring well fluids to surface once reservoir pressure alone can no longer do it, such as gas lift, rod pumps or ESPs.
Switching a well to a different lift method.
A chemical flood that combines alkali, surfactant and polymer to lower interfacial tension and control mobility together.
A heavy hydrocarbon additive used to seal shale microfractures and reduce fluid loss.
Heavy, polar molecules in crude oil that can precipitate when pressure or composition changes, plugging rock, tubing and equipment.
Change of asphaltene content with depth, used to judge reservoir connectivity.
A chemical that keeps asphaltenes from depositing.
The pressure at which asphaltenes start to come out of oil as pressure falls.
Dissolving asphaltene deposits with aromatic solvents.
A polymer with groups that link to each other, giving high viscosity at low concentration.
The largest bitumen deposit in Alberta, Canada, developed by surface mining and in-situ thermal methods.
A degasser that sprays mud against a baffle at atmospheric pressure.
A ring-shaped reef around a lagoon.
A needle-shaped clay that builds viscosity in salt water, where bentonite will not hydrate.
LWD resistivity from the loss of amplitude of an electromagnetic wave between receivers, which reads deeper than phase.
Calculating an attribute along a horizon or within a window.
Clay that grew in place in the pore space after deposition, often lining or bridging pores.
A cost estimate for a planned operation, such as drilling a well, that partners approve before money is spent. Abbreviated AFE.
The cross-correlation of a signal with itself, used in deconvolution and to spot repeating multiples.
Using algorithms to adjust model parameters until they match field data.
Scaling seismic amplitudes in a moving window so weak and strong signals display at similar strength. Abbreviated AGC.
Drilling in which software makes routine control decisions.
An inflow control device that automatically chokes back water or gas while letting oil through. Abbreviated AICD.
Software that follows a seismic horizon automatically from a seed point.
The thickness-weighted mean porosity of the net reservoir.
The volume-weighted mean pressure in the drainage area of a well or reservoir, used in material balance.
The depth to a reflector divided by its one-way travel time.
The Rutherford-Williams classification (classes 1 to 4) of gas-sand reflections by how their amplitude changes with offset.
A plot of AVO intercept against gradient, where anomalous points can indicate hydrocarbons.
The rate at which reflection amplitude changes with the square of the sine of the incidence angle.
The zero-offset reflection amplitude in a linear AVO fit.
Computing the expected AVO response for given rock and fluid properties.
Processing designed to keep amplitude changes with offset for AVO analysis.
Intercept times gradient, an attribute that highlights class III anomalies.
The compass direction of the wellbore, measured clockwise from north.
The local direction of dip of seismic events.
A density measurement while drilling split by direction around the hole, used for imaging and geosteering.
A density measurement around the borehole circumference from an LWD tool, used for geosteering and dip picking.
A resistivity measurement while drilling that is sensitive to direction, used to see bed boundaries for geosteering.
The slope of the magnitude-frequency relation of earthquakes.
The angle at which a PDC cutter tilts back from the rock face.
The sheltered area behind a reef, often a lagoon.
A basin that forms behind a volcanic arc by extension.
Unscrewing the drillstring at a joint just above the stuck point, often helped by a small explosive string shot.
A valve that keeps pressure upstream at a set value.
A gas-well deliverability test in which the well is flowed at several rates and the pressures recorded, to build its deliverability curve.
A one-way valve installed in the tubing hanger to hold well pressure while the tree or BOP is removed.
The steady low level of gas in the returns while drilling, against which shows are judged.
Pulling the drillstring out while rotating and circulating, to clean tight spots.
Averaging well-log elastic properties to seismic scale.
A tube with a valve run on wireline to collect sand or debris, or to dump material at a set depth.
The depth at which pipe weight equals the upward force of well pressure.
A mud gas ratio used with wetness to identify fluid type.
A cross section that can be restored to an undeformed state, a test that the interpretation is possible.
A cement plug placed so the fluid levels inside and outside the pipe are equal before the pipe is pulled.
A mill that grinds materials such as barite to the required fineness.
Small balls pumped with a treatment that seat on open perforations and divert fluid to other perforations.
A sleeve opened by dropping a ball, used in multistage fracturing.
A multistage system in which balls of increasing size are dropped to open sleeves and isolate stages one by one.
A stabilizer packed with clay, which raises drag and swab pressure.
Tubing shortening when internal pressure exceeds external pressure.
Inversion that recovers impedance only within the seismic frequency band.
A filter that keeps frequencies within a chosen range and removes those above and below.
The range of frequencies in a signal.
Barium sulfate (BaSO<sub>4</sub>), a heavy mineral with a specific gravity of about 4.2. It is ground fine and added to mud to raise its density.
A slurry of barite that settles quickly to form a hard plug, used to seal a well in some well-control emergencies.
Separating barite from mud with a centrifuge so it can be returned to the system.
Settling of weighting material in the mud, especially in deviated wells, which leaves uneven density in the hole.
The required density, particle size and soluble alkaline earth limits for drilling-grade barite.
The standard unit of oil volume, equal to 42 US gallons or about 0.159 cubic meters. Abbreviated bbl.
A unit that converts gas to oil on an energy basis, usually 6,000 scf of gas to one barrel, so oil and gas can be added together. Abbreviated BOE.
One part of a barrier envelope, such as a valve, plug or cement.
The set of barrier elements that together contain well pressure.
A long, narrow sand island parallel to the coast, separated from the mainland by a lagoon.
Pressure testing a well barrier to prove it holds.
A dark, fine-grained volcanic rock that can form fractured reservoirs or seals.
Swapping of cations held on clay surfaces for others in the surrounding water.
The liquid that forms the continuous phase of a mud, such as fresh water, brine, diesel, mineral oil or a synthetic oil.
The oil that forms the continuous phase of an oil-base mud, such as low-toxicity mineral oil or diesel.
The first survey in a time-lapse study.
The igneous or metamorphic rock beneath sedimentary layers.
The plate a vibrator presses on the ground to transmit its sweep.
The water, sediment and emulsion in crude oil, measured as a volume percent and limited for sales. Abbreviated BS&W.
A fan deposited on the basin floor during low sea level.
Computer simulation of a basin's burial, heating, generation and migration through time.
An overshot grapple shaped like a basket, for long catch areas.
Drilling the same section of several wells in a row before moving to the next section.
A tank in which a slurry is mixed before pumping for accurate density.
Equations for the density and velocity of oil, gas and brine at reservoir conditions.
Inversion that combines prior knowledge with data to give probabilities of rock properties.
Barrels per day, the usual unit for oil production rates. Also written BOPD (barrels of oil per day).
A pill with glass or plastic beads spotted to reduce torque and drag.
A depth migration method that propagates energy in beams, efficient for large surveys.
The replaceable orifice inside a positive choke. Its size, usually in 64ths of an inch, sets the flow rate.
The smallest named layer of sedimentary rock.
The surface between two layers, where log readings change.
The layering of sedimentary rocks.
The dip and direction of bedding measured from images or dipmeters.
A gamma ray curve that increases upward, typical of fining-upward channels.
A reference crude, such as Brent or West Texas Intermediate (WTI), against which other crude oils are priced.
A motor housing with a small built-in bend that points the bit off-axis for steering.
A short sub with a slight bend used above a motor to drill directionally.
A swelling clay made mostly of sodium montmorillonite. In fresh water it builds viscosity, gel strength and a thin filter cake.
A polymer that makes a small amount of bentonite build much more viscosity, used in low-solids muds.
A simple mix of bentonite in fresh water, often used to spud a well or as a sweep.
The barrels of 15-centipoise mud that one ton of bentonite produces.
A diverting agent that dissolves in oil or water after the treatment.
Particles above a size before a filter divided by those after, a measure of filter efficiency.
The return gravel wave filling the remaining space in a horizontal gravel pack.
Bottomhole circulating temperature: the temperature cement sees while being pumped.
Bottomhole static temperature: the undisturbed temperature at the bottom of the well.
Bicarbonate ions in a water-base mud, often from CO<sub>2</sub> or overtreatment, that cause high, hard-to-break gel strengths.
A shaped charge designed for a large entrance hole rather than deep penetration, used for gravel packs and fracturing.
A flow regime with linear flow in a finite-conductivity fracture and linear flow toward it. The derivative has a quarter slope.
A small rectangular area in a 3D survey into which all traces with midpoints in that area are gathered.
A flow model in which a fluid needs a minimum stress (the yield point) before it moves, then flows with a constant plastic viscosity.
A chemical that kills bacteria in mud, protecting polymers such as starch from fermenting.
A fragment of shell or skeleton in a sedimentary rock.
Limestone made mostly of shell fragments.
How readily a fluid is broken down by microorganisms, an important rating for offshore discharge of muds.
Bacteria consuming the lighter parts of oil in shallow, cool reservoirs, which makes it heavier and more viscous.
Gas, mostly methane, made by microbes at shallow depth and low temperature.
A molecular fossil in oil that links it to its source organisms and indicates maturity and depositional setting.
A polymer made by microbes, such as xanthan gum, used to build viscosity.
Dating and correlating rock layers using the fossils they contain.
A surfactant made by microbes.
Rock physics equations that predict how velocity changes when pore fluid changes.
A dark iron-magnesium mica found in igneous and metamorphic rocks.
Disturbance of sediment by burrowing animals, which can destroy layering and change permeability.
A depth and steering controller clamped along a marine streamer.
A very soluble magnesium chloride salt.
Sticky clay packing onto the bit's cutting structure, which sharply slows drilling.
Axial vibration where the bit lifts off and hits bottom repeatedly.
The outer diameter of a bit, and the part that holds hole size.
How pressure and flow are used at the bit to clean it and the hole bottom.
A replaceable jet in the bit that directs high-velocity mud onto the cutters and hole bottom.
The pressure lost as mud flows through the bit nozzles, often designed to be about half the total pump pressure.
A record of each bit run with footage, hours, parameters and dull grade.
The interval drilled with one bit, from going in to pulling out.
A short sub that connects the bit to the BHA.
Unplanned change of well azimuth caused by the bit and formation.
Extremely viscous petroleum that does not flow at reservoir temperature without being heated or diluted.
Separating bitumen from sand, usually with hot water and agitation.
A middle-rank coal, the most common type.
A dark shale rich in organic matter, a common source rock.
A simulation model that treats reservoir fluids as three components, oil, gas and water, using PVT tables.
A rate transient plot of normalized rate against material balance time.
A thick-walled tubing joint placed opposite perforations to resist erosion.
Bleeding annulus pressure to see whether it returns, to diagnose leaks.
Firing several sources so their signals overlap in time, then separating them in processing to survey faster.
The unit that mixes fluid, proppant and additives for a frac.
A BOP ram that closes on an open hole with no pipe in it.
A squeeze placed above and below a zone to isolate it.
Angular cavings from fractured or weak bedding, often from tectonic stress.
A gamma ray curve with sharp top and base and steady value, typical of thick clean sands.
The line that carries air and cuttings away from the well in air drilling.
Depressurizing equipment by venting its gas to flare, during an emergency or for maintenance.
An uncontrolled release of formation fluids from a well, either at surface or into another formation underground.
A stack of large valves on the wellhead that can close around pipe, seal an open hole or shear the pipe to regain control of the well. Abbreviated BOP.
A seismic wave that travels through the earth's interior: a P-wave or S-wave.
A value from cement bond logs showing the fraction of casing that is well bonded.
A high-resolution marine source that makes a pulse with an electrically driven plate.
A compressor that raises air pressure further for deep air drilling.
The unit that stores hydraulic fluid under pressure so the blowout preventers can be closed quickly, even without rig power.
A boron compound that links guar chains to make crosslinked fracturing gels.
Spalling of the borehole wall in the direction of minimum horizontal stress, seen on calipers and image logs.
A sonic tool with two transmitters that cancels hole size and tool tilt effects. Abbreviated BHC.
Adjusting a log reading for the effect of hole size and mud.
The hole size, mud, temperature and pressure conditions in which logs are run.
An electrical or acoustic picture of the borehole wall that shows bedding, fractures, dips and breakouts.
How oval a borehole is, often from breakouts.
Small-scale roughness of the borehole wall, which degrades pad-tool readings.
Seismic surveys with sources or receivers in a well, such as checkshots, VSPs and crosswell surveys.
Whether the wellbore wall stays intact, which depends on stresses, rock strength and mud weight.
Video taken downhole to see flow entries and damage.
A wiper plug pumped ahead of cement to clean the casing and separate the slurry from mud.
The lower part of the drillstring: the bit, drill collars, stabilizers, motors and measurement tools. Abbreviated BHA.
The position of the bottom of the well.
Running a gauge to measure pressure at the bottom of a well.
A fluid sample taken downhole, at reservoir pressure and temperature, before gas comes out of solution.
A tool run on wire to take a fluid sample downhole.
The temperature at the bottom of a well, usually read from logging-tool thermometers and corrected for mud cooling. Abbreviated BHT.
The pressure at the perforations during a treatment.
The time it takes mud at the bit to reach surface: annular volume divided by pump rate.
A gravity anomaly corrected for latitude, elevation and the rock between the station and datum. It reflects density changes at depth.
The ideal set of layers, from graded sand up to mud, deposited by a single turbidity current.
Fluid held in small pores or on clay that won't flow.
Water held to clay surfaces or in very small pores that cannot flow.
Flow after pressure has reached the drainage boundaries, when the whole area depletes together.
A carbonate whose components were bound together while growing, as in a reef.
The pressure derivative with respect to the log of time, the standard diagnostic in well tests.
The rotation speed of a centrifuge bowl, which sets the separating force.
A curved spring on a tool that keeps it centered or pushed to one side.
A fishing tool that screws over the outside of a fish.
A squeeze made by closing the annulus at surface and pumping down tubing or casing.
A heavy multistrand wireline used for fishing and pulling heavy tools.
A river with many shallow channels that split and rejoin around bars, typically carrying coarse sediment.
Start pumping mud after it has been static, slowly enough not to break down the formation.
The oil or gas price at which a project's NPV is zero.
The pressure at which the formation first fractures during injection.
A chemical added to a fracturing fluid to break down its viscosity after pumping so it flows back easily.
Spalling of the borehole wall where stress is highest, which shows the stress direction.
The pressure at which flow first passes a filter cake or seal.
The time when injected fluid first reaches a producer.
A rock made of angular fragments cemented together.
A North Sea crude used as a world benchmark price.
A land survey layout with source points staggered between receiver lines like bricks.
A tool set inside casing to seal off the well below it, either temporarily (retrievable) or permanently.
Forming a seal over pores or fractures with particles larger than the openings.
Sized particles that lodge in pore throats at the borehole wall so a filter cake forms quickly and seals the rock.
A fluid mixing law that ranges between uniform and patchy saturation.
An unusually strong seismic amplitude. It can indicate gas in a reservoir, but lithology can cause it too.
Water with dissolved salts. Clear brines are used as completion fluids and as the base of drill-in fluids and some muds.
Mixing two or more brines to reach a target density and crystallization point.
Whether a brine can contact formation water and rock without forming scale or damage.
The weight of a brine per unit volume, set by the type and amount of salt.
Removing solids from completion brine with cartridge or diatomaceous earth filters.
Adjusting brine density for the change caused by downhole temperature.
Hard shale that breaks into splinters when stressed.
How readily a rock fractures rather than deforming plastically. It is often estimated from quartz and carbonate content or from elastic properties.
A measure of how easily a rock fractures, from mineralogy or elastic properties.
Seismic recorded and processed to keep both very low and high frequencies, giving sharper images and better inversion.
An instrument that measures viscosity at very low shear rates.
A quick, rough stack made early in processing with approximate velocities, for a first look at the data.
Basic sediment and water: the water and solids in crude oil, measured by spinning a sample.
A flow regime with gas bubbles dispersed in a continuous liquid.
The repeated pulses produced as an air-gun bubble oscillates. Source arrays are designed to cancel it.
The speed at which gas bubbles rise through still liquid.
The pressure at which gas first comes out of solution in an oil as the pressure falls.
The classic theory of immiscible displacement that predicts how a water saturation front moves through a linear reservoir.
A well that builds angle once and then holds it to the target. Also called a J-shaped well.
How fast the inclination increases along a well, usually in degrees per 100 feet.
The part of a directional well where inclination is increased.
Interpreting pressure build-up data to find permeability, skin and reservoir pressure.
A test that measures the pressure rise after a flowing well is shut in.
Tanks and pneumatic lines that store and deliver barite in bulk.
The density of the whole rock, grains plus pore fluids, as measured by the density log. Written ρ<sub>b</sub>.
A test that measures how firm shale stays after exposure to a fluid.
Resistance of a material to uniform compression.
A constant time shift applied to a synthetic or trace.
A tank that stores powdered barite or bentonite for pneumatic transfer to the mixing system.
The fraction of rock volume holding water that won't flow. Abbreviated BVI.
Porosity times water saturation, the fraction of rock volume filled with water. Abbreviated BVW.
Pumping fluid down the well against pressure to push an influx or the wellbore fluids back into the formation.
Land the top plug on the float collar, shown by a pressure rise, ending displacement.
A slip joint that lets a fishing string deliver blows and gives free travel.
The fraction of a pipe's air weight that remains when it is immersed in mud.
The weight of pipe in mud, equal to its air weight times the buoyancy factor.
Dolomite formed deep in the subsurface by warm brines.
The record of how deep a rock layer has been buried through time, used to model when the source rock generated oil and gas.
A milling shoe on washpipe that cuts over a fish.
A device that burns oil from a well test offshore with little smoke.
The internal pressure that will split a pipe.
The heptane and heavier part of a hydrocarbon mixture, lumped together in compositional analysis.
A clamp that fixes control lines or ESP cable to tubing.
The connection between the wireline cable and the tools.
How fast a tool moves on wireline during logging.
Lengthening of wireline under tension, which must be corrected for depth.
Measuring carbonate content of cuttings by reacting them with acid.
Calcium carbonate (CaCO<sub>3</sub>), the main mineral of limestone, with a matrix density of 2.71 g/cm³.
A salt used to make dense clear brines, up to about 15.3 ppg.
Ground limestone used as an acid-soluble weighting and bridging material.
A salt used for clear brines up to about 11.8 ppg and for the brine phase of invert-emulsion muds.

Solid calcium chloride, added to water phases of oil-base mud and to brines.

Slaked lime, used to raise pH and supply calcium in lime muds.
A salt used to supply calcium or as a nitrate tracer in mud filtrate.
Gypsum or anhydrite, which contaminates water-base mud or is added to make gyp mud.
A hard calcium carbonate layer formed in soils of dry climates.
Adjusting a tool so its readings match known standards.
A measurement of borehole diameter with mechanical arms. It shows washouts and filter cake and is used to correct other logs.
A log of the inside diameter of tubing or casing to find wear and corrosion.
The period from about 539 to 485 million years ago.
A production logging sensor that measures the fluid's dielectric response to estimate water holdup.
The spread of kh values across layers, used to judge heterogeneity.
Capital expenditure: money spent on wells and facilities.
Water held in small pores by capillary forces that will not flow.

The pressure difference across the interface between two immiscible fluids in the pores. It controls the transition zone above a fluid contact.
A very small tube run into a well to inject chemicals such as foamers or inhibitors at depth.
A test that times how quickly water is drawn from a shale slurry into filter paper, used to screen inhibitors. Abbreviated CST.
Money spent on long-lived assets such as wells, platforms and pipelines. Abbreviated CAPEX.
The pulsed neutron measurement, written Σ (sigma) in capture units, that separates salty water (high) from hydrocarbons (low).
Capturing carbon dioxide from industrial sources and injecting it underground for permanent storage. Abbreviated CCS (CCUS when the CO<sub>2</sub> is also used, as in EOR).
CO<sub>2</sub> entering a water-base mud from the formation or from degraded additives, forming carbonates and bicarbonates.
The ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12, used to tell biogenic from thermogenic gas.
A pulsed neutron log that measures the carbon-to-oxygen ratio to find oil saturation behind casing where water is fresh or unknown.
A sedimentary rock made mainly of calcite (limestone) or dolomite (dolostone). Many large reservoirs are carbonates, often with fractures and vugs.
Any local mound of carbonate rock above its surroundings.
Carbonate ions in a water-base mud that cause poor rheology and high gels, usually treated with lime or gypsum.
A thick, flat-topped buildup of carbonate sediment in warm shallow seas.
A carbonate platform with a gently sloping margin rather than a steep edge.
Injecting water saturated with CO<sub>2</sub>, which moves into oil and swells it.
The period from about 359 to 299 million years ago, known for coal.
A cellulose-based polymer (CMC) used to control fluid loss and add viscosity in water-base muds.
A starch derivative used for fluid-loss control in salty mud.
A soluble potassium-magnesium chloride salt that is hard to drill without washouts.
A share in a venture whose costs are paid by other partners, often repaid from production.
A permeable layer through which oil and gas migrate from source to trap.
The liquid that carries solids such as gravel, proppant or LCM into the well.
The ability of a mud to lift and transport cuttings, which depends on its velocity, density and rheology.
The electronics section of a logging tool.
A replaceable filter element used to remove fine solids from brine.
A completion in which casing or a liner is cemented across the reservoir and then perforated to let fluids in.
A gravel pack placed inside perforated casing, with gravel also packed into the perforations.
Logging carried out after the casing is set, for example to evaluate cement, corrosion or saturation behind pipe.
Large-diameter steel pipe run into a drilled hole and usually cemented in place. It supports the hole, isolates zones and provides pressure control.
A magnetic tool that detects the thicker steel at casing collars, used for depth correlation. Abbreviated CCL.
A tool with expanding knives that cuts casing from the inside.
Splits or swelling in casing, sometimes caused by perforating.
Drilling with casing as the drillstring so it is left in place.
Cutting a window through casing to drill a sidetrack.
The device that suspends a casing string in the wellhead and seals it.
The lowest wellhead component, attached to the surface casing, which supports the next casing string.
The pressure in the tubing–casing annulus at surface.
A hole in casing where fluid enters or leaves.
A sleeve set inside damaged casing to seal a leak.
The depth where a casing string is set.
The plan of casing sizes, weights, grades and setting depths for a well.
Fixing damaged casing with patches, liners or squeeze cement.
A tool with blades that cleans the inside of casing before setting packers or plugs.
The bottom end of a casing string, usually fitted with a rounded guide shoe. The term also refers to the depth at which the casing is set.
How centered casing is in the hole, as a percentage.
A rheological model with a yield stress that fits some muds between Bingham and power law.
A fault rock made of crushed and broken grains.
The stage of burial in which kerogen breaks down into oil and gas.
Preventing corrosion of steel by making it the cathode of an electrochemical cell, using sacrificial anodes or impressed current.
The amount of exchangeable positive ions a clay can hold. It indicates how much the clay adds to rock conductivity. Abbreviated CEC.
A polymer with positive charges that bonds strongly to clay and helps stop shale hydration.
The ramp beside the rig floor where pipe is laid out before being lifted.
A lignite or tannin dissolved in caustic soda, used as a thinner.
Potassium hydroxide, used to raise pH while adding potassium for shale inhibition.
Sodium hydroxide, added to raise the pH and alkalinity of water-base mud.
Lignite pre-mixed with caustic soda so it dissolves easily as a thinner.
Pieces of rock falling from the hole wall.
Rock pieces that fall from the borehole wall rather than being cut by the bit. Their shape tells what is failing.
A pit dug under the rig floor to give room for wellhead equipment.
Thin plastic flakes used as a flaky lost circulation material.
A fibrous lost circulation material made from wood or plant fibers.
An additive that shortens thickening time, such as calcium chloride.
Dry cement mixed with dry additives before shipping to the rig.
An acoustic log that shows how well cement is bonded to the casing, to judge zonal isolation. Abbreviated CBL.
A gap in the cement sheath through which fluids can move between zones.
Mud left in a channel through cement, which allows flow between zones.
Cement drilled out after casing jobs that raises pH and calcium in water-base mud and flocculates it.
An additive that thins a slurry so it mixes and pumps easily.
Pumping fluid behind the cement to place it in the annulus.
Checking cement quality behind casing with acoustic logs and pressure tests.
Extra cement pumped above the calculated volume to allow for hole enlargement.
The fitting on top of casing that holds plugs and connects cement lines.
The operation of mixing and placing cement in a well.
A column of cement set inside the wellbore to isolate zones, for abandonment, sidetracking or curing losses.
A drillable packer with a valve, used to squeeze cement below it and then hold it there.
An additive that lengthens thickening time for hot wells.
The ring of set cement between casing and formation.
A mix of cement, water and additives pumped into the well.
Forcing cement through perforations or leaks under pressure to seal them.
Placing cement in a loss zone to seal it when other treatments fail.
Precipitation of minerals between grains, which binds them and reduces porosity.
The porosity exponent m in the Archie equation, linked to pore geometry. It is about 2 in many sandstones.
A liner cemented in place across the reservoir, then perforated or fitted with frac sleeves.
Pumping cement slurry into the annulus between casing and hole to support the casing, isolate zones and protect it from corrosion.
The pumps and mixer used to place cement.
The geologic era from 66 million years ago to the present.
A unit of viscosity, one hundredth of a poise. Water at room temperature is about 1 cP.
Keeping casing centered in the hole with centralizers so cement surrounds it.
A spring or solid device clamped to casing to keep it centered in the hole so cement surrounds it evenly.
A pump that uses a spinning impeller, used for mixing and transfer of mud on the rig.
Measuring capillary pressure by spinning core samples.
Manufactured proppant, stronger and rounder than sand, for deep, high-stress wells.
A very dense formate salt, used for clear brines up to about 19 ppg in high-pressure wells.
The radioactive gamma ray source used in density tools.
A soft, fine-grained limestone made of microscopic plankton skeletons. It can be very porous but has low permeability.
The probability that an exploration well finds hydrocarbons, combining the chances of source, reservoir, trap, seal and timing. Abbreviated COS or Pg.
Wellbore storage that changes during a test, for example from phase redistribution.
An elongated cut filled with sediment, seen on seismic slices and sections.
The number of receiver channels a system records at once.
Coarse material left at the base of a channel.
A long, narrow reservoir with parallel boundaries, seen as linear flow in tests.
A deepwater channel with raised banks built by overflowing turbidity currents.
An attribute that measures how disordered the reflections are.
Disordered reflections, typical of slumps, salt or reefs.
A mud gas ratio used to separate oil and gas shows.
The metal cup that holds the explosive and liner of a shaped charge.
The thin metal cone inside a shaped charge that collapses into the high-velocity jet.
A centrifugal pump that feeds mud to the main pump suction under pressure.
The chance that enough hydrocarbons did not reach a trap.
The amount of explosive in a shot hole.
Water injected behind a chemical or solvent slug to push it through the reservoir.
Adjusting sonic log times to match checkshot times.
Measuring the travel time from a surface source to receivers at known depths in a well, to tie the well to seismic.
A chemical that binds metal ions such as calcium or iron so they stay in solution, used to treat contamination and dissolve scale.
Porosity loss from dissolution at grain contacts and re-precipitation.
A tool that cuts tubing downhole with a jet of highly reactive chemical, leaving a clean cut.
Breaking of polymer chains by oxygen, iron or other chemicals.
EOR using injected chemicals: polymers, surfactants, alkalis or combinations.
EOR using chemicals such as polymers, surfactants or alkali.
Safe storage, mixing and disposal of mud chemicals.
A small tube that delivers treatment chemicals downhole.
A tubing component that injects chemicals, such as scale or corrosion inhibitors, deep in the well through a dedicated line.
A small pump that injects treatment chemicals into a flow stream.
The driving force for water to move between mud and shale.
Injecting resin into a weak formation to glue the grains together near the wellbore so the sand stays in place.
Whether shale keeps its strength when in contact with the mud.
Using gels or polymers to stop water production.
Correlating rocks using their chemical composition.
A hard, fine-grained rock of microcrystalline silica, often found as nodules in limestone.
The concentration of chloride ions in the mud filtrate, measured by titration to track salt and saltwater influx.
Measuring chloride in mud filtrate with silver nitrate.
An iron-rich clay mineral that coats grains and can prevent quartz cement, preserving porosity.
A fixed or adjustable restriction that controls the flow rate and pressure of a well.
A high-pressure line from the BOP stack to the choke manifold.
An arrangement of valves and adjustable chokes used to control flow from the well while a kick is circulated out.
The diameter of a choke opening, usually in 64ths of an inch.
Cold heavy oil production with sand: deliberately producing sand with the oil, without heat, which creates high-permeability channels in the reservoir.
The assembly of valves, spools and fittings on top of a completed well that controls and directs the flow.
A lignosulfonate thinner complexed with chromium for temperature stability. Its use has declined for environmental reasons.
Tubing made of chromium steel to resist CO<sub>2</sub> corrosion.
A lignosulfonate without chromium, made to meet environmental limits.
Organizing rock layers by time, so surfaces of equal age can be traced.
A chaotic flow regime between slug and annular flow.
An older shaker that moves the screen in a circular path.
Pump fluid down one path and up another to replace well fluids.
A fitting screwed onto pipe to circulate through it.
A gravel pack placed by circulating gravel down the tubing and up the annulus.
Pump pressure while circulating.
A sub that opens side ports to circulate above the BHA.
The pumps, lines, drillstring, annulus and pits through which mud moves.
A valve in the tubing that opens to circulate between tubing and annulus.
The volume of mud pumped per minute.
A weak acid used to lower pH and to treat cement contamination.
The most common basic oilwell cement, used with additives over a wide range of depths.
A basic oilwell cement similar to Class G but coarser.
Sedimentary rock made of broken fragments of older rocks, such as sandstone, siltstone, shale and conglomerate.
The behavior of clay minerals in water, such as swelling, dispersion and flocculation.
The amount of active clay in a mud, usually estimated by methylene blue test.
Clay absorbing water into or around its layers, which makes it swell and soften.
The types and amounts of clay minerals in a rock.
Fine, sheet-structured minerals such as smectite, illite, kaolinite and chlorite. They affect logs, permeability and formation damage.
A chemical, such as potassium chloride or a quaternary amine, that stops clays swelling or moving when water contacts them.
The number of barrels of 15-cp mud that one ton of clay produces, a measure of clay quality.
Water held on clay surfaces, part of total porosity but not of effective porosity.
A sedimentary rock made mostly of clay-size particles without fissility.
The log values chosen to represent clean reservoir rock.
A perforation tunnel free of debris and crushed rock.
Sand with little or no shale, which reads low on the gamma ray log.
Flowing a well to remove mud, filtrate and debris before the main test.
A solids-free salt solution used as a completion fluid.
A sloping depositional surface, such as the front of a prograding delta or shelf margin, often clear on seismic.
A reservoir with no-flow boundaries all around.
A drillstem test in which the formation flows into a closed pipe, measuring the pressure rise.
Drilling with a closed mud system that measures flow in and out closely to spot gains and losses.
A solids-control setup that processes all mud and cuttings in tanks without reserve pits.
The vertical distance between the top of a trap and its spill point.
The straight-line horizontal distance from surface location to a point in the well.
The fluid pressure at which a fracture closes, roughly equal to the minimum horizontal stress.
Using remote, on-demand computing and storage over the internet, for example for large simulations or shared subsurface data.
The temperature at which wax first makes an oil look cloudy as it cools, close to the wax appearance temperature.
A glycol that comes out of solution above a set temperature, forming droplets that help seal shale pores.
The distance between perforation clusters in a fracturing stage.
Traces that share a common midpoint, displayed side by side by offset, used for velocity analysis.
When injected CO<sub>2</sub> reaches a producer.
Injecting carbon dioxide, which swells the oil, lowers its viscosity and can become miscible with it, to recover more oil.
Foam made with CO<sub>2</sub> to control its mobility.
A pipeline that carries dense-phase carbon dioxide to fields.
Separating produced CO<sub>2</sub> and injecting it again.
The fraction of injected CO<sub>2</sub> that stays in the reservoir.
Long-term storage of carbon dioxide in rock formations such as depleted fields or saline aquifers.
Keeping carbon dioxide underground permanently, often combined with EOR.
The volume of CO<sub>2</sub> injected, or retained, per barrel of extra oil recovered.
Enhanced oil recovery by injecting carbon dioxide.
Small particles joining together into larger ones, making them easier to remove from water or mud.
A combustible rock formed from compacted plant material, a source of gas and of coalbed methane.
The maturity of coal, from lignite through bituminous to anthracite.
Natural gas adsorbed in coal seams, produced by lowering pressure, usually by pumping off water. Abbreviated CBM.
Equipment that helps small droplets merge into larger ones so they separate faster.
Large ground marble particles used to plug fractures and large pores.
Large mica flakes used to seal larger losses.
Drilled solids larger than about 74 microns, removed mainly by shakers.
A succession whose grain size increases upward, as in prograding deltas and shorefaces.
An empirical equation estimating permeability from NMR porosity and the free-to-bound fluid ratio.
A seismic attribute that measures how similar neighboring traces are. Faults and channel edges appear as low-coherence lines.
Unwanted seismic energy that lines up from trace to trace, such as ground roll and multiples.
Marine acquisition in which the vessel sails in overlapping circles to record all azimuths.
A continuous length of steel tubing stored on a reel and run into the well without connections. It is used for cleanouts, acid jobs, nitrogen lift and logging.
Placing acid through coiled tubing for accurate placement.
The tools attached to the end of coiled tubing for a job.
Placing cement through coiled tubing, often for squeezes or plugs.
Using coiled tubing to circulate sand, scale or debris out of a well.
The fitting that joins the end of the coiled tubing to the tool string.
Running production logging tools on coiled tubing in deviated wells.
Drilling with coiled tubing instead of jointed pipe, often underbalanced and for sidetracks.
Cumulative damage to coiled tubing from bending on and off the reel, tracked to decide when to retire it.
The machine that grips coiled tubing with chain-mounted blocks and pushes it into or pulls it out of the well.
Running logging tools on coiled tubing, often in horizontal wells.
Milling plugs, scale or restrictions using coiled tubing.
A small mud motor run on coiled tubing for milling and drilling.
How out-of-round coiled tubing has become, which lowers its collapse rating.
The large spool on which coiled tubing is stored and run.
The continuous length of steel tubing wound on a reel for coiled tubing work.
The truck or skid package with reel, injector head, control cab and power pack used for coiled tubing work.
A refining process that cracks heavy residue into lighter products and coke.
Producing heavy oil without heat, using natural reservoir energy and sometimes sand production.
The external pressure that will crush a pipe.
Particles so small, roughly 1 nm to 1 µm, that they stay suspended and strongly affect mud viscosity and filtration.
A weak gel of polymer and crosslinker used to divert flow deep in the reservoir.
The color scale used to display seismic amplitudes or attributes.
A fast inversion that shapes seismic to match the impedance spectrum of wells.
The vertical thickness of hydrocarbons in a trap.
A BOP with rams that combine functions, such as shear-seal or pipe-slip.
A trap formed by both structural and stratigraphic features.
The moving zone where oil burns in in-situ combustion.
A lab test that burns oil in a packed tube to measure fuel and air needs.
Producing two or more zones together through the same tubing.
The subsurface point that reflects energy for several source-receiver pairs. Equal to the common midpoint for flat layers. Abbreviated CDP.
Migrated traces at one location sorted by offset or angle. Flat events show the velocity model is right.
The surface point halfway between a source and a receiver. Traces that share it are sorted together and stacked. Abbreviated CMP.
Traces with the same source-receiver offset, displayed side by side.
All traces recorded by one receiver from many shots.
Reduction of sediment volume and porosity under the weight of overlying layers.
The operator's representative at the wellsite who directs the work for the company that owns the well.
Division of a reservoir into separate units by sealing faults or barriers, so they do not share pressure.
A neutron tool with two detectors whose ratio reduces borehole effects.
The hardware and work that turn a drilled well into one that can produce or inject safely: tubing, packers, perforations, sand control and the wellhead equipment.
Choosing the equipment and methods to connect a well to the reservoir and produce it safely.
How well a completion lets fluid flow compared with an ideal undamaged well.
The engineer who designs and oversees well completions.
A clear, solids-free brine kept in the well during completion work. It is dense enough to control pressure and chosen to avoid damaging the reservoir.
The ability of a completion to hold pressure and isolate zones.
How much fluid, proppant and stages are used per length of lateral.
A rig used to install completions.
A diagram showing every component in a well's casing and completion strings with depths and sizes.
Skin from the completion, such as perforations or a gravel pack.
All the tubing and equipment run to complete a well.
Pressure and function testing a completion after installation.
A frac plug made largely of composite materials so it can be drilled out quickly.
A log combining many curves and interpretations in one display.
A reservoir model with zones of different properties, such as a damaged ring or fluid bank.
Measuring the mole fraction of each component, from nitrogen and methane to heavy ends, in a reservoir fluid.
Change of fluid composition with depth caused by gravity and temperature.
A simulation model that tracks each hydrocarbon component and uses an equation of state, needed for gas condensates and gas injection.
How much mud volume shrinks under pressure, important for HPHT density.
The time a P-wave takes to travel one foot through the formation, in microseconds per foot. Written Δt<sub>c</sub>.
The load per unit area a set cement can bear before crushing.
A machine that raises the pressure of gas, for example for pipeline transport, gas lift or reinjection.
Using algorithms to interpret images and video, for example to analyze core photos or detect safety hazards.
A log plot showing the results of computer log analysis. Abbreviated CPI.
An agreement giving a company rights to explore and produce in an area in return for royalties and taxes.
Firing a charge into a concrete target to measure penetration.
A hard, rounded mass formed by cement growing around a nucleus.
Light hydrocarbon liquid that drops out of gas when it is cooled or its pressure is reduced, at surface or in the reservoir.
A ring of liquid condensate around a gas well below the dew point, which reduces gas flow.
A sample of liquid condensate from a gas well.
A column that removes light components from condensate so it can be stored and shipped at atmospheric pressure.
Condensate produced per million standard cubic feet of gas.
The volume of condensate produced per volume of gas, often in barrels per million standard cubic feet. Abbreviated CGR.
A thin interval deposited slowly during a rise in sea level, often rich in organic matter or fossils.
A miscible process in which rich gas gives intermediate components to the oil until they become miscible.
A fracture that appears dark on resistivity images because it is filled with mud or water.
Water-base mud that conducts electricity, suited to laterologs.
How well a fluid carries electric current, the inverse of resistivity.
Installing conductor pipe offshore by washing it into soft sediment with jets.
The first and largest string of casing, set at shallow depth to stop loose surface sediments caving in.
Cutting and removing conductor pipe at the end of abandonment.
The solids-rich stream discharged from the bottom of a hydrocyclone.
Treatments, such as gels or mechanical isolation, that make injected fluids sweep the reservoir more evenly.
An amplitude anomaly whose edge follows a structural contour, a sign of a fluid contact.
A coarse sedimentary rock of rounded pebbles and cobbles set in a finer matrix.
Water rising from below, or gas moving down from above, toward a producing well in a cone shape because of the pressure drawdown, which cuts oil production.
Two sets of faults formed at the same time at an angle to each other.
The pore volume in pressure communication with a well.
Adding a joint or stand of pipe to the drillstring as the hole deepens.

The time taken to add a joint or stand while drilling.
The coefficient K of the power-law model, a measure of how thick the fluid is at low shear rates.
A lab instrument that measures how a slurry thickens under temperature and pressure.
Sand cemented enough to hold together.

Stacks made with a range of fixed velocities, compared to choose the best one.
A boundary where pressure stays fixed, such as a strong aquifer or gas cap. The derivative falls at late time.
The angle a liquid drop makes with a solid surface, a measure of wettability.
A substance that enters mud and harms its properties, such as salt, cement, gas or drilled solids.
Watching fluid properties while pumping to decide when filtrate is low enough to sample.
The gentle apron of sediment at the base of the slope.
The shallow, flat edge of a continent under the sea.
The steep seafloor between the shelf and the deep ocean.
Quantities estimated to be recoverable from known accumulations that are not yet commercial, for example because there is no market or no approved plan.
The fluid in which other phases are dispersed: water in water-base mud, oil in invert-emulsion mud.
A spinner flowmeter that runs at a constant speed through the zone.
The difference in value between neighboring contour lines.
Sediment deposited or reworked by deep ocean bottom currents flowing along the slope.
A small stainless-steel tube strapped to the tubing that carries hydraulic pressure from surface to hold the safety valve open.
A marine method that sends electromagnetic signals into the seabed to detect resistive layers, such as hydrocarbon reservoirs. Abbreviated CSEM.
Cutting a full core with a core bit and barrel on drillpipe.
Extra pressure loss from flow converging into perforations or a partial completion.
A wave that changes type at a boundary, usually a P-wave that reflects as an S-wave. Recorded in multicomponent surveys.
A mathematical operation that blends one signal with another, such as a wavelet with a reflectivity series.
The model that treats a seismic trace as the reflectivity series convolved with the wavelet, plus noise.
Cooling of the wellbore near a zone taking cold injected fluid.
The datum and projection that define map coordinates. Abbreviated CRS.
A polymer made from two or more different monomers, often designed for better temperature or salt tolerance.
A limestone made of broken shells loosely cemented together.
A cylinder of rock cut from a well with a special bit and barrel. It gives the most direct measurement of rock properties.
Laboratory measurements on core samples, such as porosity, permeability, saturation and grain density.
The tube that holds core as it is cut.
A bit with a hole in the center that cuts a cylinder of rock.
A written record of a core's rock types, structures and features.
A lab test that measures permeability before and after fluid exposure.
A gamma ray log measured on core at surface, used to depth-match the core to the wireline logs.
A small cylinder drilled from a core for lab tests.
Sealing core at the wellsite to keep its fluids and state.
The length of core recovered divided by the length cut.
The depth adjustment that aligns core to logs.
Permeability measured on core samples.
Calibrating log interpretation against measurements on core.
Correcting core depths to match log depths so both measure the same rock.
A lab test that pushes fluids through a core to measure recovery or permeability.
A flowmeter that measures mass flow directly from the twisting of a vibrating tube.
A display of logs from several wells side by side for correlation.
A stack of upgoing VSP waves near the first arrival, used to tie wells to seismic.

Cracking from repeated stress in a corrosive environment.
A chemical that forms a protective film on metal surfaces to slow corrosion in wells and pipelines.
A log that checks metal loss in casing or tubing.

A metal such as chrome steel that resists corrosion. Abbreviated CRA.
An attribute that shows reflection continuity regardless of amplitude.
An alcohol or similar chemical added to reduce viscous phases in surfactant flooding.
In a production sharing contract, the share of production that repays the contractor's costs.

A cheap fibrous lost circulation material.
An ion with charge opposite to the particle surface it surrounds.
Phases moving in opposite directions in the well.
The standard NMR pulse sequence used to measure T2 relaxation.
A method that predicts five-spot waterflood performance including areal sweep.
An old, stable part of a continent.

A fan of sediment deposited where a flood breaks through a levee.

The porosity above which sediment acts like a suspension rather than a rock frame.

A feature that cuts another must be younger than it.
Finding fluid moving between zones in the well.

Flow from one zone into another through the wellbore, which happens when zones at different pressures are open to each other.
A vertical section through a 3D seismic volume at right angles to the inlines.

A lost circulation pill that sets into a firm, rubbery mass in the loss zone.
A short sub that joins pipes with different thread types or sizes.
A tool that directs gravel slurry from the tubing into the annulus and returns from the annulus back up the wash pipe.

Porosity found by combining two logs, such as neutron and density, to remove the effect of lithology.
A survey with the source in one well and receivers in another, giving high-resolution images between them.
The fixed set of sheaves at the top of the derrick that the drilling line passes over.
Common-reflection-surface stacking, which uses neighboring midpoints to boost signal.
A full analysis of a crude's properties and product yields.
Unrefined liquid petroleum as it comes out of the ground.
The thin ring of crushed, lower-permeability rock around a perforation tunnel left by the jet.
X-ray computed tomography used to image cores without cutting them.
Total steam injected divided by total oil produced. Abbreviated CSOR.
A measure of how sharply a mapped surface bends, used to find subtle faults, folds and fractures.
A short code naming a log curve, such as GR or RHOB.
The point where ownership of a product changes hands, where its quantity and quality are measured to the highest accuracy.
Oil streaming from cuttings when a solvent is added, a sign of movable oil.
Cutting casing and pulling it out during abandonment.
The particle size that a solids control device removes half of.
A threshold on a property, such as porosity, shale volume or water saturation, used to decide which rock counts as net reservoir or net pay.
The teeth or cutters of a bit that break the rock.
Chips of rock broken by the bit and carried up by the mud. Geologists examine them to identify the rocks being drilled.
Examining cuttings for rock type, shows and mud effects.
A layer of cuttings settled on the low side of a deviated hole. It increases drag and can cause stuck pipe.
A container that holds cuttings for shipping to shore for disposal.
Equipment, such as a vertical centrifugal dryer, that strips mud from cuttings before disposal to cut waste and recover fluid.
Grinding drilled cuttings into a slurry and injecting it into a suitable formation for disposal. Abbreviated CRI.
The net upward velocity of cuttings divided by the annular velocity. A higher value means better hole cleaning.
Rinsing cuttings before describing them.
Protecting computer systems and data from attack.
A sonic log spike caused by the detector missing the first arrival.
Injecting gas into a well, letting it soak, then producing from the same well. Also called huff-n-puff.
Injecting steam into a well, letting it soak, then producing the heated oil from the same well, and repeating. Also called huff and puff.
Dating rocks using regular cycles caused by changes in earth's orbit.
The non-Darcy flow coefficient used in rate-dependent skin, S' = S + Dq.
A normalized drilling-rate parameter used while drilling to detect overpressure.
A 2D NMR display of diffusion against T2, used to identify gas, oil and water.
The size at which 50 percent of particles go to underflow and 50 percent to overflow.
A guide that sets the D90 of bridging particles equal to the largest pore throat.
The mud engineer's daily record of properties, treatments and volumes.
The cause of reduced permeability near the well.
The ratio of ideal to actual productivity index.
Fractured rock surrounding a fault core.
The basic law of flow through porous rock: flow rate is proportional to permeability, area and pressure gradient, and inversely proportional to viscosity.
A vertical seismic profile recorded with distributed acoustic sensing on a fiber in the well.
The computers and sensors that record pressures, temperatures and rates during a test.
Rules and roles that keep data accurate, secure and consistent.
A spool with ports for pressure and temperature sensors and sampling, placed upstream of the test choke.
A database designed to store large volumes of time-stamped sensor data and serve it for trending and analysis.
A central store that keeps large volumes of raw data in their original formats until they are needed.
Organizing, storing and sharing data so it is reliable and easy to find.
How accurate, complete and consistent data are.
Interpolating seismic data onto a regular grid to fill gaps and help processing.
A screen of charts showing live or recent operations data.
A plot of well depth against days, used to plan and track drilling.
The end of drilling line fixed to the anchor, opposite the fast line.
Oil from which the dissolved gas has been released at atmospheric conditions.
A trace with no signal because of a faulty receiver or connection.
A buried anchor used to tie down guy lines.
A lab method that distills water and dissolves oil out of a core sample to measure its fluid saturations.
A dense, flowing mass of mud and coarse debris that deposits poorly sorted sediment.
A tool that catches debris in the string.
A rotating bowl separator that removes very fine solids from mud, or recovers barite from weighted mud, by high-gravity settling.
The tilt of a shaker screen deck, which changes how long cuttings stay on it.
Fitting a well's past rate history with exponential, hyperbolic or harmonic decline equations to forecast future rates and reserves.
Safely ending production: plugging wells and removing or making safe the facilities at the end of a field's life.
A processing step that compresses the wavelet and removes reverberations, which sharpens the seismic image.
Replacement of dolomite by calcite.
LWD resistivity that maps boundaries several meters from the well.
A resistivity reading far from the borehole, close to true resistivity.
A shaped charge designed to reach as far into the formation as possible, beyond the damaged zone.
Drilling an existing well to a greater depth.
An additive that cancels the attraction between clay particles, so the mud becomes thinner. Also called a thinner or dispersant.
Breaking up clumps of clay particles so they repel each other, which thins the mud.
A chemical that breaks foam and releases trapped air from mud.
A product that prevents foam when mixing brines.
Breaking foam in mud so it doesn't trap air.
A soft particle that squeezes into pore throats and fractures to seal them.
A thin zone of crushed grains in porous sandstone that lowers permeability.
A unit that removes gas bubbles from the returning mud before it is pumped back downhole.
Removing the ghost reflections from the sea surface to restore lost frequencies.
The fraction of acrylamide groups converted to acrylate in HPAM.
The average number of groups added per sugar unit in cellulose derivatives such as CMC.
An absolute temperature scale using Fahrenheit-sized degrees: °R = °F + 459.67.
Removing water from gas or oil.
A false high reading on older laterologs below thick resistive beds.
A breaker built to act slowly so a filter cake stays in place until the completion is run.
A test that measures how a gas well's rate depends on flowing pressure, used to predict its performance.
A body of sediment built where a river enters a lake or sea. Deltas contain sand bodies that form important reservoirs.
The sloping, sand-rich zone of a delta where river sediment enters standing water.
The low, flat landward part of a delta crossed by distributary channels.
A chemical that helps break oil–water emulsions so the water droplets can join together and settle out.
Reordering recorded samples into separate traces.
The amount a density tool adjusts its reading for mudcake and standoff. Symbol Δρ.
An LWD image of borehole wall density around the hole.
A log of formation bulk density measured with a gamma-ray source and detectors. It is used to calculate porosity.
A record of mud weight in and out over time.
Porosity calculated from bulk density and known matrix and fluid densities.
The setting in which sediment accumulated, such as a river channel, delta, beach, deep-sea fan or reef.
Methods that make log depths accurate and consistent.
Converting seismic travel times to depths using a velocity model, so that maps can be used to plan wells.
Tying the depth of a tool to the reference log depth, usually with a casing collar locator and gamma ray log, so the right interval is perforated.
The difference between predicted and actual depth of a horizon.
Producing seismic images directly in depth using a velocity model and depth migration.
Shifting logs from different runs so that the same features line up in depth.
How deep each cutter bites into the rock per revolution.
How far into the formation a logging tool reads, from a few inches for pad tools to several feet for deep resistivity.
A horizontal section through a seismic volume that has been converted to depth.
A map of horizon depth after depth conversion.
The depth to crystalline rock under sediments, often estimated from magnetics.
Reducing noise in the pressure derivative by using a wider time window.
A dip in the derivative of a dual-porosity reservoir as the matrix starts to feed the fractures.
The tall steel tower over the well that supports the hoisting equipment and racked pipe.
The crew member who handles pipe at the top of the derrick during trips and usually looks after the mud pumps.
The crew member who works in the derrick and tends the mud system.
A hydrocyclone, typically with 6- to 12-inch cones, that removes sand-sized particles from drilling fluid.
A safety margin applied to pipe ratings in design.
Processing that shapes the source wavelet to a known, usually zero-phase, form.
A hydrocyclone with smaller cones than a desander, typically 4 inches, used to remove silt-sized particles.
The release of adsorbed gas from rock surfaces as pressure falls.
Removing sharp, isolated noise bursts from data.
A glass tube with a chemical that changes color to measure gases such as H<sub>2</sub>S on site.
A surfactant added to water-base mud to reduce bit balling and sticking.
A single best estimate made from one set of chosen input values, as opposed to a probabilistic range.
Log analysis that calculates results step by step with set equations.
An explosive cord that carries the detonation along a perforating gun to set off every charge.
The device that starts the explosive train in a perforating gun.
A well drilled to produce a known field.
Changes in flow behavior as well angle increases, such as segregation of phases.
Negative skin from a well crossing a layer at an angle.
The period from about 419 to 359 million years ago, with important reefs and source rocks.
The pressure at which the first drop of liquid forms from a gas.
Separating water from waste mud with chemicals and centrifuges so solids can be disposed of and water reused.
Equipment that uses chemicals and a centrifuge to remove solids from water-base mud and recover clean water.
Diagnostic fracture injection test: a small injection used to find closure stress and permeability.
The physical and chemical changes in sediment after it is deposited, such as compaction, cementation and dissolution. They change porosity and permeability.
A log-log plot of pressure change and its derivative used to identify flow regimes.
The deflection read on a rotational viscometer at a set speed, such as θ<sub>600</sub>, used to calculate rheology.
Increase in coiled tubing diameter from repeated bending under pressure.
A body of salt or mud that has pushed up through overlying rocks.
A soft, porous silica rock used as a filter aid and in high-fluid-loss pills.
A light, porous rock made of diatom shells, which can hold oil with very low permeability.
A log that measures how the formation stores electrical energy, mainly to find water volume independently of salinity.
Measuring the dielectric properties of rock to find water volume independent of salinity.
How strongly a material stores electrical energy. Water has a much higher permittivity than oil or rock.
A traditional base oil for oil-base muds, now limited by toxicity and environmental rules.
A slurry of bentonite in diesel that sets into a stiff plug when it meets water in the loss zone.
A factor for drainage-area shape and well position used in pseudosteady-state flow.
A PVT test in which gas is removed from the oil as it is released at each pressure step, like reservoir depletion below the bubblepoint.
The difference in pressure between two points.
The speed difference between a centrifuge bowl and its scroll, which controls solids discharge.
Sticking that happens when stationary pipe is pressed into a thick filter cake because mud pressure is higher than formation pressure.
A log of the change in temperature over a short interval, which highlights small anomalies.
Energy scattered from a sharp feature such as a fault edge, which forms a hyperbola on unmigrated seismic.
The equation describing how pressure spreads through a porous medium.
Using sensors, communications, data management and analytics to monitor and optimize oil and gas operations in near real time.
