A virtual model of a physical asset, such as a well or plant, kept up to date with live data to monitor and test changes.
Shear thickening: becoming thicker as shear rate increases.
Diluted bitumen: bitumen blended with a light diluent so it can flow through pipelines.
A light hydrocarbon, such as condensate or naphtha, blended with heavy oil to lower its viscosity for pipelining.
The volume of new mud needed per volume of drilled solids left in the system.
The volume of new fluid added per volume of hole drilled to keep drilled solids at an acceptable level.
A weaker-than-expected reflection, which in some settings can indicate hydrocarbons.
Fracture conductivity divided by formation permeability times half-length. Symbol FCD.
Pressure change scaled by rate and reservoir properties, so different tests can be compared with one type curve. Written p<sub>D</sub>.
Time scaled by reservoir properties and wellbore radius, written t<sub>D</sub>.
The angle a rock layer or fault makes with the horizontal, measured at right angles to strike.
The local dip of seismic events computed across a volume.
A filter that removes events with certain dips.
A processing correction for dipping reflectors so that they stack properly. Abbreviated DMO.
A tool that measures the dip and direction of beds and fractures from several pads around the borehole.
A sonic tool that bends the borehole wall to measure shear-wave velocity, even in slow formations.
An emulsion of oil droplets in water, as in oil-emulsion mud.
A seismic feature, such as a bright spot, flat spot or AVO anomaly, that may show hydrocarbons are present. Abbreviated DHI.
Rows of injectors and producers directly opposite each other.
Seismic energy that travels straight from source to receiver near the surface without reflecting.
Steering a well deliberately along a planned path that departs from vertical, to reach targets away from the surface location.
A measurement of inclination and azimuth at a known depth. A series of them is used to calculate the well's position.
The maximum amount of oil or other material allowed in discharged cuttings or fluid.
An unconformity between parallel layers.
The interest rate used to convert future cash flows into present value, reflecting the time value of money and risk.
A well that finds a significant accumulation of hydrocarbons.
A chemical that keeps particles separated and spread through a fluid.
Small gas bubbles spread evenly through fast-flowing liquid.
A water-base mud treated with thinners so its clay stays in fine, separated particles, keeping viscosity low at high solids.
The droplets or particles spread through the continuous phase, such as brine droplets in an invert emulsion.
The fraction of oil removed from the pores that the injected fluid actually contacts.
The sequence of spacers and pills used to replace mud with clean brine.
Dissolving of minerals by pore fluids, which can create porosity.
A frac plug made of materials that dissolve in well fluids, so it doesn't need milling out.
How far the well is from a bed boundary, from directional resistivity.
A branch of a river that spreads water and sediment across a delta.
Turning an optical fiber into thousands of acoustic sensors along a well, used to monitor flow, fracturing and seismic. Abbreviated DAS.
Measuring temperature continuously along the full length of an optical fiber in a well, using backscattered laser light. Abbreviated DTS.
A magnetic correction for daily changes in the earth's field.
A biopolymer viscosifier with strong low-shear viscosity and good temperature stability.
An ion with a charge of two, such as calcium or magnesium, which tends to flocculate clay.
A material or tool that redirects treatment fluid from zones already taking fluid into zones that are not.
A flowmeter that diverts all the flow through its measuring section.
Material that temporarily blocks treated zones so fluid goes into others.
A formula that converts RMS velocities at two reflectors into the interval velocity of the layer between them.
Digital Log Interchange Standard: a binary format for well log data.
A sharp bend or change of direction in a wellbore, which adds torque, drag and casing wear.
The small building on the rig floor used as the driller's office.
How sharply a well's direction changes, usually given in degrees per 100 feet or per 30 meters.
Calcium magnesium carbonate, CaMg(CO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, with a matrix density of 2.87 g/cm³.
The replacement of calcite by dolomite in a carbonate rock, which can create or destroy porosity.
A carbonate rock made mostly of the mineral dolomite, often formed by alteration of limestone. Often simply called dolomite.
A fold that dips away from a central high in all directions.
The frequency with the most energy in a seismic signal. It controls the wavelength and therefore the resolution.
Thread compound applied to pipe connections to seal and prevent galling.
Injecting gas into a watered-out zone to drain the remaining oil downward.
The layer of ions around a charged clay particle that controls how it interacts with others.
A reservoir model with fractures that flow and a matrix that stores fluid.
Thickening of the ionic layer on rock surfaces in low-salinity water, which can release oil.
A logging run lowering the tool down the well.
The part of a VSP traveling downward, mainly the direct wave and multiples.
A camera run into a well to see damage, fish or debris.
Heating the near-wellbore region with electric cables or resistive elements to reduce oil viscosity.
Optical and other sensors in a formation tester that measure fluid composition, gas-oil ratio and contamination before a sample is taken. Abbreviated DFA.
A tubing section that holds a permanent pressure and temperature gauge.
An electric heater placed in the well to warm heavy oil.
Receivers in a nearby well that record microseismic events.
A motor in the drillstring, driven by mud flow, that turns the bit.
Closing a valve near the reservoir rather than at surface, which reduces wellbore storage effects in a buildup test.
A burner placed in the well to make steam at depth.
A valve in the test string near the reservoir that opens and closes to make the flow and shut-in periods.
Layers ending downward against a surface below them, typical of sediment building out into deeper water.
Refining crude oil, processing gas and marketing and selling the products to consumers.
The pressure after a choke, valve or meter.
Calculating a potential field as if measured lower, which sharpens shallow effects.
A small fold formed next to a fault as layers are dragged by movement.
Lowering turbulent friction by adding long-chain polymers.
The area of reservoir that supplies fluid to a well.
A capillary pressure curve as a non-wetting phase displaces a wetting phase.
The difference between average reservoir pressure and the flowing bottomhole pressure. It is the pressure difference that drives fluid into the well.
Permeability over viscosity estimated from a formation tester pretest.
A test in which a well is flowed, ideally at constant rate, and the fall in bottomhole pressure is recorded and analyzed.
The rig's main hoisting winch. It spools drilling line to raise and lower the drillstring.
The guaranteed minimum internal diameter of a pipe, checked by passing a gauge tool (drift) through it.
A correction for slow changes in an instrument's reading over time.
A plot of the difference between sonic and checkshot times with depth.
A multiphase flow model that relates phase velocities through a distribution parameter and drift velocity.
Heavy, thick-walled pipe placed just above the bit. It supplies weight on bit and keeps the drillpipe above it in tension.
The working platform of the rig where pipe is handled.
The steel wire rope that runs over the blocks and holds the drillstring.
Using the noise of the drill bit as a seismic source.
A clean, low-damage fluid used to drill the reservoir section. Its bridging solids can later be removed with acid or other breakers.
A test that finds the best weight on bit by watching how fast the bit drills off weight.
How easily a rock can be drilled.
A well that has been drilled but not yet fractured and put on production. Abbreviated DUC.
Rock fragments produced by the bit. Fine drilled solids that are not removed degrade mud properties and slow drilling.
The crew member who operates the rig controls.
Depth measured by the length of drillpipe in the well.
A two-circulation kill method. The first circulation removes the influx with the original mud; the second replaces the mud with kill-weight mud.
Control systems that carry out drilling tasks such as weight-on-bit control or tripping with little manual input, for consistency and safety.
A rig mounted on a barge for drilling in shallow, sheltered water.
A sudden increase in penetration rate, which can mean a new formation or a kick.
The company that owns and runs the rig for the operator.
The engineer who designs the well and plans the drilling operations.
The fluid pumped down the drillstring and back up the annulus while drilling. It carries cuttings to surface, holds back formation pressure, cools and lubricates the bit and supports the hole wall.
A product added to mud to change a property such as viscosity, density or fluid loss.
Mass of mud per unit volume, measured with a mud balance and reported as ppg, lb/ft³, g/cm³ or specific gravity.
The specialist who designs, tests and treats the mud on the rig.
The plan for mud types and properties for each hole section.
The design of flow rate, pressures and nozzle sizes to clean the bit and hole while keeping ECD within limits.
A tool in the drillstring that stores energy and releases it as a sharp hammer blow to free stuck pipe.
The wire rope threaded between the crown and traveling blocks, wound on the drawworks drum.
The written plan for drilling a well, with casing, mud, bits and procedures.
The machinery used to drill a well, including the derrick or mast, hoisting system, rotating equipment, mud pumps and power.
A surface-active additive in mud used as an emulsifier, wetting agent, defoamer or detergent.
Used mud, cuttings and other material produced while drilling.
Handling cuttings and spent fluids by treatment, recycling, reinjection or approved disposal to meet environmental rules.
A thin fracture created in the borehole wall by drilling, aligned with maximum horizontal stress.
Seamless steel pipe with threaded tool joints that makes up most of the drillstring's length.
Metal loss on the drillstring caused by oxygen, carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide or salt in the mud.
The strength rating of drillpipe steel, such as E-75, X-95, G-105 or S-135.
Checking drillpipe for wear, cracks and corrosion.
A ship equipped to drill in deep water, held over the well by anchors or dynamic positioning.
A temporary completion that uses the drillstring to flow a formation, take samples and record pressures before deciding to complete the well. Abbreviated DST.
The connected drillpipe, drill collars and tools that link the rig to the bit and carry mud down to it.
Axial, lateral or torsional shaking of the drillstring that damages tools and slows drilling.
The natural source of energy that pushes fluids to the wells: solution gas, gas cap, water drive, rock compaction or gravity drainage.
Using unmanned aircraft to inspect flare stacks, pipelines and facilities.
A section where inclination is reduced.
In-situ combustion with air only.
A well that finds no commercial hydrocarbons.
Tripping out with the drillpipe empty of mud thanks to a slug.
The stiffness of the rock frame with empty pores.
The weight of a dry additive, as opposed to a liquid product.
The pressure record from a drillstem test.
The tubing, packer, valves and gauges run for a drillstem test.
A common mnemonic for compressional sonic slowness.
A well completed to produce two zones separately through two tubing strings or a tubing and the annulus.
Two one-way valves near the end of coiled tubing that stop well fluids entering the string.
An induction log with deep and medium readings, often run with a shallow focused log.
A laterolog with deep and shallow readings, run in conductive mud.
A model where both fracture and matrix systems can flow to the well.
A reservoir model with two connected pore systems, typically fractures that carry flow and matrix blocks that store fluid.
A shaly-sand model that treats clay-bound water and free water as two separate conductive waters.
Offshore drilling in which the riser has a lighter fluid than the hole so pressure better matches the formation.
A shaker that can switch between linear and elliptical motion.
A formation tester section with two packers that isolates an interval for testing.
A streamer with hydrophones and motion sensors so the receiver ghost can be removed.
A standard way of describing how a bit has worn after a run, including cutter wear, location and reason pulled.
A blank device placed in a side-pocket mandrel instead of a gas-lift valve.
Controlling solids by discarding mud and adding new fluid.
A bailer that carries cement or sand down the well and releases it at a set depth.
A valve in a mud pit used to drain settled solids or fluid.
A scheme for carbonate rocks based on depositional texture: mudstone, wackestone, packstone, grainstone and boundstone.
A stack of thrust slices bounded by a floor and roof thrust.
A double-acting pump with two cylinders, older than triplex pumps.
Measures that limit dust when adding dry products.
Air drilling in dry rock where cuttings return as dust.
A measure of vertical permeability variation, from 0 (uniform) to 1 (extremely variable), used to predict waterflood sweep.
Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio and other elastic constants calculated from sonic and density logs.
Fluid loss while mud is circulating, which erodes the filter cake and is usually higher than static fluid loss.
Mud lost to the formation while circulating.
A reservoir simulation model that predicts flow over time.
An elastic modulus calculated from wave velocities and density.
Computer-controlled thrusters that hold a floating vessel over a fixed point without anchors. Abbreviated DP.
The ratio between the largest and smallest signals a recording system can capture.
Barite settling while mud is circulating slowly, especially in deviated holes, worse than sag at rest.
A short pressure drawdown created right after the charges fire, using special gun chambers, to clean perforations even without static underbalance.
An explosive used as a land seismic source in shot holes.
A plot of polished-rod load against position over a pump stroke, used to diagnose rod-pump problems.
A low-angle detachment surface, often in salt or shale, on which rocks above slide.
Radial flow around a horizontal wellbore before the top and bottom boundaries are felt.
The first part of a test, dominated by wellbore storage and skin.
A method of estimating pore pressure from how far sonic or resistivity readings depart from their normal compaction trend.
A device that pushes a logging tool against the borehole wall.
The time between NMR echoes, which affects what fast-relaxing fluids are seen.
The production rate at which a well's revenue just covers its operating costs. Below it the well loses money.
Processing data close to where it is collected, such as at the wellsite, instead of sending everything to a central server.
Highlighting abrupt changes in seismic, such as faults and channel edges.
Clay plates linking edges to faces, which builds structure and gel strength.
A titration with EDTA to measure calcium and magnesium hardness.
The percentage drop in rate over one period, such as a year, easier to quote than the nominal rate.
The interconnected pore volume that can hold movable fluid, excluding isolated pores and water bound to clay.
The viscosity a non-Newtonian fluid shows at a particular shear rate, such as the rate in the annulus.
An angle-dependent version of acoustic impedance used to invert far-offset data for lithology and fluids.
A synthetic gather that models amplitude change with angle.
How well rubber seals, such as in motors and packers, resist swelling or hardening in a given mud or brine.
Wireline with insulated conductors that power downhole tools and carry data. Also called e-line.
A multistage centrifugal pump with an electric motor, run on the tubing into the well. It suits high liquid rates. Abbreviated ESP.
Heating a reservoir with electric current or downhole heaters.
A probe that tells water from hydrocarbon by electrical conductivity.
Mapping resistivity in 2D or 3D from many electrode measurements.
A test that applies a rising voltage across an invert-emulsion mud until it conducts. A higher breakdown voltage means a more stable emulsion.
An instrument that finds the voltage needed to break an invert emulsion.
The pull between charged particles in mud, mainly clays, which controls yield point and gel strength.
Groups of depth intervals with similar log responses, used as stand-ins for rock types.
A dissolved salt that splits into ions in water. Electrolytes affect clay behavior and polymer performance in mud.
A tool that measures dielectric properties near the borehole with high-frequency waves. Abbreviated EPT.
A survey that measures the earth's response to electromagnetic fields to map resistivity.
A tool that measures metal loss in casing and tubing from electromagnetic signals, even through more than one string.
A log that measures the gamma rays from neutron capture to estimate the elements present and from them the mineralogy.
Time corrections for differences in surface elevation.
Clamps hung from the blocks that grip pipe for lifting.
The region within which a well's true position probably lies, given survey errors.
A shaker that moves the screen in an elliptical path.
An automatic system that shuts in wells and isolates equipment when a dangerous condition is detected. Abbreviated ESD.
A valve that closes automatically to shut in a well or system in an emergency. Abbreviated ESDV.
Acid dispersed in oil, which reacts more slowly and penetrates deeper into carbonates.
A surfactant that keeps brine droplets small and evenly spread in an invert-emulsion mud.
A mixture of two immiscible liquids in which one is dispersed as fine droplets in the other, such as water droplets in crude oil.
A viscous emulsion formed near the wellbore that reduces productivity.
Formation damage from a viscous emulsion forming in the pores.
How well the water droplets in an invert mud resist merging and separating.
Arranged in parallel, overlapping steps, as with some faults and folds.
A high-molecular-weight polymer that coats cuttings and shale.
Long-chain polymers coating cuttings and wellbore shale so the shale does not take up water and disperse.
A layout with all receivers on one side of the source.
The mobility ratio using end-point relative permeabilities.
Fracturing fluid with gas such as nitrogen or CO<sub>2</sub> to help flowback.

Methods that recover oil beyond primary and secondary recovery by changing the properties of the oil, the injected fluid or the rock–fluid system. The main groups are thermal, gas and chemical methods. Abbreviated EOR.
Gas with added intermediates such as ethane and propane to help miscibility.
The hole a perforating jet makes in the casing. Its size matters for sand control and hydraulic fracturing.
A depth where fluid enters the well.
The capillary pressure at which a non-wetting fluid first enters the largest pores.
The instantaneous amplitude of a seismic trace, independent of phase.
Meeting rules for discharge and disposal of mud and cuttings.
An adjustment of a log reading for borehole size, mud type, temperature and other conditions.
Release of produced fluids to the environment, which tests must control and record.
A breaker that uses enzymes to digest polymer in filter cakes or fracturing fluids.
The epoch from about 56 to 34 million years ago.
Early diagenesis near the surface.
The costs, oil gain and value of an EOR project.
Watching injection, production, pressures and tracers to manage an EOR project.
A small field test of an EOR method on a few wells, done before full-field expansion.
Planning a small field trial of an EOR method.
Comparing a reservoir's properties, such as oil gravity, viscosity, depth and permeability, with the ranges in which each EOR method has worked.
The remaining oil volume an EOR project aims to recover.
Made of fragments eroded from older rocks.
A neutron slightly above thermal energy. Tools counting these are less affected by absorbers such as chlorine.
A division of geologic time smaller than a period.
A line connecting two mud tanks so their levels match.
A mathematical relation between pressure, volume and temperature of a fluid, such as Peng-Robinson, used to predict phase behavior.
The density the formation effectively feels while mud is circulating: the static mud weight plus the annular friction pressure, converted to a density. Abbreviated ECD.
The effective mud density at a depth with no circulation, including temperature and pressure effects. Abbreviated ESD.
A modified shut-in time (Agarwal's) that lets buildup data be analyzed with drawdown type curves.
A major division of geologic time, such as the Mesozoic.
A large desert area covered by a sea of wind-blown sand dunes.
An indicator dye used in hardness titrations.
Layers cut off at the top by erosion.
The flow velocity above which a fluid will erode pipe, often estimated with the API RP 14E equation.
Electrical submersible pump: a downhole multistage centrifugal pump driven by an electric motor.
Pulling and replacing an electrical submersible pump.
A synthetic-base mud using esters, which biodegrade readily and suit environmentally sensitive offshore areas.
The total volume a well is expected to produce over its whole life. Abbreviated EUR.
A drowned river mouth where fresh and salt water mix and tides rework the sediment.
An anisotropy parameter that controls nonhyperbolic moveout in VTI media.
A method to estimate depths of magnetic or gravity sources.
Estimated ultimate recovery: the total a well is expected to produce over its life.
Worldwide change in sea level.
Rock formed when salty water evaporates, such as halite (rock salt), anhydrite and gypsum. Evaporites make excellent seals.
A basin where evaporation formed thick salt and gypsum layers.
Finding the position of a microseismic event from arrival times.
A neutron reading that is too low in gas zones because gas reduces hydrogen.
Undissolved lime held in reserve in a lime mud or invert emulsion, measured to make sure there is enough to treat contaminants.
The pressure above the expected water gradient, which can show a separate compartment.
An area around a seismic source that must be clear of marine mammals before firing.
A screen that is expanded downhole to press against the borehole wall, reducing the annular gap where sand could move.
Cement that expands slightly as it sets to seal better.
The ratio of thickness across a growth fault, showing when it was active.
A joint that lets tubing lengthen and shorten.
The probability-weighted average value of a decision, such as drilling a prospect: EMV = Pg × NPV(success) − (1 − Pg) × cost of failure.
A gun whose charges are exposed or lightly encased and break up when fired, leaving debris in the well.
A structured way to choose combinations of uncertain inputs to run, so their effects on the result can be measured efficiently. Also called design of experiments (DoE).
A modeling trick that treats every reflector as a source firing at time zero, used in post-stack migration.
A well drilled to test whether a prospect holds hydrocarbons.
Rules for handling, storing and arming explosives.
Decline at a constant percentage rate, q = q<sub>i</sub>e<sup>−Dt</sup>. It is the Arps case with b = 0 and the most conservative.
The function Ei that appears in the line-source solution.
The line-source solution written with the Ei function.
The release of generated oil and gas from a source rock, the first step of migration.
The fraction of generated hydrocarbons that leave the source rock.
Cement with extenders that add water and lower density and cost.
A generalization of elastic impedance that projects to chosen rock properties. Abbreviated EEI.
A leak-off test continued past breakdown to measure fracture closure and the minimum stress.
Drilling wells whose horizontal reach is far greater than their vertical depth, often more than twice the TVD. Abbreviated ERD.
A production test lasting weeks or months that gathers reservoir and fluid data before committing to full field development.
Oil denser than water, with API gravity below 10°, that may still flow at reservoir temperature.
A gravity correction for the motion of a ship or aircraft.
Filtering seismic data in the frequency–wavenumber domain to remove noise with particular dips, such as ground roll.
Acid reacting at the borehole face instead of forming wormholes, usually from too low a rate.
Clay plates stacking together, which lowers viscosity.
A body of rock whose features, such as grain size, structures and fossils, record the environment in which it was deposited.
Assigning each point in a seismic volume to a rock type using attributes.
A 3D model of rock types in a reservoir.
A model of changing wellbore storage that rises with time.
Deposits laid down while relative sea level is falling.
A test in which an injection well is shut in and the decline in pressure is recorded and analyzed.
An alluvial fan that builds directly into standing water.
A dial reading from a rotational viscometer at a set speed.
A dimensionless factor used to compute frictional pressure loss in pipe.
The longest source-receiver distance in a gather.
A stack of large-angle traces.
Diverting agents that plug the far part of a fracture so flow goes elsewhere.
Acquiring an interest in a license from its holder, usually by paying part of the exploration or drilling costs. The holder's side of the deal is a farmout.
The end of drilling line that runs to the drawworks drum.
The direction of the faster shear wave, which often matches the maximum horizontal stress.
An AVO approximation written in terms of P-impedance, S-impedance and density reflectivity.
A soap-forming emulsifier made from fatty acids and lime, used in invert-emulsion muds.
A fracture in the Earth's crust along which the rocks on either side have moved. Faults can trap hydrocarbons or let them leak.
The central part of a fault zone where most slip occurs, often with gouge.
The distance to a fault estimated from a well test.
Fine, crushed rock along a fault, which can form a seal.
The horizontal displacement across a fault.
Marking fault traces on seismic sections.
The outline of a fault cut on a horizon map.
A fault that stops hydrocarbons moving across it, for example because shale has been smeared along the fault plane.
A zone of poor or distorted imaging beneath a fault caused by velocity changes across it.
The vertical offset of a layer across a fault.
A trap where a fault seals one side of a reservoir.
A band of many faults and fractures rather than a single plane.
A fold formed as a rock layer rides over a bend in a thrust fault.
A fold that forms ahead of the tip of a growing fault.
Fossil groups follow each other in a set order through time.
An empirical relation of velocity to depth and resistivity.
The pressure of mud fed to hydrocyclones, usually in feet of head.
A sealed path for control lines or cables through a packer or hanger.
A group of aluminosilicate minerals common in sandstone. Feldspars can dissolve to create secondary porosity.
A set of linked cross-sections showing geology in three dimensions.
Bacterial breakdown of natural polymers such as starch in mud, which ruins their performance and causes odors.
Bacterial breakdown of starch that sours the mud and lowers its fluid-loss control.
A lignosulfonate with iron and chromium salts, once the standard dispersant for water-base mud.
Type curves combining transient and decline curve behavior.
Glass fibers used to send data and to sense temperature, strain and sound along a well.
A pill of fibers pumped to sweep cuttings or seal losses.
Coiled tubing with an optical fiber inside for real-time downhole data.
Lost circulation material made of fibers that mat across openings.
Recording field readings and inspections digitally on mobile devices.
The plan for how a discovered field will be produced, covering wells, facilities, schedule, costs and expected recovery. Abbreviated FDP.
Sand, debris or settled solids that build up inside the wellbore and can cover the perforations.
A trap filled with hydrocarbons down to its spill point.
The period in a waterflood when injected water refills gas space before oil response.
A corrosion inhibitor that forms a protective film on steel.
The layer of mud solids left on the borehole wall when the mud's liquid seeps into permeable rock. A thin, tough cake limits further fluid loss.
A treatment, such as an enzyme, oxidizer or acid, that breaks down filter cake after drilling the reservoir.
Removing filter cake from the reservoir face before production.
The thickness of the cake left on the filter paper in a fluid-loss test, reported in 32nds of an inch or millimeters.
Hardened paper used in filter press tests.
A test comparing filtration times to check whether a polymer solution will plug the formation.
The liquid that passes from the mud into a permeable formation, leaving the mud solids behind as filter cake.
Mud filtrate mixed into a formation fluid sample, which must be measured and kept low for good PVT data.
Formation damage from mud filtrate, such as clay swelling or precipitation.
Mud filtrate entering the formation around the well.
Keeping the volume of filtrate and the thickness of filter cake low, using clays, polymers and bridging particles.
The flat reference level to which processed seismic times are referred.
The last shut-in period of a drillstem test, usually long enough to analyze permeability and skin.
The stack produced at the end of processing.
Small ground marble or limestone particles used for bridging pores.
Small mica flakes used as a seepage loss material.
Very small particles, usually silt and clay size, that can plug pore throats and screens.
Movement of tiny particles such as clay through the pores, where they can plug pore throats and reduce permeability.
A succession whose grain size decreases upward, as in many channel fills.
A fracture whose own flow resistance affects the well test.
Migration that solves the wave equation using finite differences.
Detectors and logic that sense fires and gas leaks and trigger alarms, shutdowns and firefighting.
Another name for in-situ combustion.
The device at the top of a perforating gun that starts the detonation, triggered electrically, by pressure or by a dropped bar.
The first arrival of seismic energy at a receiver, picked to compute near-surface corrections.
The temperature at which the first crystals show in a cooling brine. Abbreviated FCTA.
Miscibility reached as soon as the injected fluid meets the oil, as with LPG solvents.
Anything lost or stuck in a well that must be recovered.
Recovering equipment, called the fish, that has been lost or stuck in a well.
A jar used to free stuck tools during fishing.
A strong magnet run to recover small steel debris from the bottom of a well.
The machined top of a downhole tool designed to be gripped by a retrieving tool.
The pipe and tools run to recover a fish.
Any tool used to recover lost equipment from a well.
The tendency of shale to split along thin layers.
A waterflood pattern with an injector at the center of a square and producers at the four corners, or the reverse.
A choke with a fixed bean size. Also called a positive choke.
Lost circulation material made of flat flakes, such as mica, that bridge across pore openings.
A burner, usually on a tall stack or boom, that safely disposes of gas that cannot be processed, used or sold, especially during upsets.
An arm that holds a flare or burner away from an offshore rig.
A tall stack where unusable gas is burned safely.
Sand with thin mud drapes in ripple troughs, typical of tidal settings.
A PVT test in which gas released from oil stays in contact with it, like a single-stage separator.
The lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapor to ignite. A safety property of base oils and fuels.
A synthetic-base mud designed so its gel strength and yield point change little between cold seabed and hot downhole temperatures.
A horizontal reflection that cuts across dipping layers, often caused by a gas–water or gas–oil contact.
Rig time spent not making hole, such as tripping, casing and cementing.
Cement with a lower elastic modulus that resists cracking under load changes.
Sinking caused by the crust bending under a load, as in foreland basins.
A borehole wave from a dipole source, used to measure shear velocity.
A one-way valve near the bottom of a casing string that stops cement flowing back into the casing.
The float shoe and float collar with one-way valves at the bottom of casing.
A guide shoe with a one-way valve at the bottom of casing.
A one-way valve in the drillstring that stops backflow.
A smooth reference surface near the topography used for processing.
A chemical that causes fine solids to clump together so they settle or can be removed by a centrifuge.
Clay particles clumping into loose clusters, which raises the yield point and gel strength of a mud.
The leading edge of injected fluid moving through the reservoir.
A surface where water depth suddenly increased.
The flat land beside a river that floods and receives fine sediment.
A unit that removes oil droplets from water by floating them on gas bubbles.
The exponent n of the power-law model. A value below 1 means the fluid is shear-thinning; exactly 1 means Newtonian.
Fluid flowing in the annulus behind casing, outside the wellbore.
Stopping the pumps and watching the well to see whether it flows, the basic test for a kick.
A factor that relates flow through a meter or valve to pressure drop.
A thick-walled section placed above and below restrictions to resist turbulent erosion.
The ratio of a well's actual productivity index to the productivity index it would have with zero skin.
The pipe that carries mud from the well to the shakers.
The temperature of mud returning to surface.
A chart that predicts the flow regime from gas and liquid velocities.
A stage of a well test during which the well produces at a controlled rate, followed by a shut-in or a different rate.
How the production or injection rate is distributed along the open interval of a well.
Measuring how much oil, gas and water a well produces.
The arrangement of phases in a pipe, such as bubble, slug, churn or annular flow. It depends on rates, fluid properties and inclination.
A paddle or meter in the flowline that measures return flow so gains and losses are spotted quickly.
Flowing a well to measure rates and pressures.
A reservoir interval with consistent properties that control fluid flow, distinct from the intervals around it.
The speed of fluid moving in the well.
A value derived from the reservoir quality index that groups rock into hydraulic flow units. Abbreviated FZI.
The recovery to surface of fracturing fluid and proppant after the treatment, before or as the well starts producing.
A pattern of faults that branch upward from a strike-slip fault, looking like a flower on seismic.
A valve assembly at the top of a test string that controls flow and allows tools to enter.
The pressure at the bottom of a well while it is producing. Written p<sub>wf</sub>.
Measuring pressure at several depths in a flowing well.
A method that estimates in-place volume from flowing pressures and rates.
A production logging run made while the well flows.
A temperature log run while the well flows.
The pressure at the wellhead while the well flows. Abbreviated FWHP.
The pipe that carries production from a wellhead to a manifold or processing facility.
The pressure in the line downstream of the wellhead choke.
A log of fluid velocity along the well from a spinner or other flowmeter.
Injecting combustion exhaust, mainly nitrogen and CO<sub>2</sub>, for pressure support or EOR.
A boundary between two fluids in a reservoir, such as the gas–oil contact or the oil–water contact.
Mass per unit volume of a fluid, usually in ppg or specific gravity for mud.
A production logging tool, such as a gradiomanometer, that measures the average density of the fluid mixture in the well to infer the phases present.
The fraction of fracturing fluid that remains in the fracture at shut-in instead of leaking into the formation.
The part of a mud pump with the liners, pistons and valves that move mud.
An AVO attribute designed to highlight departures from the wet-rock trend, which can indicate hydrocarbons.
The rate of pressure change with depth in a fluid column, set by its density.
Telling oil, gas and water apart in the wellbore.
A tiny droplet of fluid trapped in a mineral as it grew, which records past temperatures and fluids.
The depth of the liquid surface in a well.
The volume of filtrate a mud loses through a filter paper in a standard test, such as 30 minutes at 100 psi. It shows how well the mud seals permeable rock.
Permeability divided by fluid viscosity, k/μ. Formation testers measure it from the pretest drawdown.
The bulk modulus of the pore fluid.
A sharp impact in a rod pump when the plunger hits liquid in a partly filled barrel, caused by pumping faster than the well can supply.
Calculating how logs or seismic would change if the pore fluid were different, usually with the Gassmann equation.
Identifying oil, gas or water in the formation from logs.
Any additive, such as starch, PAC or fine bridging solids, that reduces filtrate loss.
A pill placed across open perforations or screens to stop completion fluid flowing into the formation.
An acid that releases hydrofluoric acid slowly for deep sandstone treatment.
Light given off by oil in cuttings under ultraviolet light, used by mud loggers to detect oil.
Fluid pumped after the slurry to clear proppant from the well.
The part of the invaded zone nearest the borehole, where mud filtrate has displaced almost all the movable formation fluid.
The resistivity of the flushed zone, measured by shallow microresistivity tools and written R<sub>xo</sub>.
A scoop-shaped mark on a bed base that shows current direction.
Relating to rivers. Fluvial reservoirs are channel sands that are often narrow and discontinuous.
A pozzolan from coal-burning power plants used as a cement extender.
Removing fill with foam, which carries solids well and keeps hydrostatic pressure low.
Using foam to divert acid from taken zones.
Drilling with stable foam as the circulating fluid, used in low-pressure zones.
Injecting gas as foam to reduce its mobility, control gravity override and improve sweep.
Fracturing with a foam of gas in liquid.
The volume percent of gas in a foam at given conditions.
How long foam lasts before collapsing.
Cement with nitrogen foamed into it to lower density and add flexibility.
Unwanted foam in the mud, which lowers density and disturbs pump suction.
A surfactant that makes stable foam.
Heavy oil in which gas bubbles stay dispersed instead of forming a separate gas phase, which can help keep production up.
The fault orientation and slip direction of an event, from its radiation pattern.
A probe with a guard ring that draws contaminated fluid away from the sample line.
A formation-tester probe design that draws contaminated fluid through an outer ring so the center collects cleaner reservoir fluid.
A bend in rock layers caused by deformation, such as an anticline or syncline.
The number of traces in each bin.
The line of greatest curvature on a fold.
The side of a fold between hinges.
The number of times each subsurface bin is sampled in a survey, a basic measure of data quality.
The block of rock below an inclined fault plane.
Single-celled organisms with tiny shells, widely used to date and correlate marine rocks.
Shoreline moving seaward because sea level falls.
The seaward slope of a reef, with reef debris.
A basin between a trench and a volcanic arc.
A basin that forms in front of a mountain belt as the weight of the mountains bends the crust down.
The beach zone between high and low tide.
A clear brine of sodium, potassium or cesium formate. It reaches high densities with low corrosion and environmental impact.
The pressure at which the formation fractures during a leak-off test.
A loss of permeability around the wellbore caused by drilling, completion, workover or production, for example from fines, clay swelling or scale.
A core flood that measures how a mud or completion fluid affects a rock's permeability.
Determining a formation's rock and fluid properties, and whether it can produce, from logs, cores, samples and tests.
The planned logs, cores, tests and samples for a well.
Measuring formation properties with LWD tools during drilling.
The ratio of the resistivity of a fully water-saturated rock to the resistivity of the water. Written F = R<sub>o</sub>/R<sub>w</sub> = a/φ<sup>m</sup>.
A sample of the fluid in a formation, taken by a tester or during a test.
A pressure test below the casing shoe up to a planned value, stopping before leak-off, to confirm the formation can hold the planned mud weights.
A downhole valve that isolates the reservoir during completion work.
The pressure of fluids in the pores of a formation.
A wireline or LWD tool that measures pore pressure at points in the well and can take fluid samples.
The ratio of resistivity of a water-filled rock to that of the water. Symbol F.
A tool that seals against the borehole wall to measure formation pressure and collect fluid samples at chosen depths.
A small drawdown by a formation tester probe to measure pressure and mobility.
The small tube on a formation tester pressed against the wall to measure pressure.
The depth where a formation starts in a well.
The ratio of a fluid's volume at reservoir conditions to its volume at standard surface conditions, such as B<sub>o</sub> for oil and B<sub>g</sub> for gas.
Formation water entering the mud, changing its salt content and density.
The resistivity of the water in the rock's pores, written R<sub>w</sub>. It falls as salinity and temperature rise.
An organic acid used in hot wells because it reacts slowly.
Combustion in which the burning front moves in the same direction as the air.
The weight on bit above which penetration rate stops increasing.
A caliper with two pairs of arms that measures hole shape and breakouts.
A trap closed on all sides by dip, such as a dome.
A mathematical method that splits a signal into its frequencies.
A floating production, storage and offloading vessel: a ship-shaped facility that processes oil offshore, stores it and offloads it to tankers.
The set of pumps, blenders and other units used to fracture a well.
Chemicals added to fracturing fluid, such as biocides, breakers and scale inhibitors.
A fitting on the frac tree where treating lines connect.
A pressure or fluid response in a nearby well caused by fracturing a new well, which can damage or interrupt the older well.
A completion that combines a short, wide hydraulic fracture with a gravel pack. It controls sand and bypasses near-wellbore damage.
A plug set to isolate fractured stages below, later drilled out or dissolved.
A high-pressure pump that injects fracturing fluid.
Sized quartz sand used as proppant.
A sliding sleeve opened by a dropped ball, coiled tubing or pressure, used to isolate and treat one fracturing stage at a time.
A chemical or radioactive tracer pumped to show which stages produce or where proppant went.
A high-pressure valve assembly on the wellhead used during fracturing.
The fraction of the total flowing stream that is water (or another displacing phase) at a given saturation. Written f<sub>w</sub>.
Separating a liquid mixture into products such as ethane, propane and butane by distillation.
The width of an open fracture.
The point when a fracture closes on its proppant or faces as pressure falls.
The degree to which a hydraulic fracture branches into a network rather than one planar fracture.
How easily fluid flows along a propped fracture: fracture permeability times propped width, in mD·ft.
The number of fractures per unit length of borehole.
Damage on fracture faces from fluid leakoff.
The height, length and width of a hydraulic fracture.
The pressure per unit depth at which a formation breaks down and starts accepting fluid. It sets the upper limit on mud weight and ECD.
The distance a hydraulic fracture extends from the wellbore on one side. Written x<sub>f</sub>.
The vertical extent of a hydraulic fracture, controlled mainly by stress contrast between layers.
A model that predicts fracture size and shape from rock and pumping data.
Pore space provided by fractures. It is usually small in volume but can greatly increase permeability.
The pressure needed to keep a fracture growing after breakdown.
The opening of a fracture between its faces, which sets how much proppant it can hold.
A reservoir in fractured igneous or metamorphic rock, where oil is stored mainly in fractures.
Shale broken by natural fractures, which can cave in and cause losses.
The fluid pumped to create and fill a hydraulic fracture and carry proppant, such as slickwater, linear gel or crosslinked gel.
A gel that forms quickly to suspend solids but breaks easily, limiting pressure surges when circulation restarts.
The larger grains that support a sandstone.
The porosity filled with movable fluid, as measured by NMR logs. Abbreviated FFI.
Gas held as a compressed gas in pores and fractures, as opposed to adsorbed or dissolved gas.
Casing with no cement behind it, which rings strongly on a bond log.
Water that separates on top of a cement slurry at rest.
The depth where capillary pressure is zero. The oil–water contact usually sits slightly above it.
A gravity anomaly corrected for latitude and elevation but not for the rock mass between station and datum.
A tool that measures stretch and twist in stuck pipe to find the deepest point that is still free.
A vessel that removes the free water that settles quickly from the wellstream before the oil is treated further.
An attribute that measures loss of high frequencies, sometimes a sign of gas.
A plot of how much energy a seismic signal has at each frequency.
A water-base mud made with fresh water, in which bentonite hydrates fully.
The area of a reflector that contributes to a reflection at one point. It limits horizontal resolution before migration.
Removing friction effects from pressure-derived fluid density.
Pressure lost to fluid friction as mud flows through the drillstring, bit and annulus.
A polymer that cuts friction pressure in turbulent flow, the key additive in slickwater fracturing.
The movement of a saturation front through a reservoir during displacement.
A basin with little or no exploration.
Cleaning water and solids from bitumen froth after mining extraction.
The coke-like residue left ahead of the combustion front that burns as fuel.
A BHA with a stabilizer near the bit and flexible collars above it, which builds angle.
Measuring all components of the gravity gradient to map density changes in detail.
A survey with offsets recorded in every direction.
A ball valve kept on the rig floor to stab into pipe and close it during a kick.
A synthetic seismogram that includes multiples and transmission losses.
A computing-intensive method that builds a detailed velocity model by matching complete recorded waveforms. Abbreviated FWI.
A spinner flowmeter with blades that open to cover most of the casing.
The Marsh funnel reading in seconds per quart. It is useful for spotting changes at the rig but is not a true viscosity.
A gamma ray curve that decreases upward, typical of coarsening-upward deposits.
A noise filter that predicts signal across traces in the frequency domain.
The acceleration of a shaker screen, a multiple of gravity.
A time function used to analyze pressure decline after a minifrac.
Amplitude corrections that compensate for spreading and absorption.
An LWD image of natural radioactivity around the hole.
The scaled position of a gamma ray reading between clean and shale values, used to estimate shale volume.
A log of the formation's natural radioactivity. Shales usually read high and clean sands and carbonates low, so it is used to pick lithology and correlate wells.
An empirical relation between density and P-wave velocity, ρ ≈ 0.31V<sup>0.25</sup> (g/cm³, m/s).
A test kit that measures sulfides or carbonates in mud filtrate by releasing them as gas.
Free gas sitting above the oil in a reservoir. Its expansion helps drive oil to the wells.
Gas bubbles carried out of a separator with the liquid.
A vertical zone of disturbed seismic caused by gas leaking upward.
An instrument that separates and measures the components of a gas sample.
The fractions of methane, ethane and other components in a gas.
The ratio of a real gas's volume to the volume an ideal gas would occupy at the same pressure and temperature. Written Z and read from the Standing–Katz chart.
Removing water vapor from natural gas, often with glycol or desiccant, to prevent hydrates and corrosion and meet pipeline specifications.
An instrument in the mud logging unit that measures gas from the mud.
The way gas makes density porosity read too high and neutron porosity too low, creating the classic crossover.
A depth where gas flows into the well.
A correction in orifice flow equations for gas expanding through the plate.
A compressor that raises gas pressure for export.
The fraction of pipe area filled by gas.
An ice-like solid of water molecules caging gas molecules. It forms at high pressure and low temperature and can block pipelines.
Injecting gas into the tubing through valves at depth. The gas lightens the fluid column, so the reservoir can push fluid to surface.
Changing gas lift valve settings or depths to suit new well conditions.
A valve in a side-pocket mandrel that lets gas from the annulus into the tubing.
Replacing gas lift valves with slickline.
A pump condition in which gas fills the barrel and the valves cannot open, so no liquid is pumped.
The straight pipe section containing an orifice plate and its taps.
Gas moving through cement as it sets, which can create channels to surface.
A facility that treats natural gas to sales quality by removing water, acid gases and heavier hydrocarbons.
The volume of gas produced per day.
Using ratios of methane to heavier gases in mud gas to guess the fluid type in a zone.
A sample of gas taken from a separator, wellhead or downhole.
An increase in gas detected in the mud from a formation.
Treatments that stop unwanted gas production.
The ratio of a gas's density to that of air at the same conditions, equal to its molecular weight divided by 28.97.
Removing hydrogen sulfide and carbon dioxide (acid gases) from natural gas.
A device in the flowline or shaker tank that extracts gas from returning mud for analysis.
The arbitrary units mud loggers use to report gas detected in mud.
The rate a gas well can deliver against a given back-pressure.
The temperature range, above the oil window, in which source rocks mainly generate gas.
Injecting gas at the top so oil drains down to horizontal producers. Abbreviated GAGD.
Mud with gas bubbles in it, which lowers its density. It can come from drilled gas or from an influx.
The deepest depth where gas is proven. Abbreviated GDT.
Total gas produced per barrel of total liquid. Abbreviated GLR.
The depth that separates gas from oil in a reservoir. Abbreviated GOC.
The volume of gas produced per volume of oil, usually in standard cubic feet per stock-tank barrel (scf/STB). Abbreviated GOR.
A slurry designed to stop gas migration while it sets.
A clean synthetic base oil made from natural gas. Abbreviated GTL.
The depth that separates gas from water in a reservoir. Abbreviated GWC.
A liquid with gas injected to lower its density.
A rock-physics relation that predicts how a rock's elastic properties change when the fluid in its pores changes.
Processing prestack gathers, by flattening, denoising and balancing, before AVO analysis or inversion.
The network of flowlines and pipelines that carries production from many wells to a central facility.
How close a gauge reading is to the true pressure.
A test string component that holds pressure and temperature gauges.
A slickline tool with a sharp ring run to check tubing drift and scrape off scale or wax.
A slow false change in a gauge's reading over time.
Pressure measured relative to the surrounding atmosphere, in psig. Absolute pressure is gauge plus atmospheric.
The smallest pressure change a gauge can detect.
A ring run on wireline to check that tubing is clear to a given size.
A calibrated tank used to measure liquid volumes during a well test.
A fluid that has developed structure at rest, or a slang term for bentonite.
The extra pump pressure needed to break the gel when starting circulation.
A thick, viscous pill used to sweep the hole or seal losses.
Polymer left in the fracture after breaking, which lowers conductivity.
The shear stress needed to start a mud moving after it has rested, usually measured after 10 seconds and 10 minutes. It shows how well the mud holds cuttings in suspension when the pumps stop.
Excessive thickening of mud at high temperature, often in bentonite muds.
Acid thickened with polymer to slow reaction and aid placement.
The amount of hydrocarbons a source rock can still generate.
AI that creates new text, images or other content from patterns in data.
A log that measures elements in the formation to estimate mineralogy.
A reference model of the earth's shape used for positions, such as WGS 84.
A map showing rock units, faults and structures at the surface.
A division of geologic time smaller than an era, such as the Jurassic.
A time-rock unit smaller than a series, such as the Maastrichtian.
The division of earth history into eons, eras, periods and epochs.
The probability that a prospect holds moving hydrocarbons, found by multiplying the chance of each element.
A vertical slice through the subsurface showing rock layers, faults and fluids between wells.
A mappable body of rock with consistent characteristics, given a name such as the Nido Limestone.
A 3D representation of a reservoir's structure, layers and properties.
The study of how rock deforms and fails under stress, used for wellbore stability, sanding and fracturing design.
Skin caused by well geometry, such as partial penetration or deviation.
Linking each trace to its source and receiver positions.
A sensor planted on land that converts ground motion into an electrical signal during a seismic survey.
Several geophones wired together and spread out to cancel noise.
How well a geophone is planted to move with the ground. Poor coupling distorts the signal.
Any survey that measures physical properties of the earth, such as seismic, gravity or magnetics.
Inversion that makes many high-resolution impedance models consistent with seismic and wells.
Statistical methods that describe how properties vary in space and estimate them between wells.
Adjusting the well path in real time, using logging-while-drilling data, to keep the bit in the best part of the reservoir.
The rate at which temperature increases with depth, commonly around 25–30 °C per kilometer.
The undisturbed temperature with depth in a well.
Energy reflected from the sea surface just above a marine source or receiver, which interferes with the primary signal.
A field with more than about 500 million barrels of recoverable oil equivalent.
A natural asphalt added to muds to help seal shale microfractures and reduce fluid loss.
Small solid glass spheres added to mud as a mechanical lubricant.
A green, potassium-bearing clay mineral formed on the seafloor. It raises gamma ray readings in otherwise clean sands.
Dehydrating gas by contacting it with a glycol, usually triethylene glycol (TEG), which absorbs the water and is then regenerated by heating.
A water-base mud containing a polyglycol, which reduces shale hydration and improves lubricity.
A banded, high-grade metamorphic rock.
The curved guide arch on top of a coiled tubing injector that bends the tubing from the reel into the well.
A block of crust dropped down between two normal faults.
A bed in which grains get finer upward.
The depth where two fluid gradients cross, used to find a fluid contact.
A volume of AVO gradient values.
A tool that measures the pressure difference between two points to find fluid density in the well.
The way grains touch, such as point, long or sutured contacts.
The density of the solid grains in a rock sample.
The diameter of sediment particles, classified as clay, silt, sand, granules, pebbles and larger.
A grain-supported carbonate with no lime mud between the grains, often with good porosity.
A coarse-grained igneous rock of quartz and feldspar, often part of basement.
Lost circulation material made of hard granules, such as nut shells or carbonate, that wedge into fractures.
A resilient carbon material used as a lost circulation and wellbore strengthening material and as a lubricant.
The gripping part of an overshot that holds the fish.
Sized sand or ceramic beads placed around a screen to stop formation sand.
A sand-control method that packs sized gravel between a screen and the formation, so the gravel holds back formation sand.
How completely gravel fills the space around a screen.
Logging to check how well gravel fills the space around a screen.
The packer that seals above a gravel pack and isolates it from the casing above.
Extra pressure loss through a gravel pack and its perforation tunnels.
Choosing gravel size to stop formation sand, often from a sieve analysis.
An instrument that measures tiny differences in gravity.
The difference between measured gravity and expected gravity after corrections.
Oil draining downward under gravity, typically in thick or steeply dipping reservoirs with good vertical permeability.
Measuring the rate of change of gravity in several directions, which sharpens detail of shallow density contrasts.
The ratio of gravity to viscous forces, which predicts gravity override.
Lighter injected fluids, such as gas or steam, rising to the top of the reservoir and bypassing oil lower down.
Measuring tiny differences in the Earth's gravity to map density changes underground, such as salt domes or basin depth.
A seal for braided line or e-line that uses injected grease to stop leaks.
A seal for braided or electric line that uses pressurized grease around the cable.
A method to predict shear velocity from compressional velocity for mixed lithologies.
A poorly sorted, dark sandstone with a muddy matrix and rock fragments.
The angle between true north and grid north on a map projection.
A model divided into cells for numerical solution.
A centrifuge test that separates water and sediment in an oil sample to measure BS&W.
A family of type curves for wells with wellbore storage and skin.
Shaped blocks on the injector chains that grip coiled tubing.
A false high reading on a laterolog under a thick resistive bed.
The total rock volume of a reservoir between its top surface and the fluid contact. Abbreviated GRV.
The total thickness of a zone from top to base.
Calcium carbonate made from marble, used as acid-soluble bridging and weighting material.
Slow, low-frequency surface waves in land seismic that can mask reflections. Processing tries to remove it.
A stratigraphic unit made of two or more formations.
The distance between the centers of neighboring receiver groups.
A normal fault that moved while sediment was being deposited, so beds are thicker on the downthrown side.
Layers deposited while a fault or fold was moving, thickening toward it.
A natural polymer from guar beans, used as a viscosifier in drilling fluids and as the base of many fracturing gels.
An electrode in a laterolog that focuses current into the formation.
A rounded nose on the bottom of casing that guides it down the hole.
Soft, sticky clay that balls bits and plugs flowlines.
A sudden flood of sticky clay at surface that overloads shakers and lines.
A coarse screen or chute ahead of the shakers that catches gumbo.
The tube that holds the charges in a perforating gun.
The gap between the perforating gun and the casing wall, which affects entrance-hole size and penetration.
Releasing guns after firing so they fall to the bottom of the well.
Choosing gun size and charges for well size, temperature and goals.
Several guns connected and run together.
The increase in outside diameter of a hollow-carrier gun after firing, which must stay small enough for the gun to be pulled.
A mixture of bentonite in diesel oil that sets into a stiff plug when it contacts water in a loss zone.
Short for gypsum, calcium sulfate dihydrate.
A calcium-treated water-base mud using gypsum, designed to tolerate anhydrite and limit shale swelling.
Hydrated calcium sulfate, an evaporite that turns to anhydrite when buried.
A directional survey using a gyroscope, unaffected by magnetic interference.
Procedures for detecting hydrogen sulfide and protecting people during operations.
Measuring hydrogen sulfide in gas, for example with detector tubes or analyzers.
A 1/2 slope on the log-log derivative, showing linear flow.
A basin bounded by a fault on one side only, so the fill tilts toward the fault.
Rock salt (sodium chloride). It flows under pressure and forms excellent seals and salt domes.
A plot of cumulative pressure-time against cumulative injection used to track injectivity.
A thermal cuttings processor that uses friction from rotating hammers to boil off oil and water.
The block of rock above an inclined fault plane.
A hard alloy layer on tool joints that reduces wear.
The amount of calcium and magnesium dissolved in water or filtrate.
The Arps case with b = 1, in which the decline rate is proportional to the production rate.
Unwanted energy at multiples of the sweep frequency produced by a vibrator.
The narrowest upper and lower limits on a mixture's elastic moduli, used in rock physics models.
A straight-line form of the material balance equation used to find original oil or gas in place.
A wave that travels along a boundary at the faster layer's velocity, created at the critical angle. Used in refraction surveys.
A fracture filled with mineral cement.
The rate at which heat moves up through the crust, which controls source rock maturity.
Heat escaping from steam to wellbore surroundings and to rock above and below the reservoir.
A vessel that heats an oil–water emulsion, often with chemicals, so the water separates and the oil meets sales specifications.
The heat released when gas burns, in BTU per standard cubic foot.
A system that keeps weight on bit steady as a floating rig moves up and down.
A dense completion brine, such as calcium bromide or zinc bromide.
Mercury, cadmium and other metals in barite, limited by discharge rules.
Dense minerals such as zircon and garnet used to trace sediment sources.
Dense, viscous crude oil, commonly defined as having an API gravity below about 22°. It usually needs heat, dilution or special lifting to produce.
A reservoir holding viscous oil that is hard to produce without heat or special methods.
Processes that turn heavy oil into lighter, more valuable oil.
The denser fluid in multiphase flow, usually water.
A small batch of mud heavier than the active system pumped before a trip.
Cement weighted with hematite or similar materials for high-pressure wells.
Thick-walled drillpipe placed between the drill collars and normal drillpipe to ease the stiffness change and reduce fatigue.
A magnesium-lithium clay used as a high-temperature viscosifier.
A dimensionless number used with Bingham plastic fluids to find the laminar-turbulent transition.
The start of a horizontal well's lateral, where it turns from the curve into the target zone.
A model of changing wellbore storage that fits phase redistribution.
Pipe bending into a spiral under compression.
An instrument that measures grain volume using helium and Boyle's law.
An iron oxide weighting material with a specific gravity of about 5, used when barite cannot reach the required density.
Fine sediment near continents made of both settled ocean material and land-derived mud.
The Louisiana pipeline hub whose price is the main benchmark for US natural gas.
Cross-beds dipping in opposite directions, typical of tidal currents.
A three-parameter flow model that adds a yield stress to power-law behavior. It usually describes drilling muds most accurately.
Contact theory that gives the stiffness of a pack of spheres under pressure.
A squeeze cement job that pumps in stages with pauses to build filter cake.
Variation of rock properties from place to place within a reservoir.
A gap in time in the rock record.
Removing cuttings in deviated wells, where they settle on the low side and need high rate and rotation.
A lost-circulation slurry that dewaters quickly in the loss zone, leaving a firm plug of solids.
Dense solids such as barite or hematite that are added to mud on purpose to raise its weight.
A water-base mud with advanced inhibitors and polymers, designed to perform close to oil-base mud in reactive shale.
A gravel pack pumped at high rate with brine above fracture pressure.
Seismic acquired with high frequencies and close spacing to image shallow targets in detail.
A centrifuge run at high g-force to remove fine low-gravity solids.
Bentonite mud flocculating and setting into a stiff gel at high temperature.
Mud designed to keep its properties above about 300 °F.
Combustion of fuel in the reservoir at high temperature.
A thick pill pumped to carry cuttings out of the hole.
Deposits laid down late in a sea-level rise and during the early fall, typically building seaward.
A simple AVO approximation based on normal-incidence reflectivity and Poisson's ratio contrast.
A crossplot of resistivity transformed against porosity used to estimate water resistivity and saturation.
Adjusting a simulation model until it reproduces the field's past production rates and pressures.
An explosive more stable at high temperature than RDX, used in hotter wells.
The fraction of the pipe cross-section occupied by one phase. Because phases slip past one another, it differs from that phase's share of the flow rate.
Removing cuttings from the wellbore. It depends on flow rate, mud properties, pipe rotation and hole angle.
Widening of the hole beyond bit size by washout or caving.
Cuttings or caved rock collected on bottom after a trip.
A tool that enlarges an existing hole.
A reusable steel tube that holds the charges and contains most of the debris when fired.
Tiny hollow glass beads added to mud to lower its density without adding air or gas.
The current epoch, the last 11,700 years.
The total weight hanging from the hook, including the drillstring in mud. It is read on the weight indicator.
A shaker screen with hooked edges that is tensioned on the shaker.
A biomarker derived from bacterial membranes.
Displaying seismic with a horizon made flat to restore the depositional view.
Picking a seismic horizon across a survey.
Tracking a reflection across a seismic volume.
A slice through a seismic volume that follows a picked horizon.
The horizontal distance from the surface location to a point in the well.
Permeability along the bedding. Symbol kh.
Resistivity measured along the bedding. Symbol Rh.
A subsea tree whose valves are on the side, so the tubing can be pulled without removing the tree.
A well that turns to run roughly parallel to the reservoir layer, so it contacts far more rock than a vertical well.
Production logging in a horizontal well, where phases segregate and tools must be pushed in.
A test in a horizontal well, with flow regimes such as vertical radial, linear and pseudoradial.
A buildup plot of shut-in pressure against log[(t<sub>p</sub> + Δt)/Δt]. The slope of its straight line gives kh, and extrapolating the line gives p*.
The ratio (tp + Δt)/Δt used as the time axis on a Horner plot.
A block of crust raised between two normal faults.
Circulating heated oil through a well to melt and remove paraffin.
Ageing mud samples in sealed cells rolled in an oven to simulate downhole temperatures before testing.
Injecting hot water to warm and displace viscous oil; less effective than steam but simpler.
A shale test that rolls cuttings in a mud at temperature and measures how much survives, to rate inhibition.
Hydrolyzed polyacrylamide, the most common synthetic polymer for polymer flooding.
A heated, high-pressure fluid-loss cell, typically run at 300 °F with 500 psi differential, to show how a mud seals under downhole conditions.
Filtrate volume at high temperature and 500 psi differential, doubled to match the API filter area.
A drilling fluid designed to stay stable at high pressure and high temperature, usually above 300 °F.
A viscometer that measures rheology at high temperature and pressure.
Health, safety and environment: the discipline and management system for protecting people and the environment.
Hydraulic horsepower per square inch of bit area, a measure of bit cleaning.
Horizontal transverse isotropy: rock whose properties vary with horizontal direction, often caused by vertical fractures.
A relation that estimates interfacial tension from the solubilization ratio.
The screens operators use to monitor and control a process. Abbreviated HMI.
Gently curved layers formed by storm waves on the shelf.
A bit combining roller cones and PDC blades.
A treatment combining slickwater and crosslinked gel stages.
A material that swells with water to plug loss zones.
A chemical such as methanol or glycol that prevents gas hydrates.
Calcium hydroxide, used in lime mud and to treat carbonate contamination.
Uptake of water by clay or other materials, causing swelling.
k/(φμct): how fast pressure spreads through a reservoir.
A tool released by pressure or a dropped ball to leave a stuck BHA behind.
Pumping fluid into a well above the rock's breakdown pressure to create a fracture, then propping it open with proppant to give the reservoir a high-conductivity flow path.
The power delivered by the mud stream. At the bit it is often quoted per square inch of hole area.
A jar that delays its blow with hydraulic fluid, letting the operator build load.
A downhole pump driven by power fluid pumped from surface.
Workover using a hydraulic unit rather than a conventional rig.
A compact rig that uses hydraulic jacks to run and pull pipe, with or without pressure in the well.
A packer set by applying pressure inside the tubing, useful in deviated wells.
A compound made only of hydrogen and carbon. Crude oil and natural gas are mixtures made mainly of hydrocarbons.
The volume and timing of oil and gas supplied to a trap.
The vertical height of a hydrocarbon accumulation, from its top to the deepest fluid contact.
Removing heavier hydrocarbons from gas so liquids won't drop out in the pipeline.
Injecting produced or rich hydrocarbon gas to keep up pressure or achieve miscible displacement.
Porosity times hydrocarbon saturation times thickness, summed over a zone.
The pore volume filled with hydrocarbons: rock volume × net-to-gross × porosity × hydrocarbon saturation. Abbreviated HCPV.
A large region with many related oil and gas fields.
The fraction of pore volume filled with oil or gas, equal to 1 − S<sub>w</sub>.
HCl, the main acid for stimulating carbonates and removing carbonate scale.
Cracking heavy oil with hydrogen and a catalyst to make lighter products.
A cone-shaped separator that uses swirling flow to separate fluids or solids by density, used for produced water and mud solids.
A trap where flowing water holds hydrocarbons in place, often with a tilted contact.
HF, an acid that dissolves silica and clays, used with HCl in sandstone treatments.
Loss of steel toughness when hydrogen atoms enter the metal.
The amount of hydrogen in a material compared with fresh water. It controls how neutron and NMR tools respond.
H<sub>2</sub>S, a toxic, flammable, corrosive gas found in sour oil and gas. It smells of rotten eggs at low levels but deadens the sense of smell at higher ones.
A chemical, usually zinc-based, that reacts with hydrogen sulfide in the mud to form a harmless solid.
Attracted to water. Hydrophilic solids are water-wet.
A scale of how water-loving or oil-loving a surfactant is. Abbreviated HLB.
Repelled by water. Hydrophobic, or oil-wet, surfaces prefer oil.
A sensor that records pressure changes in water, used in marine seismic streamers and some borehole surveys.
A sealed bailer that sucks up debris when its seal is broken at bottom.
A packer that sets using the pressure of the fluid column.
Pressure testing pipe or equipment with water.
Dolomite formed by hot fluids moving up faults.
A non-ionic cellulose polymer (HEC) used as a clean viscosifier in brines and completion fluids.
A modified guar used to thicken water-base fluids.
A starch derivative for fluid-loss control in drill-in fluids and brines.
Decline whose rate slows over time, q = q<sub>i</sub>/(1 + bD<sub>i</sub>t)<sup>1/b</sup>, with 0 < b < 1 for conventional wells.
Reflection time increasing with offset along a hyperbola.
A standard code that describes a bit by type, intended formation hardness and design features.
A group of trace fossils typical of a particular environment.
A method of choosing bridging particle sizes so they pack to seal pores of a range of sizes.
Rock formed by cooling of molten magma, such as granite and basalt.
International Geomagnetic Reference Field: the standard model of the earth's main magnetic field.
A non-swelling, often hair-like clay mineral that can sharply reduce the permeability of sandstones.
An iron-titanium oxide weighting material, denser than barite.
A log that shows a picture of the borehole wall from resistivity or acoustic data.
An imaginary well used to model a boundary's effect on pressure.
Turning recorded seismic data into a picture of the subsurface, mainly through migration.
A capillary pressure curve as a wetting phase displaces a non-wetting phase.
A series of thrust faults that branch from one detachment and overlap like roof tiles.
Displacing oil with a fluid that does not mix with it, such as water.
Injecting gas that does not mix with the oil, mainly to maintain pressure and displace oil.
The force of the mud jets striking the hole bottom, one criterion for optimizing bit hydraulics.
The difference in acoustic impedance across a boundary, which controls reflection strength.
A bit with diamond grit throughout its matrix, used in very hard rock.
A tool with a soft face run onto a fish to take an imprint of its shape.
Any method that increases recovery beyond what a reservoir would give on its own, including waterflooding, infill drilling and EOR. Abbreviated IOR.
Calibrating spinner response from passes at different speeds in the well itself.
Burning part of the oil in the reservoir by injecting air. The heat and gases from the combustion front drive the remaining oil to producers. Also called fireflooding.
Surfactant formed when alkali reacts with acids in crude oil.
The natural stresses in the rock before drilling: vertical stress and the two horizontal stresses.
The part of the pore space too small for large polymer molecules to enter, which makes polymer travel slightly faster than water.
The angle between a seismic ray and the normal to the reflector.
A valley cut by a river during a fall in sea level and later filled, often with sand.
The angle between the wellbore and vertical, in degrees.
The extra oil produced by a project beyond what would have come from the existing operation.
Extra oil recovered by a project beyond what would be produced without it.
A fossil of a species that lived for a short time over a wide area, so it pins rock age.
A heater in which a bath heats the well fluid coil, used to prevent hydrates.
An empirical saturation equation for shaly sands with fresh formation water.
A fracture created in the formation by mud pressure exceeding its breakdown pressure, usually causing losses.
Water treatment in which gas bubbles attach to oil droplets and carry them to the surface for skimming. Abbreviated IGF.
Magnetism a rock has because of the present earth field.
A method that measures how the ground stores electric charge, useful for minerals and clays.
Earthquakes caused by human activity such as injection or production.
A resistivity log that induces currents in the formation with coils. It works best in fresh or oil-base mud and resistive formations.
Networks of connected sensors and devices on industrial equipment that share data automatically. Abbreviated IIoT.
Measuring gamma rays from fast neutron collisions to find elements such as carbon.
Solids that don't react with water, such as sand and barite.
Extra lines acquired to fill gaps in coverage.
Drilling extra wells between existing ones to reach bypassed oil and speed up production.
The period when pressure changes linearly with the logarithm of time because no boundary has yet been felt. It is used to find permeability-thickness.
A fracture with no pressure drop along it.
A packer with an element that is filled with fluid to seal, able to set in larger holes.
A nozzle or channel in a screen joint that restricts flow so a long horizontal well produces evenly along its length. Abbreviated ICD.
The rate contributed by each zone at different drawdowns.
The relationship between flowing bottomhole pressure and the rate the reservoir delivers into the well. Abbreviated IPR.
The rate contributed by each perforated or open zone.
Reducing pressure above a barrier to check that nothing leaks in through it.
Preventing shale from hydrating and swelling.
A brine such as potassium chloride or formate that limits clay swelling.
A mud designed to limit the reaction between its water and the shale being drilled, for example a KCl-polymer or glycol system.
Pumping inhibitor into the formation so it returns slowly with production.
The first shut-in period of a drillstem test, used to measure initial reservoir pressure.
A test that measures pressure decline after injection into a well stops.
Running production logging tools in an injection well.
The layout of injection and production wells, such as five-spot or line drive.
The pressure at which fluid is injected.
How injected water or gas is distributed among the open zones of an injection well.
Changing where injected fluid enters a well, for example with gels.
The volume of fluid injected per day.
An injection well's rate per unit of pressure above reservoir pressure, the injector's equivalent of productivity index.
Injecting fluid into a well to measure how easily the formation takes it.
A vertical section in a 3D survey running in the direction the data was acquired. The perpendicular direction is the crossline.
Running smart pigs through a pipeline to measure wall loss, cracks and dents. Abbreviated ILI.
A small, fixed-blade spinner used at higher flow rates.
Cementing large casing through drillpipe stung into the float shoe.
A valve installed in the drillstring to stop upward flow. Abbreviated IBOP.
The strength of the seismic signal at each time sample regardless of phase, computed with the Hilbert transform. Also called the envelope or reflection strength.
The rate of change of instantaneous phase at each sample. Abrupt drops can indicate gas or fractures.
