The phase angle at each sample of a trace, independent of amplitude. It helps trace weak reflectors and terminations.
The pressure right after pumping stops in a fracture treatment, with friction removed. Abbreviated ISIP.
The way a recording system changes the amplitude and phase of a signal.
Tubing designed to reduce heat loss from steam to the surroundings.
A linked model of reservoir, wells and facilities used to optimize the whole system.
A completion with permanent downhole sensors and remotely operated valves that allow zones to be monitored and controlled without intervention.
A multiple that bounces between layers below the surface.
A volume of AVO intercept values.
Pore space between crystals, as in dolomite.
The energy per unit area at the boundary between two immiscible fluids, such as oil and water. Abbreviated IFT.
Measuring tension between oil and water, often with a spinning drop tensiometer.
A test that changes the rate in one well and measures the pressure response in another, to check connectivity between them.
Casing set between surface and production casing to isolate troublesome zones such as lost-circulation or high-pressure intervals.
A synthetic hydrocarbon used as the base of many synthetic-base muds, with low toxicity and good low-temperature properties.
The discount rate at which a project's net present value equals zero. Abbreviated IRR.
Networks of connected sensors and devices that share data. Abbreviated IoT.
In a dual-porosity model, how easily fluid moves from the matrix into the fractures. Written λ.
Two faults meeting at an angle, which form a wedge-shaped drainage area.
A downhole valve operated from surface that controls flow from one zone. Abbreviated ICV.
The average seismic velocity within one layer between two reflectors.
Injecting a tracer in one well and monitoring its arrival in others to map flow paths and sweep.
A fragment of partly hardened sediment reworked within the same basin.
A broad, slowly subsiding basin in the interior of a continent.
Energy loss to heat as waves pass through rock.
The region around the borehole where mud filtrate has pushed out some or all of the original formation fluids.
Using several resistivity depths to estimate Rt and the invasion diameter.
How the resistivity changes from the borehole into the undisturbed formation.
Later compression that reverses an old basin, pushing former lows up into structures.
An emulsion of water droplets dispersed in a continuous oil phase. It is the structure of oil-base and synthetic-base muds.
Oil-base or synthetic-base mud with water droplets dispersed in oil.
A basin that was later squeezed so its center rose.
A pattern with the injector in the center and producers around it.
Time lost to slow performance within normal operations, compared with best practice.
An atom or group of atoms with an electric charge.
A measure of the total concentration of ions in a solution.
A connected sensor that sends data over a network.
An additive that keeps dissolved iron from precipitating as acid is spent.
A specially treated iron oxide that reacts with hydrogen sulfide in mud.
A machine that makes up and breaks out pipe connections on the rig floor.
The lowest water saturation a rock can reach under normal displacement; this water is held by capillary forces and will not flow. Written S<sub>wirr</sub>.
A map of time thickness between two seismic horizons.
A gas-well deliverability test with flow periods of equal length, each starting from shut-in, which suits slow-to-stabilize, low-permeability wells.
Taking a sample from a flowing stream at the same velocity as the stream, so the sample represents the flow.
A packer that separates two zones.
A thickness map computed between two seismic horizons.
A contour map showing the thickness of a rock unit.
The balance of the crust floating on the denser mantle.
A small container used to collect mud gas samples for isotope analysis.
A dimensionless form of capillary pressure that lets data from different rocks be compared.
A mobile offshore rig with legs that are lowered to the seabed to raise the hull above the waves. Used in shallow water.
A tool in the drillstring that stores energy and releases it as a sharp blow to free stuck pipe.
The fast stream of metal formed when a shaped charge fires.
A tool that uses a circular shaped charge to cut tubing or casing downhole.
A downhole pump with no moving parts that uses a high-velocity power fluid passing through a nozzle to lift well fluids.
The speed of mud leaving the bit nozzles, which cleans the cutters and hole bottom.
A coiled tubing end tool with high-pressure jets for cleanouts and scale removal.
A tool with nozzles that cleans tubing or perforations with fluid jets.
A natural fracture along which there has been no visible movement.
The contract among partners in a license that sets out how operations are run, costs shared and decisions made. Abbreviated JOA.
Cooling of gas as it expands into the wellbore, which marks gas entries on temperature logs.
Temperature change of a gas or liquid as it expands through a restriction.
A valve that cools gas by letting it expand through a pressure drop, used to condense liquids.
A sealed friction bearing in a roller cone bit.
A tool that catches small debris, such as metal pieces, in the well.
A mill with a flat, hard-faced bottom used to grind up debris in the hole.
The channel between blades of a PDC bit that carries cuttings away.
The geologic period from about 201 to 145 million years ago, with major reservoirs such as in the North Sea.
What rock lies against what across a fault, which decides whether reservoirs connect or seal.
A non-swelling clay mineral whose loose platelets can migrate and plug pore throats (fines migration).
A precise lab method for measuring very small water contents in oil.
Landscape and cave systems formed by dissolution of limestone. Buried karst can make highly porous reservoirs.
A square or hexagonal pipe turned by the rotary table to rotate the drillstring on older rigs.
On many rigs, the reference point on the rig floor from which depths are measured. Abbreviated KB.
A valve on the kelly that can close to stop flow up the drillstring.
Solid organic matter in sedimentary rock that does not dissolve in ordinary solvents. It breaks down to oil and gas when heated during burial.
Breakdown of kerogen into hydrocarbons by heat.
A classification of organic matter: Type I (lacustrine algae, oil-prone), Type II (marine, oil-prone), Type III (land plants, gas-prone) and Type IV (inert).
A slot worn into the side of a dogleg by the drillpipe, which can trap larger tools.
A 2D fracture model (Khristianovich-Geertsma-de Klerk) for short fractures with width set by the length.
An unplanned flow of formation fluid into the wellbore, which happens when pressure in the well drops below formation pressure. If not controlled it can become a blowout.
Methods for spotting an influx early: pit volume, flow out, pump pressure, gas and drilling breaks.
The largest influx that can be shut in and circulated out without fracturing the weakest exposed formation.
A hard cement plug set to start a sidetrack.
The depth at which a planned well starts to deviate from vertical. Abbreviated KOP.
A slickline tool that deflects into the pocket of a side-pocket mandrel to set or pull gas-lift valves.
Fluid dense enough to balance formation pressure, used to kill a well before work.
A high-pressure line connected below the closed BOP rams for pumping fluid into the well.
Mud weighted to the density needed to balance formation pressure and stop an influx during well control.
The pump pressure at the slow circulating rate.
A small pipe left in a well to pump kill fluid.
Fill the well with fluid dense enough to stop formation fluids flowing, so work can be done safely.
Fluid heavy enough to balance formation pressure and stop a well flowing.
Viscosity divided by density, often in centistokes.
A migration method that sums energy along diffraction curves, widely used for its flexibility.
Gas permeability measured in the laboratory reads higher than liquid permeability because gas molecules slip along pore walls. The correction gives the equivalent liquid permeability.
A vessel that separates liquid droplets from a gas stream, for example upstream of a compressor or flare.
A flexible joint in a tool string that lets pads follow the hole wall.
A factor that describes how heterogeneity and viscosity cause fingering in miscible floods.
A geostatistical interpolation method that uses the variogram to give the best linear unbiased estimate between data points.
Lease automatic custody transfer equipment that measures, samples and checks the quality of oil as it is sold into a pipeline.
Formed in or relating to lakes. Lake shales can be rich source rocks.
The time for cuttings or gas to travel from the bit to the surface, used to assign samples to the right depth.
The depth from which a cuttings sample came, after correcting for lag time.
A shallow body of water protected from the open sea by a barrier or reef, where fine sediment accumulates.
An approach that converts impedances into λρ (incompressibility) and μρ (rigidity) to separate fluids and lithology.
Lamé's lambda times density, an incompressibility attribute sensitive to fluids.
Smooth flow in parallel layers, typical in the annulus at normal rates and gentle on the borehole wall.
Thin sand layers between shale layers, which make logs average the two and underestimate pay.
Shale with fine layers, often organic-rich.
Very thin layering in sedimentary rock, less than 1 cm thick.
Two elastic constants, lambda and mu, that describe an isotropic material.
Spreading oily cuttings on land so soil microbes break down the oil.
Recording seismic on land with geophones or nodes and sources such as vibrators or dynamite.
A collar inside casing where wiper plugs land.
A short tubing section with a machined internal profile where plugs, valves or gauges can be locked in place.
Pipe used to run and land a completion or tubing hanger.
A curve describing how much gas is adsorbed on a surface at each pressure. It is used to estimate adsorbed gas in shale and coal.
The pressure at which half the Langmuir volume of gas is adsorbed. Written P<sub>L</sub>.
An AI model trained on large amounts of text that can read, summarize and generate language, used for searching reports and documents.
The frequency at which protons spin in a magnetic field, used to tune NMR tools.
Log ASCII Standard: a simple text format for well log data.
The temperature at which the last crystals disappear in a warming brine. Abbreviated LCTD.
The last part of a test, when boundaries affect the pressure.
The horizontal section of a horizontal well that lies in the target zone.
The length of the horizontal section of a well.
Getting tools into a chosen branch of a multilateral well.
The smallest horizontal distance between features that seismic can separate. Migration improves it toward a quarter wavelength.
A resistivity log that focuses current into the formation with guard electrodes. It works best in salty mud and resistive formations.
A gravity correction for the change of gravity with latitude.
In undisturbed layers, older rocks lie below younger ones.
A depth conversion model built from flat-lying velocity layers.
The concentration of a substance that kills half the test organisms in a set time, used to rate the toxicity of mud and additives.
A sub or valve that lets coarse LCM bypass downhole tools.
A possible trap that needs more data before it can be called a prospect.
A slickline tool with a soft lead face that takes an imprint of the top of a fish or obstruction.
The first, usually lighter, slurry pumped in a cement job.
The cable between the vessel and the first active section of a streamer.
Finding where fluid enters or leaves the well through holes or bad seals.
The point on a leak-off test where pressure stops rising linearly with volume.
A test that pressures the open hole just below the casing shoe until the formation starts taking fluid. It gives the fracture gradient and the maximum safe mud weight.
Loss of fracturing or drilling fluid from a fracture or wellbore into the surrounding rock.
Natural gas with few heavier hydrocarbons, mostly methane.
A legal agreement granting rights to explore for and produce oil and gas from a defined area. The term is also used for the area itself.
An iterative migration that corrects for uneven illumination and gives more balanced amplitudes.
A natural phospholipid used as an oil-wetting agent and emulsifier.
A step in the hole wall, often at a hard bed, that hangs up pipe.
Mud with isolated lenses of sand, typical of tidal flats.
A raised ridge of sediment along a channel bank, deposited when floods overtop the channel.
A device that keeps liquid level in a vessel by opening or closing a dump valve.
A dimensionless form of capillary pressure that lets curves from rocks of different permeability and porosity be compared and averaged.
Gas released from cuttings as they are ground up by the bit.
The pressure needed to lift filter cake off the formation when flow starts.
The operating cost of producing one barrel of oil or one barrel of oil equivalent.
A low-density brine such as sodium or potassium chloride.
The less dense fluid in multiphase flow, such as oil or gas.
Intervention from a vessel without a riser, such as wireline work on subsea wells.
A cement slurry made lighter with extenders, foam or beads to avoid losses.
A soft coal ground and treated with caustic soda, used as a thinner and fluid-loss additive in water-base mud.
A thinner made from wood-pulp by-products that lowers the viscosity and gel strength of water-base mud.
Calcium hydroxide, used to raise alkalinity, to treat carbon dioxide and as a key ingredient of invert-emulsion muds.
The amount of excess lime in an oil-base or lime mud.
A calcium-treated water-base mud using lime, which inhibits shale and resists contamination.
A carbonate rock made mostly of calcite, often from shells, skeletons and lime mud.
Neutron porosity calibrated as if the rock were limestone.
Using few perforations so friction forces fluid to split between several clusters.
Using deliberately few perforations so the pressure drop across them spreads fracturing fluid over several zones or clusters.
A flood pattern in which rows of injectors alternate with rows of producers.
A rubber that wipes fluid off wireline as it comes out of the well.
The solution for pressure around a well modeled as a line in an infinite reservoir.
A straight-chain olefin used as a synthetic base fluid.
A reservoir model with a property change across a straight boundary.
A flow regime in which streamlines are parallel, as toward a fracture. The derivative has a half slope on a log-log plot.
A fracturing fluid of water thickened with uncrosslinked polymer, more viscous than slickwater.
A shale shaker whose screens move back and forth in a straight line, which conveys cuttings well with fine screens.
Time shift that increases linearly with offset, as for direct and refracted waves.
Noise with straight-line moveout, such as ground roll and guided waves.
A straight-chain paraffin used as a synthetic base fluid.
An instrument that measures how much a compressed shale sample swells in contact with a fluid over time.
A string of casing that does not reach surface. It is hung from near the bottom of the previous casing string.
Cementing a liner through the drillpipe and liner running tool.
A completion with a liner across the reservoir, either cemented and perforated or slotted.
Drilling with a liner as the drillstring.
The tool that grips the previous casing and supports a liner's weight.
A packer at the top of a liner that seals the overlap between liner and casing.
Water sprayed on pump liners to cool and lubricate the pistons.
Natural gas cooled to about −162 °C so it becomes a liquid that can be shipped. Abbreviated LNG.
Propane and butane stored and sold as a liquid under moderate pressure. Abbreviated LPG.
Liquid building up in a gas well when the gas velocity is too low to carry it to surface. The backpressure reduces flow and can kill the well.
A shore-based facility that mixes, stores and recycles drilling and completion fluids for offshore rigs.
A shale play whose gas contains significant condensate or natural gas liquids, which improves its economics.
A curved normal fault that flattens with depth.
A sandstone rich in rock fragments.
Turning loose sediment into rock by compaction and cementation.
A density tool that also measures the photoelectric factor, giving both porosity and lithology.
The physical character of a rock: its mineral composition, grain size and texture.
The rock type track on a mud log, made from cuttings.
A log used to identify rock type, such as gamma ray, photoelectric factor or spectroscopy.
Estimating rock type from seismic properties.
Dividing rock layers by their physical type.
Oil that still contains dissolved gas at reservoir or separator pressure.
Working in a well that is under pressure, using pressure control equipment.
A bulge on the base of a sand bed where it sank into soft mud.
The part of a wireline device that latches into a landing nipple to hold it in place.
The point where friction stops coiled tubing from going deeper, no matter how hard it is pushed.
Interpreting well logs to find porosity, saturation, lithology and pay.
Programs used to load, correct, crossplot and interpret well logs.
Simplifying logs into layers of constant value.
Removing spikes and bad data from logs.
The block at the top of a log print with the well, tool and mud details.
Using well logs to identify lithology, porosity, fluids and pay.
The logarithmic average of the T2 distribution.
The shape of a log curve, such as bell or funnel, used to interpret environments.
Adjusting logs from many wells so they read consistently.
Checking logs for calibration, repeatability and correct depth before interpretation.
The thinnest bed a log can measure correctly.
Joining logs from different runs into one continuous curve.
The set of logs run in a well.
A column on a log print showing one or more curves.
Permeability estimated from logs using a correlation.
Logging, injecting a fluid with a different capture cross section, and logging again to measure residual oil.
A plot with logarithmic scales on both axes, used for diagnostic plots and type curves.
The service company that runs logging tools.
The engineer who runs logging operations and checks data quality at the wellsite.
A part of a tool pressed against the borehole wall to measure close to the formation.
The list of logs to run in each hole section.
How fast a tool is pulled up the well, which affects data quality.
Running small logging tools through the bit after drilling.
Measuring formation properties with sensors built into the drillstring while the hole is being drilled. Abbreviated LWD.
A multiple that arrives well after its primary and looks like a separate reflection.
The far detector on a density or neutron tool, reading deeper into the formation.
A sonic tool with long spacing that reads beyond altered rock near the wellbore.
LWD resistivity that senses formations ahead of the bit.
A number from 0 to 1 describing how unevenly flow capacity is spread among layers. Zero means a perfectly uniform reservoir.
A concentrated batch of lost circulation material pumped to the loss zone.
A formation interval where mud is being lost.
Loss of whole mud into the formation through natural or induced fractures, caverns or very permeable zones. Severe losses can drop the fluid level and cause a kick.
Fibrous, flaky or granular material, such as nut shells, mica or graded carbonate, added to mud to plug the paths through which it is being lost. Abbreviated LCM.
A surface wave with horizontal side-to-side particle motion.
A filter that removes frequencies below a set value.
A gun designed to keep debris inside the carrier.
The 6- and 3-rpm viscometer readings, which indicate hole cleaning and suspension in slow-moving parts of the annulus.
A smooth background model of impedance, usually from well logs, added to seismic inversion to supply missing low frequencies.
Drilled solids and clays with a specific gravity of about 2.6, as distinct from heavy weighting materials. Too much of them slows drilling.
A mud designed to seal pores almost instantly so very little filtrate enters the formation.
Hydrocarbon-bearing rock that reads low resistivity because of clay, fine grains, conductive minerals or laminations, and is easily missed.
The extra oil released when injected water has lower salinity than formation water.
Injecting water with lower salinity than the formation water, which can change wettability and release extra oil in some reservoirs.
Yield stress estimated from the 3- and 6-rpm readings, a guide to hole cleaning. Abbreviated LSYP.
Viscosity measured at very low shear rates, such as with a Brookfield viscometer, which shows how well mud suspends cuttings at rest. Abbreviated LSRV.
A mud kept low in clays and drilled solids to drill faster, usually with polymers for viscosity.
Oxygen reacting with oil at low temperature, forming oxygenated products instead of burning.
A refined mineral oil with low aromatics used as base oil.
The part of a completion across the reservoir, such as screens, perforations, sleeves or a gravel pack.
Deposits formed when relative sea level is low, often including deepwater fans with good reservoirs.
An additive that reduces friction between pipe and hole.
A well-control method that pumps small volumes of heavy fluid in and bleeds gas off in turns to replace gas with liquid.
A pressure-rated pipe assembly mounted on the wellhead that lets wireline or slickline tools enter a live well.
The friction coefficient measured by a lubricity tester.
A lab device that measures the coefficient of friction of a mud between steel surfaces.
A carbonate classification based on grain size, sorting and pore types, used for permeability.
Acoustic measurement while drilling.
The cementation exponent in Archie's law, usually near 2.
A crossplot of lithology numbers M and N, computed from sonic, density and neutron logs, used to identify mixed minerals.
Maximum allowable annular surface pressure: the highest surface pressure the annulus can take before the weakest formation, usually at the shoe, fractures.
Algorithms that learn patterns from data, used for example to predict equipment failure or estimate properties from logs.
A brine made with magnesium chloride, sometimes used when drilling magnesium-rich salts.
Magnesium from seawater or formation brines that consumes alkalinity and can flocculate water-base mud.
Added to some polymer muds and brines as a pH buffer and to improve temperature stability of polymers.
A fishing tool that picks up small iron pieces.
A local departure from the expected magnetic field, caused by rocks with different magnetic properties.
The angle between true north and magnetic north at a location.
Distortion of magnetic surveys by nearby casing or magnetized steel.
Measuring variations in the Earth's magnetic field, usually from aircraft, to map basement depth and large structures.
How strongly a material becomes magnetized in a magnetic field.
An instrument that measures the strength of the magnetic field.
Dating and correlating rocks using reversals of the earth's magnetic field.
A survey that uses natural electromagnetic fields to map resistivity at depth. Abbreviated MT.
A method that uses natural electromagnetic fields to map electrical resistivity deep in the earth.
The longest flow period of a test, used for analysis.
The torque used to tighten a connection.
The water used to build new mud or replace water lost from the system.
A deepwater gas-condensate field offshore northwest Palawan, Philippines, a major source of the country's natural gas for power.
Drilling with a closed, pressurized mud system and adjustable surface backpressure to hold bottomhole pressure in a narrow window. Abbreviated MPD.
A very fine, acid-soluble weighting material used where barite would damage the reservoir or sag.
A method of showing the curved earth on a flat map, such as UTM.
A metamorphic rock formed from limestone or dolostone.
The extra pull available above the hook load before the pipe's tensile limit.
A person who watches for marine mammals and halts shooting when they come close.
The large pipe that connects a floating rig to the subsea blowout preventer and returns mud to the rig.
Recording seismic at sea with towed streamers or seabed sensors and air-gun sources.
A distinctive, widespread layer that is easy to recognize and correlate between wells.
A mixed rock of clay and carbonate.
A cone-shaped funnel for a quick rig-site viscosity check. The result is the number of seconds one quart of mud takes to drain.
Sediment moved downslope as a slide, slump or debris flow.
A portable derrick that is raised as one unit, common on land rigs.
The main shutoff valve on the Christmas tree, directly above the tubing head. Many trees have an upper and a lower one.
Applying conservation of mass to a reservoir: produced fluids are balanced against fluid expansion and influx to estimate volumes in place and the drive mechanism.
Cumulative production divided by rate, used to analyze variable-rate data.
A document describing the hazards and safe handling of a chemical. Abbreviated MSDS or SDS.
The solid framework of a rock, excluding pores.
Acid injection below fracture pressure so the acid flows through the pores and removes damage close to the wellbore.
The density of the solid grains, used to calculate porosity: about 2.65 g/cm³ for sandstone, 2.71 for limestone and 2.87 for dolomite.
A well-explored basin with many fields.
Maximum allowable wellhead operating pressure for an annulus.
The surface marking the farthest landward reach of the sea during a transgression. It is often a widespread shale that is easy to correlate.
The largest source-receiver distance recorded, which limits the angles available.
The Matthews-Brons-Hazebroek method that converts p* to average reservoir pressure.
One thousand standard cubic feet of gas; MMcf is one million and Bcf one billion.
Miller-Dyes-Hutchinson plot: buildup pressure against log of shut-in time, used when the producing time was long.
A river with a single winding channel that migrates across its floodplain.
The length of the well measured along its actual path. Abbreviated MD.
Downhole sensors that measure inclination, azimuth and drilling data and send them to surface while drilling, usually by mud-pulse telemetry. Abbreviated MWD.
A wheel device that measures how much wire has gone into the well.
Porosity loss from grains rearranging and packing tighter under load.
A cutter with blades that cut pipe as it rotates.
Breaking of polymer chains by high shear in chokes, pumps or perforations.
Skin from formation damage or stimulation, excluding geometry effects.
The energy used to remove a unit volume of rock, used to judge drilling efficiency. Abbreviated MSE.
Whether the hole stays open given stresses, rock strength and mud weight.
Using plugs, packers or patches to stop water production.
A packer set by rotating or moving the tubing up and down.
A filter that takes the middle value in a window, used to remove spikes and separate wavefields.
A named subdivision of a formation.
How well shale acts as a membrane that lets water through but holds back ions.
Nitrogen made on site by passing air through membranes that remove oxygen.
A gauge that records data downhole for retrieval later.
Production logging with data stored in the tool and read later.
A logging tool that stores its data in internal memory instead of sending it to surface. It can be run on slickline or coiled tubing.
A small digital accelerometer used as a seismic receiver.
A sulfur compound with a strong smell found in some crudes and gases.
A lab test that forces mercury into a rock sample at rising pressure to measure its pore-throat size distribution. Abbreviated MICP.
The number of openings per linear inch of a screen. Higher mesh means finer openings.
Diagenesis during deep burial.
The geologic era from about 252 to 66 million years ago.
The high-temperature stage after catagenesis, when only dry gas forms.
A friction reducer pumped in coiled tubing jobs to extend reach.
Rock changed by heat and pressure, such as slate, schist and marble.
Changes to sediment caused by fresh rainwater.
A correction number applied to a meter's reading, found by proving it against a known volume.
Checking a flowmeter's accuracy against a calibrated volume to determine its meter factor.
Measuring the quantity of oil, gas or water that flows, for well allocation, reservoir management or sales.
A packaged set of meters and provers for measuring flow.
Measuring methane leaks with sensors, cameras or satellites.
Injecting methanol into a well or pipeline to lower the hydrate formation temperature.
Modeling boundaries with image wells and superposition.
The pH 4.3 endpoint used to measure Mf alkalinity.
A titration that measures how much reactive clay a mud contains, reported as pounds per barrel of bentonite equivalent. Abbreviated MBT.
The filtrate methyl orange alkalinity: total acid needed to bring the filtrate to pH 4.3. Pf and Mf together show carbonate problems.
A flaky mineral used as a lost circulation material.
Microcrystalline carbonate mud, the fine matrix of many limestones.
A very thin gap between the casing and the cement, often caused by pressure or temperature changes.
Using microorganisms or their products, such as biosurfactants and gases, to help release oil from the rock. Abbreviated MEOR.
Using microbes or their products to help recover oil.
A thermodynamically stable mixture of oil, water and surfactant with extremely low interfacial tension, the target state in surfactant flooding.
A focused pad resistivity log that reads the flushed zone.
A pad log with two shallow resistivity curves whose separation shows mudcake over permeable beds.
Barite ground extremely fine so it sags less and gives lower viscosity in heavy muds.
A pad tool that reads resistivity in the first few inches from the borehole wall, used to estimate R<sub>xo</sub> and see thin beds.
Recording the tiny earthquakes caused by hydraulic fracturing to map where the fractures are growing.
An undersea mountain chain where plates move apart and new crust forms.
A microemulsion that coexists with excess oil and water, where interfacial tension is lowest.
The part of a test showing radial flow, used to find permeability.
Transporting, storing and processing oil and gas between the field and the refinery or market, for example by pipeline, ship or gas plant.
The movement of oil and gas out of the source rock (primary migration) and through carrier beds toward a trap (secondary migration).
The width of data used to migrate each point. Too narrow and steep dips are lost.
A false feature, such as a smile, created by migration.
The route hydrocarbons take from source to trap.
A curved artifact made when migration spreads noise or a spike.
The velocity field used to migrate seismic data.
Cycles in earth's orbit and tilt that change climate and can leave cycles in sediment.
A downhole tool with hard cutting surfaces that grinds metal.
A roller cone bit with teeth cut from the cone steel, for soft rock.
A unit of gravity acceleration, one thousandth of a gal (1 cm/s²).
Grinding away metal downhole, such as a stuck fish, packer or casing section, with a mill.
The set of minerals and fluids assumed in a multimineral log analysis.
A refined, low-aromatic oil used as a less toxic base for oil-base mud than diesel.
A short test using a wireline formation tester with packers to flow a small zone.
A sediment-filled basin that sinks into underlying salt.
A small injection test before the main fracture job, used to measure closure pressure, leakoff and fluid efficiency. Also called a data frac.
The standard method of calculating a well's trajectory between survey stations by fitting a smooth arc.
The smallest horizontal compressive stress in the rock. Fractures open against it and grow perpendicular to it.
The least amount of intermediate gases needed to make a gas miscible with an oil.
The lowest pressure at which an injected gas becomes miscible with a given reservoir oil. Abbreviated MMP.
A wavelet with its energy concentrated as early as possible, typical of explosive and air-gun sources.
The geologic epoch from about 23 to 5 million years ago, host to many deltaic and deepwater reservoirs.
A mismatch in time or amplitude where two seismic lines or surveys cross.
The ability of two fluids to mix in all proportions without forming an interface.
Displacing oil with a fluid that mixes with it completely, leaving very little behind.
Injecting a gas or solvent that mixes completely with the reservoir oil, removing the interface between them so very little oil is left behind where the flood reaches.
A charge or gun that fails to fire.
Air drilling with a small amount of water and foamer added to handle water inflow.
A flow regime with liquid carried as droplets in continuous gas.
The water used to mix a cement slurry.
A positively charged additive that gives bentonite mud very high low-shear viscosity. Abbreviated MMH.
A funnel and jet used to add dry materials to mud.
A centrifugal pump used to circulate mud through the hopper.
The transition zone where solvent and oil mix behind the front.
The total flow rate divided by pipe area.
Permeability divided by viscosity, a measure of how easily fluid flows.
The ratio of mobilities between two zones of a composite reservoir.
The mobility of the displacing fluid divided by the mobility of the displaced oil, where mobility is relative permeability divided by viscosity. A value above 1 is unfavorable and leads to fingering.
How much foam or polymer lowers the mobility of the injected fluid.
One of many equally probable versions of a stochastic reservoir model.
Inversion that updates a starting impedance model until its synthetic matches the seismic.
An isochronal test with shut-ins equal to the flow periods, which saves time.
Starch treated chemically to resist temperature and bacteria better.
Pores left where grains or shells dissolved, keeping their shape.
The mass of a molecule. In mud polymers it largely controls viscosity.
A magnitude scale based on the seismic moment of an event.
A repeat survey compared against the baseline.
The derrickman's platform high in the derrick, used to rack pipe during trips.
A completion with nearly the same internal diameter from the reservoir to surface, which simplifies interventions.
A fold with a single step-like bend in otherwise flat or gently dipping layers.
A glycol (MEG) injected into gas pipelines to prevent hydrates, then recovered and regenerated.
A sonic source that sends waves equally in all directions.
An ion with a charge of one, such as sodium or potassium.
Running log analysis many times with varying inputs to estimate uncertainty.
Sampling uncertain inputs at random many times to build a probability distribution of the result, such as oil in place.
An opening in a floating rig's hull through which the riser and equipment pass.
A coiled tubing assembly with a downhole motor driving a mill.
Reflections forming a hump, as over reefs or fans.
A hole in the rig floor where the next joint is held ready for a connection.
A sand bar deposited where a distributary channel enters the sea or a lake.
Sw divided by Sxo. Values near one mean the hydrocarbons did not move.
Micro-spherically focused log: a pad tool that measures flushed-zone resistivity.
Shear modulus times density, a rigidity attribute from LMR analysis.
A mixture of hydrochloric and hydrofluoric acids used to dissolve clays and fines in sandstone.
A material added to mud to adjust its properties.
A simple beam balance with a fixed-volume cup, used at the rig to measure mud density.
Checking a mud balance with fresh water to read 8.33 ppg.
The layer of solids left on the borehole wall as mud filtrate enters the formation.
Drilling with total losses by pumping a heavy mud cap into the annulus and sacrificial fluid down the drillpipe, used in fractured carbonates.
A routine set of tests on the mud: density, viscosity, fluid loss, solids, pH, chlorides and more.
An older name for the mud engineer.
A desilter mounted over a fine vibrating screen. It removes drilled solids while returning barite to the mud.
A service company that supplies drilling fluid products and engineers.
Circulating and treating mud to bring its properties back into specification.
Any unwanted material in the mud, such as cement, salt, gas, carbonates or drilled solids, that changes its properties.
A heat exchanger that lowers mud temperature in hot wells to protect electronics and elastomers.
The cost of drilling fluid for a well, often tracked daily.
Polygonal cracks in mud that dried out, a sign of exposure.
Mass of mud per unit volume, also called mud weight.
Adding base fluid or new mud to reduce the concentration of drilled solids or contaminants.
The specialist at the rig who tests the drilling fluid, keeps records and prescribes treatments.
The resistivity of the mud filtrate, written R<sub>mf</sub>, needed to interpret SP and flushed-zone logs.
Gas released from formation into the drilling fluid.
A vessel that separates gas from mud coming through the choke during well control and vents the gas safely. Also called a poor-boy degasser.
The hydrostatic pressure per foot of mud column: 0.052 × mud weight in ppg, in psi/ft.
A nozzle that jets mud into a tank to stir it.
A funnel and jet nozzle used to mix dry additives into the mud system.
A depth log of drilling rate, gas, lithology and shows made by the mud logger.
The person who monitors returns, gas and cuttings and keeps the mud log.
Continuous monitoring at the rig of cuttings, gas shows and drilling data while the well is drilled.
The wellsite cabin with gas detectors, sensors and microscopes used by the mud logging crew.
An additive that reduces friction between the drillstring and the borehole wall, lowering torque and drag.
Rig slang for the mud engineer.
Adding and dispersing materials to build mud.
A positive-displacement downhole motor driven by mud flow. It turns the bit without rotating the whole drillstring and is used for directional work.
Whether a mud's chemistry and solids are safe for motor elastomers and bearings.
A carbonate buildup made mostly of mud with few frame-building organisms.
A steel tank, or on older sites an earthen pit, that holds drilling fluid at the surface.
The plan for mud types and properties for each hole section.
The measured characteristics of mud, such as weight, viscosity, fluid loss and solids.
Sending data to surface as pressure pulses in the mud column.
A high-pressure reciprocating pump, usually triplex, that circulates drilling fluid down the drillstring and up the annulus.
A summary report of mud properties, products and problems for a well.
Clearing mud from the annulus before cement fills it.
The daily record of mud properties, chemical treatments, volumes and losses.
The resistivity of the drilling mud, written R<sub>m</sub>, measured on a surface sample and corrected to downhole temperature.
The mud coming back from the well to surface.
A ring of sticky cuttings that builds up in the annulus in air drilling when water is present, restricting flow.
Passing new mud through high-shear equipment so polymers and clays disperse and hydrate quickly.
The whole set of tanks, pumps, solids-control equipment and lines that hold and treat the drilling fluid.
A mixer in a mud pit that keeps solids suspended and the mud uniform.
The temperature of mud at the pump suction.
The temperature of mud at the flowline.
A standard measurement of a mud property.
Adding chemicals or water to correct mud properties.
Convert a well from water or spud mud to a full drilling fluid.
A cone of mud formed where overpressured mud and gas erupt at the surface or seafloor.
The total amount of mud in hole and pits.
The density of the drilling fluid, usually in pounds per gallon (ppg). It sets the hydrostatic pressure the mud column exerts on the formations.
A drop in mud weight, often from gas, water or dilution.
The density of mud entering the well.
The density of mud returning from the well.
A planned sequence of mud weight increases as a well drills into higher pore pressure.
The range of mud weights between the pore pressure (or collapse pressure) and the fracture gradient.
Correction for the effect of mudcake on pad tools.
The resistivity of the filter cake on the borehole wall, written R<sub>mc</sub>.
A fine sedimentary rock such as shale, mudstone or siltstone.
Castagna's linear relation between P- and S-wave velocities in water-saturated clastic rocks.
A fine-grained sedimentary rock of clay and silt that, unlike shale, does not split into thin layers.
A survey recorded in several sailing directions over the same area.
A survey acquired by a contractor at its own cost and licensed to several companies.
Towing several streamers side by side to record a 3D swath.
A ship-mounted sonar that maps water depth across a wide swath beneath the vessel.
Exchange of ions between clay surfaces and brine, one proposed cause of the low-salinity effect.
Recording ground motion in three directions, plus pressure at sea, so S-waves and converted waves can be used.
A tool with many arms that measures the internal shape of casing or tubing to detect corrosion, wear and deformation.
A well with two or more branches drilled from one main bore to reach more reservoir from a single surface location.
A test designed to find properties of separate layers.
Solving many logs at once for volumes of several minerals and fluids.
The simultaneous flow of more than one phase, such as gas, oil and water, in a pipe or in the rock.
A meter that measures oil, gas and water rates in the flow line without first separating the phases.
Processing that removes or reduces multiples.
Miscibility that develops as gas and oil exchange components through repeated contact in the reservoir.
Running a production logging tool up and down at several speeds to calibrate the spinner.
A geostatistical method that copies patterns from a training image to build more geologically realistic models.
A test at several flow rates, often to measure deliverability and skin.
A test with several flow rates in sequence, analyzed with superposition.
A completion that divides a long lateral into isolated stages for separate fracturing or production.
Hydraulically fracturing a horizontal well in many separate, isolated stages along its lateral.
A completion designed so a horizontal well can be fractured in many separate stages.
A light-colored mica common in sandstones and granites.
Zeroing parts of seismic traces, such as noisy first arrivals or stretched far offsets, before stacking.
A solvent that dissolves in both oil and water, used to clean and water-wet surfaces.
A toxicity test that uses mysid shrimp to measure LC50 of mud.
The saturation exponent in Archie's law, usually near 2.
A microscopic fossil of calcareous plankton, used for dating marine sediments.
One billionth of a darcy. Shale matrix permeability is often measured in nanodarcies.
Using tiny particles to change wettability, stabilize foam or reduce interfacial tension.
Particles under 100 nanometers used to plug shale pores in some muds.
The unit used for magnetic field anomalies.
A large sheet of rock pushed far over other rocks by thrusting.
A survey with offsets mostly in one direction, as in conventional towed streamer.
An oil and gas company owned or controlled by a government. Abbreviated NOC.
A crack in rock formed by geological stress, which can greatly increase permeability.
The frequency at which a geophone's spring and mass resonate.
A gaseous mixture made mainly of methane, with smaller amounts of heavier hydrocarbons and non-hydrocarbon gases such as CO<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>S.
Ethane, propane, butanes and heavier hydrocarbons separated from natural gas as liquids. Abbreviated NGL.
Algorithms that read and interpret written text, such as daily reports.
Adding source and receiver positions to recorded data.
The shortest source-receiver distance in a gather.
A stack of small-angle traces.
A sensor placed close to the bit to see formation and inclination sooner.
A stabilizer placed just above the bit.
A model of velocity and thickness of the shallow layers, used to compute statics.
Winding fracture paths near the well that add pressure loss.
The period from about 23 to 2.6 million years ago.
Revenue minus all costs, royalties and taxes in a period.
Purchased CO<sub>2</sub> per barrel of incremental oil.
The stress on a core sample minus pore pressure, used to simulate reservoir conditions.
The thickness of reservoir rock that contains hydrocarbons and can produce them, after cutoffs for porosity, shale volume and water saturation are applied.
The sum of a project's future net cash flows discounted to today's value at a chosen rate. A positive value means the project earns more than that rate. Abbreviated NPV.
The fracture fluid pressure minus the closure pressure. It controls fracture width and growth.
A map of the total thickness of sand in an interval.
The fraction of the gross reservoir thickness that is net reservoir rock. Abbreviated N/G or NTG.
The revenue per barrel after deducting transport, royalties and production costs.
A machine learning model built from layers of connected nodes that learn patterns from examples.
The point in the drillstring where axial load changes from compression to tension.
A log that responds mainly to the amount of hydrogen in the formation, which relates to the liquid-filled porosity. Gas makes it read low.
The porosity read by a neutron tool, usually scaled to limestone. It responds to hydrogen, so shale reads high and gas reads low.
Where neutron porosity reads lower than density porosity on a log, usually a sign of gas.
The gap between neutron and density porosity curves, which indicates shale (neutron higher) or gas (density higher).
A fluid whose viscosity doesn't change with shear rate, such as water or light oil.
A pattern with one well surrounded by eight others.
The grooves inside a nipple that a lock mandrel engages.
Drilling with nitrogen gas as the circulating fluid.
Injecting nitrogen for pressure maintenance, gravity drainage or, at very high pressure, miscible displacement.
Pumping nitrogen through coiled tubing to lighten the fluid column and start a well flowing.
Pumping nitrogen through coiled tubing to lighten the fluid column in a well so it starts flowing again.
Distortion of the wavelet to lower frequency at far offsets after normal-moveout correction, usually muted.
Porosity measured by an NMR log, mostly independent of lithology.
The spread of relaxation times measured by NMR, which relates to pore sizes.
A barrier, such as a sealing fault or a pinch-out, across which no fluid flows.
A shoulder in a nipple or tool that stops a device at a set place.
Recording with autonomous receivers that store data without cables.
Splitting the production system at a point, usually bottomhole, and intersecting the inflow and outflow curves there to predict the well's rate.
A small rounded mass of a mineral, such as chert or pyrite, in a rock.
Processing steps that reduce random and coherent noise while keeping the signal.
A record of sound in the well, used to detect flow through leaks, channels behind casing or perforations.
A field test recording noise to choose array and source parameters.
A log-log plot of net pressure against time used to judge fracture growth.
The instantaneous decline rate D, the slope of the natural log of rate against time.
Flow with extra pressure loss from inertia at high velocity, common near gas wells.
A fluid whose viscosity changes with shear rate, as most drilling muds do.
Rig time lost to unplanned events such as stuck pipe, losses or equipment failure. Abbreviated NPT.
Any drilling fluid with an oil or synthetic continuous phase. Abbreviated NAF.
Oil-base mud that doesn't conduct, which needs induction tools.
An unconformity where sediments lie on igneous or metamorphic rock.
A water-base mud without thinners, so clay particles stay grouped. Common for shallow and fast drilling.
Moveout that departs from a hyperbola at long offsets because of anisotropy or layering.
A surfactant with no electric charge on its head group.
A drill collar of nonmagnetic alloy that houses magnetic survey sensors.
The expected change of a property, such as sonic travel time, with depth in normally pressured shale.
A fault where the hanging wall has moved down relative to the footwall, caused by stretching of the crust.
The increase in reflection time with source–receiver offset. It is corrected so reflections line up before stacking. Abbreviated NMO.
Shoreline moving seaward because sediment supply outpaces rising accommodation.
Pseudopressure scaled to have pressure units.
The main petroleum-producing basin of the Philippines, offshore northwest Palawan, home to fields such as Malampaya, Nido and Galoc.
A filter that removes a narrow band of frequencies, such as electrical power-line noise.
A common mnemonic for neutron porosity.
Normalized root-mean-square difference: the standard measure of 4D repeatability.
Nephelometric turbidity unit, used to measure brine clarity.
Fluid density measured by gamma ray absorption.
A log that measures how hydrogen in pore fluids relaxes after a magnetic pulse. It gives porosity independent of lithology, pore-size distribution and free-fluid volume. Abbreviated NMR.
A small, deliberate deviation near surface to keep wells apart.
Interpreting a test with a numerical model instead of analytical solutions.
Ground nut shells used as a granular lost circulation material.
The highest frequency that can be recorded without distortion: half the sampling frequency.
Building facies models by placing geometric shapes, such as channels or lobes, into the grid.
A clinoform with steep foresets and toplap, formed with little accommodation.
Removing the effect of oil-base mud filtrate from sample analysis.
A well used to watch pressure changes caused by another well.
The field record of each shot, its location and any problems.
A cable with seismic sensors laid on the seafloor, used for multicomponent and obstructed-area surveys. Abbreviated OBC.
A self-contained seismic recorder placed on the seabed, used where streamers can't go or where better data is needed.
A seabed recorder for low-frequency and long-offset data. Abbreviated OBS.
With the bit lifted clear of the bottom of the hole.
The range of offsets recorded in each bin.
Traces from one common midpoint arranged by offset.
A VSP with the source at a distance from the well, imaging away from it.
Offset divided by target depth, a quick guide to the reflection angles recorded.
Located at sea, as opposed to onshore. Offshore operations use fixed platforms, jack-ups, semisubmersibles and drillships.
Disposal of cuttings and mud into the sea, allowed only under strict rules.
A zone of increased oil saturation that forms ahead of an EOR flood front as mobilized oil gathers.
Liquid droplets carried out of a separator with the gas.
The volume percent of oil in a mud, measured by retort.
Breakdown of oil into gas at high temperature.
The rise in oil fraction at producers after an EOR project starts.
A depth where oil flows into the well.
A pump that sends treated oil into an export pipeline.
Reservoir barrels of oil and dissolved gas per stock-tank barrel. Written B<sub>o</sub>, usually 1.1 to 2.0 rb/STB.
The fraction of pipe area filled by oil.
The oil-filled part of a reservoir below a gas cap.
The amount of base oil left on cuttings after solids control, regulated where cuttings are discharged. Abbreviated OOC.
A sample of oil taken from a separator, tank or downhole.
Sand or sandstone saturated with bitumen, produced either by surface mining or by thermal methods in place. Also called tar sands.
Digging shallow oil sands and separating bitumen with hot water.
A place where oil or gas leaks naturally to the surface, showing that a petroleum system is active nearby.
Immature, kerogen-rich rock that yields oil only when heated (retorted), not to be confused with shale oil.
Any sign of oil in cuttings, cores or mud while drilling, such as stain, odor or fluorescence.
Measuring how much separator oil shrinks when flashed to stock-tank conditions.
A thin film of oil on the sea surface, which can come from a natural seep.
Increase in oil volume when gas such as CO<sub>2</sub> dissolves in it.
An oil's resistance to flow, in centipoise. It falls sharply as temperature rises, which is why heat works so well for heavy oil.
The temperature range in which kerogen mainly generates oil, roughly 60 to 120 °C. Hotter rock generates mainly gas.
A drilling fluid with oil as the continuous phase and brine droplets emulsified in it. It is chosen for reactive shales, high temperatures and good lubricity.
A resistivity imager designed to work in nonconductive mud.
Mud contaminated with oil from the formation.
The deepest depth where oil is proven in a well. Abbreviated ODT.
A water-base mud with a small amount of oil emulsified in it to improve lubricity and filtration.
An instrument that measures oil in produced water.
The concentration of oil left in treated produced water, usually in mg/L, limited by discharge regulations.
Matching an oil to the source rock that generated it using its chemical fingerprint.
The depth that separates oil from water in a reservoir. Abbreviated OWC.
The split between oil and water in the liquid phase of an invert-emulsion mud, written for example as 80/20.
Describes a surface that oil coats in preference to water.
A surfactant that coats solids with oil in an invert-emulsion mud so they stay dispersed instead of clumping as water-wet solids.
Attracted to oil. Oleophilic surfaces are wetted by oil rather than water.
The epoch from about 34 to 23 million years ago.
A steam generator in which water passes through the tubes once, producing wet steam of about 75–80% quality. Abbreviated OTSG.
A rounded carbonate grain built by algae coating a nucleus.
Layers ending against an inclined surface as they lap onto it, seen on seismic as reflections ending against an older surface.
A small sphere of carbonate with concentric layers.
A limestone made of ooids, small rounded grains with concentric layers formed in agitated warm water.
An open industrial communication standard that lets equipment and software from different vendors exchange data securely.
A fracture with space that can let fluid flow.
A section of well with no casing.
A completion with no casing across the reservoir.
A gravel pack placed around a screen in an uncased reservoir section.
Logging run in a well before casing is set.
A packer that seals against the bare borehole wall to isolate zones in an openhole completion.
The pressure of a sample bottle when first opened in the lab, checked against the sampling pressure.
Ongoing costs of running operations, such as labor, power, chemicals and maintenance. Abbreviated OPEX.
Protecting industrial control systems, such as SCADA and safety systems, from cyberattack and unauthorized access.
The company that runs day-to-day operations on a license on behalf of all the partners.
Operating expenditure: day-to-day running costs.
How much light a fluid absorbs, used downhole to identify and type fluids.
A probe that detects gas bubbles by how light reflects at its tip, used to measure gas holdup.
Using infrared cameras to see gas leaks.
A probe that tells gas from liquid by how light reflects at its tip.
The salinity at which a surfactant system reaches its lowest interfacial tension, with a middle microemulsion phase.
The period from about 485 to 444 million years ago.
Rock mined for a mineral, such as barite ore.
A weaker acid, such as acetic or formic acid, used at high temperature where HCl reacts too fast.
Tiny pores within organic matter in shale.
Clay coated with amines so it swells and builds viscosity in oil.
Clay treated with amines so it swells in oil. It provides viscosity and suspension in oil- and synthetic-base muds.
Lignite treated with amines so it disperses in oil, used for fluid-loss control in oil-base mud.
A core marked so its original direction is known.
Aiming the charges in a chosen direction, for example toward maximum stress or away from a control line.
A gas meter that measures flow from the pressure drop across a thin plate with a precise hole.
A plate with a sized hole used in an orifice meter.
The total volume of oil in a reservoir before any production. In field units, N = 7758·A·h·φ·(1 − S<sub>w</sub>)/B<sub>oi</sub> (stock-tank barrels). Abbreviated OOIP.
A vast extra-heavy oil region in eastern Venezuela.
A mountain-building event in which crust is folded, faulted and thickened.
A land survey layout with source lines at right angles to receiver lines.
Anisotropy with three perpendicular planes of symmetry, as in fractured layered rock.
Open Subsurface Data Universe: an industry standard platform for subsurface and well data.
An open, industry-built data platform that stores subsurface and well data in standard formats.
Movement of water across a membrane from lower to higher salt concentration.
The pressure that drives water across a semipermeable membrane between solutions of different salinity. It can pull water out of shale toward a saltier mud.
A place where bedrock is exposed at the surface. Outcrops are studied as analogues for buried reservoirs.
A rock exposure at the surface used to understand a similar reservoir underground.
The bottomhole pressure needed to lift a given rate through the tubing and surface equipment. Also called the tubing performance curve.
Adding too much of a chemical, which can cause new mud problems.
Two streamers towed at different depths over each other to remove ghosts.
Perforating with wellbore pressure above reservoir pressure, which keeps the well under control but leaves tunnels less clean.
Fine sediment laid down when flow spills over channel banks.
The rock above a given depth, whose weight creates vertical stress.
The vertical stress caused by the weight of all the rock and fluid above a point.
The cleaned liquid leaving the top of a hydrocyclone.
Fluid pumped after a treatment to push it deeper into the formation and away from the wellbore.
Pore pressure higher than the normal hydrostatic pressure for that depth, often caused by fast burial that traps fluids.
Pull above the free weight of the string needed to move it, a sign of drag or sticking.
A fishing tool that slides over the outside of a lost tubular and grips it so it can be pulled out.
A fold in which one limb has rotated past vertical.
A breaker, such as a persulfate, that chemically breaks polymer chains.
A pulsed neutron technique that detects moving water.
A pulsed neutron measurement that detects moving water, inside or behind the casing, by activating oxygen atoms.
Corrosion of steel caused by dissolved oxygen, often seen as pitting.
S3 per gram of organic carbon, a Rock-Eval measure of kerogen type. Abbreviated OI.
A chemical, such as a sulfite, that removes dissolved oxygen from mud or brine to reduce corrosion.
Piping and instrumentation diagram: the detailed drawing of a facility's piping, equipment, instruments and control loops.
Written p*: the pressure found by extending the straight line of a Horner plot to infinite shut-in time.
A pressurized bulk tank for barite or cement.
A compressional wave in which particles move back and forth in the direction the wave travels. It is the fastest seismic wave.
Bulk modulus plus four thirds shear modulus, equal to density times Vp squared.
The speed of compressional waves in a material. Symbol Vp.
Probabilistic estimates with a 90%, 50% and 10% chance that the true value equals or exceeds them: the low, best and high cases.
Cuttings or debris jamming around the drillstring, which stops circulation and can stick the pipe.
A stiff BHA with several stabilizers that holds angle and direction.
A device that seals the annulus between tubing and casing. It isolates zones and keeps well fluids and pressure off the casing above it.
The fluid left in the annulus above a packer. It is chosen to be non-corrosive and to support the casing and tubing.
Fluid passing a packer that should seal.
Milling out a permanent packer to remove it.
A tool that mills a packer and catches it in one trip.
A tool that releases and pulls a retrievable packer.
A grain-supported carbonate with lime mud between the grains.
The proppant-free fluid pumped first in a fracture treatment to create the fracture before proppant follows.
Drilling several wells from one surface location, which cuts surface footprint, rig moves and cost.
Fluid pumped without proppant at the start of a frac to open the fracture.
An old fluid contact preserved by diagenesis or residual oil.
The epoch from 66 to about 56 million years ago.
The direction of ancient water or wind flow, read from sedimentary structures.
The period from 66 to about 23 million years ago.
Ancient karst buried in the rock record, which can form reservoirs or cause lost circulation.
An ancient soil preserved in the rock record.
The geologic era from about 539 to 252 million years ago.
The study of fossil pollen, spores and other microscopic organic particles, used to date rocks and judge their maturity.
A Radon transform that separates multiples by their parabolic moveout.
Waxy hydrocarbons that come out of crude oil as it cools and deposit in tubing, flowlines and tanks.
Taking out wax deposits by heat, solvents or scraping.
A tool that scrapes wax from tubing walls.
Reflections that stay evenly spaced, typical of uniform deposition.
A small shallowing-upward package of beds bounded by flooding surfaces.
Pressure lost to friction everywhere in the system except the bit.
An older well and a newer well drilled near it, which often performs worse.
The effect of an older (parent) well's depletion on a newer (child) well drilled nearby, which often reduces the child well's performance.
Sucker rods that have broken in the well.
Tubing that has broken in the well.
Losing some mud into the formation while still getting returns.
A well open to only part of the reservoir thickness, which adds skin.
A stack made from a limited range of offsets or angles, such as a near stack or far stack, used for AVO analysis.
Sealing pore throats or fractures with sized particles.
The spread of particle sizes in a mud or additive. Matching it to the formation's pore or fracture size improves bridging.
A continental edge with no plate boundary, built of thick sediment over an old rift.
Recording natural or induced earth vibrations without an active source, for example to monitor microseismicity.
The active receivers recording each shot in a land survey.
A small isolated reef within a lagoon or shelf.
Gas and water in separate patches in the rock, which gives higher velocities than uniform mixing.
Adjusting injection rates so each pattern is swept evenly.
A marker on a log showing intervals that pass all pay cutoffs.
A table of net pay, porosity and saturation for each zone in a well.
The time it takes for a project's cumulative cash flow to repay the initial investment. Also called the payback period.
A fixed-cutter bit with polycrystalline diamond compact cutters that shear the rock, used widely in soft to medium-hard formations.
A disk of synthetic diamond bonded to tungsten carbide, the cutting element of PDC bits.
Partly decayed plant material, the first stage of coal formation.
A multiple with an extra short bounce near a reflector, which lags slightly behind the primary.
Fine sediment that settles slowly from open ocean water, such as ooze and red clay.
A small rounded grain of carbonate mud, often fecal pellets.
A BHA with the first stabilizer high above the bit so gravity drops angle.
How far a perforation tunnel reaches into the formation beyond the casing, which affects productivity.
How fast the bit deepens the hole, usually in feet or meters per hour. Also called ROP.
A sidewall core taken by firing a hollow bullet into the borehole wall.
Perforating a zone and flowing it in the same trip with a combined string.
Metal and charge-case fragments left in the well after perforating, which can damage equipment.
Making sure guns are fired at the right depth, usually with a CCL and gamma ray.
The clean fluid in the well during perforating.
A carrier holding shaped charges that is lowered into the well and fired to shoot holes through casing and cement into the formation.
The guns, charges, firing head and accessories used together.
The extra pressure loss caused by perforation geometry and crushed zone.
Running guns on coiled tubing, often in horizontal wells.
Removing debris and crushed rock from perforation tunnels.
A short group of perforations; several clusters make up one stage in a multistage fracturing treatment.
Choosing gun size, shot density, phasing and charges for a well.
The fraction of perforations that are open and contributing to flow.
The pressure drop as fluid passes through the perforations, which depends on rate, hole size and the number of holes.
The length, diameter, density and phasing of perforations.
The diameter of the hole a charge makes in the casing.
The extra pressure drop caused by the geometry and damage of the perforations.
The channel through the casing, cement and rock created by one shaped-charge jet.
Removing crushed rock and debris from tunnels after perforating.
The permeability of the crushed zone around a perforation tunnel.
A routine test of each producing well's rates through a test separator.
Injecting water around the edge of a reservoir, often into the aquifer, to push oil toward producers in the middle.
A barrier meant to seal a well forever, such as a cement plug across caprock.
A pressure and temperature sensor installed with the completion to monitor the reservoir continuously. Abbreviated PDG.
Pressure records from gauges installed in the completion, analyzed continuously.
A packer that cannot be released once set and must be milled out to remove it.
Sensors installed permanently on the seabed to record repeated 4D surveys cheaply. Abbreviated PRM.
A rock's ability to let fluids flow through it, measured in darcies or millidarcies (mD). It depends on how large the pores are and how well they connect.
Difference between horizontal and vertical permeability. Written kv/kh.
Loss of permeability near the wellbore from mud solids or filtrate.
A fluid-loss test through a ceramic disc of chosen pore size, showing how well a mud seals permeable or fractured rock. Abbreviated PPT.
The product of permeability and net thickness, kh, which controls a well's flow capacity.
The period from about 299 to 252 million years ago, with major evaporite and reservoir deposits.
Permission from land or sea authorities to carry out a survey.
A written system that authorizes hazardous work only after the hazards are identified and controls are in place.
Gloves, goggles, masks and similar gear used when handling chemicals. Abbreviated PPE.
Describing rocks and their minerals, often with a microscope.
The study of the chemistry of source rocks, oil and gas to understand where hydrocarbons came from and how mature they are.
The combination of source rock, migration path, reservoir, seal and trap, in the right timing, that allows oil and gas to accumulate.
The equations and parameters used to turn logs into reservoir properties.
A rock property such as porosity, permeability or saturation.
A specialist who interprets logs and core to find rock and fluid properties.
The study of rock and fluid properties from logs and cores, especially porosity, permeability and saturation.
The filtrate phenolphthalein alkalinity: millilitres of 0.02 N acid needed to bring 1 mL of filtrate to pH 8.3.
A measure of how acidic or alkaline a fluid is. Water-base muds are usually kept alkaline, often pH 9 to 10.5.
An additive that holds mud pH steady when acids or bases enter, such as magnesium oxide or bicarbonate systems.
An electronic probe that measures pH more accurately than paper strips.
Test paper that changes color to show approximate pH.
The shape of a wavelet relative to its timing. A zero-phase wavelet is symmetric and centered on the reflector, which makes it easiest to interpret.
Mixing oil, brine and surfactant at different salinities to find the best formulation.
The region on a pressure–temperature diagram, bounded by the bubblepoint and dew point curves, in which a mixture exists as both gas and liquid.
Gas and liquid separating in a shut-in wellbore, which distorts early pressure data.
A change in reflection polarity along a horizon, often from a fluid or lithology change.
Changing the phase of seismic data by a constant angle, for example to make the wavelet zero-phase.
The phase of each frequency in a signal, which controls wavelet shape.
The speed of one phase in multiphase flow.
A frequency-domain migration method for layered velocity models.
LWD resistivity from the phase difference of an electromagnetic wave between receivers.
The angle between neighboring charges around the gun axis, such as 0°, 60°, 90° or 120°.
A pH indicator that turns pink above about pH 8.3, used as the endpoint in Pf and Pm alkalinity titrations.
The Philippine Department of Energy's process for offering areas to companies for petroleum service contracts. Abbreviated PECR.
A sedimentary rock rich in phosphate minerals.
A density-tool measurement of how the formation absorbs low-energy gamma rays. It is mainly a lithology indicator. Written Pe or PEF.
Partially hydrolyzed polyacrylamide, a polymer that coats and encapsulates cuttings and helps keep shale from dispersing.
Machine learning models constrained by physical laws, such as material balance, so their predictions stay realistic.
A log-log crossplot of resistivity against porosity. Lines of constant water saturation are straight, which helps find R<sub>w</sub> and m.
A device pushed through a pipeline to clean it or inspect it.
The pressure chamber at the start of a pipeline where a pig is loaded and sent into the line. The pig receiver catches it at the other end.
Running a device called a pig through a pipeline to clean it, separate products or inspect the pipe wall.
A small, specially mixed volume of fluid pumped for one purpose, such as curing losses, freeing pipe or cleaning the hole.
A small tank used to mix and hold pills and slugs.
A small hole drilled first to check geology or to guide a larger hole.
A small-scale lab test of a mud treatment before it is added to the active system.
The thinning of a rock layer until it disappears, which can form a stratigraphic trap.
A tall, isolated reef build-up, which can form a small rich trap.
Using the measured pipe size to convert fluid velocity into rate.
Bending of pipe into a sinusoidal or helical shape when it is pushed under compression.
When pipe weight exceeds the well pressure force, so the pipe falls in by itself.
When well pressure force exceeds pipe weight, so the pipe must be pushed in.
A frame that holds pipe horizontally near the rig.
A BOP ram with cutouts that seal around a given pipe size.
Moving casing up and down while cementing to improve mud removal.
Freeing and pulling stuck pipe or casing.
A list of measured pipe lengths used to know the depth of the string.
Running logging tools on drillpipe in highly deviated wells.
Managing a pipeline so it stays safe and leak-free, through inspection, corrosion control and repair.
A sample cylinder with a piston separating sample from the pushing fluid.
Tubing force change caused by pressure acting on area differences at a packer.
An ideal displacement where the injected fluid pushes oil ahead as a sharp front.
An increase in active pit volume. Without a known cause, it is a primary sign of a kick.
The height of mud in the pits, watched closely for gains and losses.
An instrument that adds up the volume in all active pits and sounds an alarm on a gain or loss. Abbreviated PVT.
Local corrosion that forms small, deep pits.
Relations between pore throat sizes, porosity and permeability from mercury injection.
A plot of mud gas ratios used to predict whether a zone holds oil, gas or water.
A 2D fracture model (Perkins-Kern-Nordgren) for long fractures of fixed height, with width set by the height.
The point on a ternary diagram where two phases become identical.
In the Bingham-plastic model, the 600-rpm viscometer reading minus the 300-rpm reading, in centipoise. It reflects friction from solids and the base fluid, and rises as drilled solids build up.
The theory that the earth's outer shell is divided into moving plates, whose interactions create basins, mountains and faults.
A rig installed on a fixed offshore production platform.
A group of prospects and fields that share the same source, reservoir, seal and trap style, so they can be explored the same way.
The area where all the elements of a play are likely present.
A dry lake bed in a desert basin.
The epoch of the ice ages, from about 2.6 million to 11,700 years ago.
The epoch from about 5.3 to 2.6 million years ago.
Permanently sealing a well with cement and mechanical plugs at the end of its life, so fluids cannot move between zones or reach surface. Abbreviated P&A.
A multistage fracturing method: set a plug to isolate the treated stage, perforate the next stage, fracture it, and repeat up the well.
Flow in which the center of the stream moves as a solid plug because of yield stress.
Lowering pipe or wire to touch a cement plug and confirm its depth.
Proving a plug is in place and holding by tagging and pressure testing.
Setting a plug to shut off a lower part of a well.
Solids used to seal pores, fractures or loss zones.
The angle a fold axis dips from horizontal.
A free-moving plunger that travels up and down the tubing, using the well's own gas to lift liquid slugs. It is used to unload gas wells.
The phenolphthalein alkalinity of the whole mud, used with Pf to estimate the lime content.
A crater on the seafloor formed by fluid or gas escaping.
A sand body built on the inside bend of a meandering river. Point bars can form good reservoirs.
Counting grains at many points on a thin section to measure mineral fractions.
A rotary steerable design that tilts the bit shaft to steer.
An attribute combining P- and S-impedance to separate fluid and lithology.
The ratio of lateral strain to axial strain in a stressed material. It relates P- and S-wave velocities and helps detect gas.
Whether an increase in impedance is shown as a peak or a trough.
A spike on LWD resistivity at a high-angle bed boundary.
The time protons are left in the magnet before measurement.
A smooth-bored tube that seal assemblies seal inside, allowing the tubing to move as it heats and cools. Abbreviated PBR.
The smooth top rod of a sucker-rod string that moves through the stuffing box at the wellhead.
A synthetic hydrocarbon made by linking alpha olefins, used as a base fluid.
A synthetic polymer widely used to thicken injection water.
A short-chain acrylic polymer that thins water-base mud without chromium.
A synthetic emulsifier for invert emulsion muds that is stable at high temperature.
An amine compound used as a shale hydration inhibitor in high-performance water-base mud.
A cellulose-based polymer (PAC) used for fluid-loss control and some viscosity in water-base muds.
A polymer with many charged groups, such as PAC or PHPA.
A glycerol polymer used to inhibit shale and reduce water activity.
A large molecule made of repeating units, used to thicken fluids or control fluid loss.
Polymer sticking to rock surfaces during a polymer flood, which removes it from solution and adds to the cost.
Breakdown of polymer by heat, shear, oxygen or microbes, which lowers viscosity.
Breakdown of mud polymers by heat, shear or bacteria.
Adding a polymer to injected water to raise its viscosity, which lowers the mobility ratio and improves sweep efficiency.
A crosslinked polymer that sets in place to block thief zones.
Equipment that dissolves and ages polymer powder before injection.
How easily polymer solution can be injected into a well.
A water-base mud that gets its viscosity and fluid-loss control mainly from polymers such as xanthan gum, PAC or PHPA rather than from clay.
A batch of polymer solution injected to control mobility behind a chemical slug.
A natural polymer built from sugar units, such as starch, cellulose, xanthan and guar.
A short drill collar used to space out a BHA.
A pressure relief valve on a mud pump that opens to protect the pump and lines.
The pressure of the fluids in a rock's pores. Mud weight must be high enough to balance it but low enough not to fracture the rock.
The rise of pore pressure near the wellbore as mud pressure leaks into shale.
The narrow connection between pores that controls permeability.
The fractional change of pore volume per unit pressure change.
The volume injected divided by the pore volume of the swept region.
The fraction of a rock's bulk volume that is pore space. Effective porosity counts only the connected pores that can hold mobile fluid.
Any log used to estimate porosity, such as density, neutron, sonic or NMR.
Estimating porosity between wells from seismic data.
The usual decline of porosity with burial depth for a rock type.
An equation relating core permeability to porosity, used to estimate permeability from logs.
Porosity times thickness, summed over a zone.
Measuring capillary pressure by pushing fluid through a sample on a water-wet plate.
The hydraulic cement used for oil wells, made by burning limestone and clay and grinding the clinker.
A meter that measures liquid by filling and emptying chambers of known volume.
A mud motor with a helical rotor in a stator that turns the bit as mud flows through. Abbreviated PDM.
Additional reserves less likely to be recovered than probable reserves. Proved plus probable plus possible makes 3P.
Migrating seismic data after it has been stacked, faster but less accurate than prestack migration.
Deposited after rifting ended, usually in a sagging basin.
A chloride-free source of potassium ions for inhibitive water-base mud.
A water-base mud that uses potassium ions to reduce clay swelling in reactive shales.
A dense, low-solids formate salt used in drill-in and completion brines.
Caustic potash: a strong base used to raise pH while adding inhibitive potassium.
The potassium cation, which fits between clay layers and reduces swelling.
A silicate used in inhibitive mud that supplies potassium as well as silicate.
A field, such as gravity or magnetic, that can be described by a potential.
The concentration of an additive in mud, in lb/bbl (ppb). One ppb is roughly one gram per 350 mL in the lab.
The lowest temperature at which an oil still flows under test conditions.
The part of a mud pump that converts motor rotation into piston motion.
A flow model with shear stress = K·γ̇<sup>n</sup>, where n is the flow behavior index and K the consistency index. It fits polymer muds well.
Hydraulic tongs used to tighten or loosen pipe connections.
A siliceous material such as fly ash that reacts with lime to form cement.
Pounds per US gallon, the usual unit of mud density. Water is 8.33 ppg.
The total fluid collected in a permeability plugging test, a measure of how well mud seals.
