Bentonite mixed and allowed to swell in fresh water before it is added to a salty mud.
All of earth history before about 539 million years ago.
Damage from solids that form when filtrate mixes with formation water.
Deconvolution that predicts and removes repeating energy, such as short-period multiples.
Scheduling maintenance based on condition data and models that predict failures, rather than at fixed intervals.
A fluid, often hydrochloric acid, pumped ahead of the main acid to remove carbonates and displace formation water.
Starch cooked and dried so it disperses readily in cold water.
Mixing bentonite in fresh water before adding it to salty mud so it swells.
A threaded joint with metal seals for high pressure and gas tightness.
A sand screen with a woven metal mesh filter.
New mud mixed ahead of time to add to the active system.
Deposited before rifting began.
A chemical, often a biocide, that stops bacteria spoiling a mud.
Equipment such as the lubricator, stuffing box and wireline BOP that contains well pressure during intervention.
Coring that keeps the core at reservoir pressure to preserve its fluids.
A factor that corrects measured gas volume to standard pressure.
The crystallization temperature of a brine at high pressure, which can be higher than at surface.
The derivative of pressure change with respect to the natural logarithm of time. Its shape is used to identify flow regimes and boundaries.
The extra pressure loss near the well caused by damage or stimulation.
The change in pressure with depth. Gas, oil and water have different gradients, so pressure plots reveal fluid types and contacts.
A plot of formation pressures against depth, where line slopes show fluid density and contacts.
The full record of pressures over the life of a well or test.
Pressure used up by friction as fluid flows.
Injecting water or gas early in a field's life to stop reservoir pressure falling.
Lining up pressure axes of data and type curve to find permeability.
A valve that opens automatically when pressure reaches a set point, to protect vessels and piping from overpressure.
The delay before an observation well feels a rate change.
A spring valve that opens to release pressure above a set point. Abbreviated PSV.
Dissolution of grains where they touch under stress, which reduces porosity and supplies cement.
Applying pressure to equipment or a well to check that it holds.
A sensor that turns pressure into an electrical signal.
Interpreting the pressure response to a change in flow rate to find permeability, skin, reservoir pressure and boundaries.
Leakoff that increases as pressure opens natural fractures.
Shale with pore pressure above normal, which tends to cave if mud weight is too low.
A mud balance whose cup is pressurized to compress entrained air or gas, giving the true density.
Seismic traces before they are stacked, which keep the offset information needed for AVO and velocity analysis.
Migrating seismic data in depth before stacking, which handles complex velocities better than time migration.
Inversion of angle gathers to get P-impedance, S-impedance and density.
Migrating seismic data in time before stacking. Abbreviated PSTM.
A shaker screen bonded to a frame under tension.
A small drawdown and buildup made by a formation tester at one depth to measure formation pressure and mobility.
A synthetic seismogram that includes no multiples.
The first barrier that prevents flow from a well, such as fluid column or tubing.
Cementing casing after it is run, to support it and isolate zones.
The main surfactant that forms and holds the water-in-oil emulsion in an invert mud.
Movement of hydrocarbons out of the source rock.
Porosity formed when the sediment was deposited, such as the spaces between sand grains.
Production that uses only the reservoir's natural energy, such as fluid expansion, gas drive or water influx.
A reflection that has bounced only once, as opposed to a multiple.
A small explosive that passes detonation from the cord to the main charge.
A biomarker ratio that indicates oxygen conditions where the source rock formed.
The Petroleum Resources Management System, the SPE-sponsored framework for classifying and reporting reserves and resources.
Log analysis that finds the best-fit mix of minerals and fluids by minimizing error.
A seismic volume giving the chance of a facies or fluid at each point.
Additional reserves less likely to be recovered than proved reserves. Proved plus probable (2P) is the best estimate.
A device that measures permeability at points on a core surface by gas flow.
The ordered steps used to turn raw seismic into a final image.
A series of vessels and equipment that treat production in sequence.
The muddy, deepest part of a delta beyond the delta front.
An open data standard for exchanging production and fluid-analysis data.
Water brought to surface along with oil and gas. It must be treated, then reinjected or disposed of.
Cleaning produced water so it can be discharged or reinjected.
The stock of mud products on the rig.
Dividing the total measured production of a field back to individual wells, usually using well tests.
The casing string across or above the reservoir, through which the well is completed and produced.
The work of optimizing how wells produce, from reservoir to surface.
A prediction of future production rates.
A manifold that combines flow from several wells.
S1/(S1+S2), a Rock-Eval measure of how much generation has occurred. Abbreviated PI.
Turning production log readings into rates for each phase and zone.
The summary of a production log job with flow profile and conclusions.
Running tools in a flowing or injecting well to measure how much fluid, and which phases, enter or leave the well at each depth.
A caliper in a production logging string that measures pipe size for rate calculations.
The question a production log is run to answer, such as where water enters.
A string of sensors, such as spinner, density, temperature and pressure, run to profile flow. Abbreviated PLT.
The sensors combined in one string for production logging.
An arrangement of pipes and valves that gathers flow from several wells and routes it to production or test equipment.
Adjusting wells and facilities to get the most value from production.
An offshore structure that holds wellheads, processing equipment and accommodation.
A test that checks whether a drill-in fluid will pass through a sand screen without plugging it.
An agreement in which the contractor bears exploration and development costs and is repaid from cost oil, with the remaining profit oil shared with the government. Abbreviated PSC.
Measuring a well's oil, gas and water rates and pressures under controlled conditions, for allocation and well performance checks.
Pipe run inside the casing that carries produced fluids to surface. It protects the casing and allows the flow to be controlled.
The production rate per unit of pressure drawdown, J = q / (p̄<sub>r</sub> − p<sub>wf</sub>), usually in bbl/d/psi.
A test to measure a well's productivity index.
In a production sharing contract, the production left after royalty and cost oil, split between the government and the contractor.
Seaward building-out of a shoreline or delta as sediment supply outpaces the creation of accommodation.
Reflections that build outward basinward over time.
A rugged industrial computer that controls equipment such as pumps and valves. Abbreviated PLC.
A pump with a helical rotor in a stator, suited to viscous oil and sand. Abbreviated PCP.
A pump in which a helical steel rotor turns inside a rubber stator, moving fluid in sealed cavities. It handles viscous oil and some sand. Abbreviated PCP.
Gel strength that keeps growing with time at rest, often a sign of high solids or contamination.
An LWD resistivity measurement from the phase shift and attenuation of an electromagnetic wave between receivers.
Burning a solid propellant downhole to create a pressure pulse that cracks the rock near the perforations.
Filling a 3D reservoir grid with porosity, permeability, saturation and facies, guided by well data and geostatistics.
Sand or manufactured ceramic grains carried into a hydraulic fracture to hold it open after pumping stops.
The amount of proppant per volume of fluid, usually in pounds per gallon.
Breaking of proppant grains under closure stress, which creates fines and reduces conductivity.
Proppant grains pressing into soft fracture faces, which narrows the fracture and cuts conductivity.
Proppant produced back out of the fracture, which can damage equipment and leave the fracture poorly propped.
The amount of proppant pumped per unit length of lateral, often in pounds per foot.
The bed of proppant inside a fracture.
A survey acquired for one company that owns the rights to the data.
A mapped potential trap that is judged worth drilling.
Quantities estimated to be recoverable from undiscovered accumulations, before any well finds them.
Reserves with reasonable certainty of being recovered: at least a 90% probability that actual recovery will equal or exceed the estimate. Also called 1P.
The origin of the sediment in a rock, including its source area and rock type.
A device of known volume used to calibrate flowmeters.
A quick mathematical stand-in for a full reservoir simulation, built from a set of simulation runs.
A fracture model that allows height growth through layers.
The mixture's equivalent critical temperature and pressure, used to calculate pseudo-reduced conditions for the Z-factor chart.
Shear thinning: becoming thinner as shear rate increases.
A transformed pressure that accounts for gas viscosity and Z-factor changes, so gas tests can be analyzed like liquid tests.
Radial flow far from a fracture or horizontal well, once the whole system acts like a large well.
Skin from flow geometry, such as partial penetration, deviation or perforations.
The flow period after all boundaries are felt, when the pressure everywhere in a closed drainage area falls at the same rate.
A time function that corrects for changing gas properties.
A basin that forms where a strike-slip fault steps over and pulls the crust apart.
A tool that latches onto a fishing neck to retrieve a device from the well.
A small rig used to pull and run rods and tubing in producing wells.
A gas-charged vessel on the pump discharge that smooths pressure surges.
A form of interference test that uses short, repeated rate pulses at one well and measures the response at another.
An electronic device that makes bursts of neutrons without a chemical source.
A cased-hole log that bursts neutrons into the formation and measures the response, used to find water and hydrocarbon saturation behind casing.
Drilling a top-hole section with mud that is discharged at the seabed.
Pulling a failed downhole pump and running a new one.
The actual output of a mud pump compared with its theoretical displacement, commonly 95–97% for triplex pumps.
The pressure at a downhole pump's inlet. Keeping it low enough maximizes drawdown while avoiding free gas.
The replaceable cylinder in which a mud pump piston moves. Its diameter sets the pump's output and pressure rating.
The volume a mud pump delivers per stroke or per minute.
The moving part in a mud pump liner that pushes mud.
The pressure at the mud pumps, which equals the total friction around the system.
Swings in pump pressure that can mean washouts, plugged nozzles or air.
A fitting on the lubricator for pumping fluid into the well.
When a rod pump removes fluid faster than it flows in, so the pump partly fills.
A formation tester pump that draws fluid from the formation before sampling.
Lost circulation material fine enough to pass through the MWD and motor.
A short length of tubing or casing used for spacing.
A rotary steerable design that pushes pads against the hole wall to steer.
Laboratory measurements of how reservoir fluids change in volume and phase with pressure, volume and temperature.
A high-pressure, high-temperature vessel in which reservoir fluid samples are tested.
A fluid sample taken for lab study of pressure-volume-temperature behavior.
Iron sulfide (FeS<sub>2</sub>), a dense, conductive mineral that can lower resistivity readings.
Processing that restores amplitude and frequency lost to attenuation.
A coiled tubing BOP with four rams: blind, shear, slip and pipe.
A sonic source used in LWD to measure shear in slow formations.
A measure of how little energy rock absorbs. Low Q means strong attenuation, which can indicate gas.
Using seismic amplitudes, AVO, inversion and rock physics to predict rock and fluid properties. Abbreviated QI.
The volume of mud, 946 mL, used to measure Marsh funnel viscosity.
A 1/4 slope on the log-log derivative, showing bilinear flow.
Silicon dioxide, the most common mineral in sandstone, with a density of 2.65 g/cm³.
A sandstone made almost entirely of quartz grains, usually well sorted and mature.
A high-accuracy pressure gauge based on a quartz crystal.
Quartz cement that grows around sand grains, reducing porosity with depth.
A hard metamorphic rock formed from quartz sandstone.
The current period, from about 2.6 million years ago to now.
A tannin extract from the quebracho tree, once widely used as a mud thinner.
A fast log analysis at the wellsite to find pay.
The platform in the derrick where stands are leaned and held during trips.
A reservoir model with different properties in a ring around the well than farther out.
A tool that cuts pipe with a ring of hot gas from burning chemicals.
Darcy's law for flow toward a well, relating rate to pressure drop.
How far into the formation a log tool can measure.
Turning off radios near the well while arming electric detonators.
Heating a reservoir with radio waves to reduce oil viscosity.
Releasing a small amount of radioactive tracer in a well and tracking it with detectors to find where fluid goes.
Finding the age of a rock from the decay of radioactive elements.
How far the pressure disturbance from a test has traveled into the reservoir at a given time.
A transform used to separate multiples from primaries by their different moveout.
A blowout preventer that closes with two opposing steel rams: pipe rams seal around pipe, blind rams seal an open hole and shear rams cut the pipe.
The part of a thrust that cuts steeply up through layers.
Unwanted energy that differs from trace to trace, such as wind or traffic. Stacking reduces it.
Processing a long, variable-rate pressure record to recover the single constant-rate response it represents.
The full record of flow rates used in superposition.
How fast the bit deepens the hole, usually in feet or meters per hour. Abbreviated ROP.
Analyzing production rates and flowing pressures over time to find reservoir properties. Abbreviated RTA.
The part of skin that grows with flow rate because of non-Darcy flow, written D·q.
A hole in the rig floor where the kelly is stored during trips.
Estimating saturation from the ratio of shallow to deep resistivity.
An erosion surface cut by waves as the shoreline moves landward.
A quick stack made early in processing to check data.
Calculating the paths and travel times of seismic waves through a velocity model.
A surface wave with rolling, elliptical particle motion. On land it forms most of the ground roll.
A relation between sonic transit time and porosity that improves on Wyllie.
A common explosive used in perforating charges.
Going back into an existing well to deepen, sidetrack or repair it.
Shale rich in swelling clay that softens, swells and disperses when it absorbs water.
Another name for gas pseudopressure.
Data sent to surface while drilling.
A central room where engineers watch live data from wells and facilities and support field crews remotely.
A tool that enlarges or smooths the borehole to the full intended diameter.
A group of geophones or hydrophones wired together to suppress unwanted noise such as ground roll.
The distance between receiver stations along a line.
A line of receivers in a land 3D survey.
Fluid flowing down on the low side while other fluid flows up in deviated wells.
Base oil recovered from cuttings or used mud.
Mixing separator oil and gas samples in the ratio produced to rebuild the reservoir fluid.
Separator oil and gas samples mixed in the laboratory in the measured gas-oil ratio, to recreate the reservoir fluid.
Completing an existing well in a different zone, for example after the original zone is depleted.
How long each trace is recorded after the source fires, for example 6 or 8 seconds.
LWD data stored in tool memory and read after the tool returns.
The equipment that collects and stores signals from receivers.
Base oil reclaimed from cuttings or waste mud.
The fraction of the hydrocarbons in place that is produced or expected to be produced.
Change of crystal size or shape without change in mineral.
A reservoir model bounded on four sides.
A fold lying on its side with a nearly horizontal axial plane.
Converting reflectivity to impedance by stepping down trace by trace.
Gas that was not removed at surface and returns down the hole.
Processing that turns magnetic anomalies into what they would look like at the magnetic pole.
A mound built by corals, algae or other organisms. Buried reefs can be highly porous carbonate reservoirs.
A trap formed by a porous reef covered by a seal.
Tension held by the reel motor on coiled tubing between reel and injector.
The fraction of the wave amplitude reflected at a boundary: (Z<sub>2</sub> − Z<sub>1</sub>)/(Z<sub>2</sub> + Z<sub>1</sub>), where Z is the acoustic impedance.
The reflection coefficient at each layer boundary down a well.
Imaging the subsurface by recording waves reflected from rock boundaries.
The size of a reflection, an attribute used to spot bright spots.
The way reflections end against a surface, such as onlap or truncation.
Updating a velocity model by minimizing residual moveout on image gathers.
The sequence of reflection coefficients with time. Convolving it with the wavelet gives a synthetic trace.
Dolomite formed by dense brines from evaporating lagoons sinking through limestone.
Static corrections computed from refracted first arrivals to model the near surface.
A seismic survey that uses waves refracted along fast layers to map their depth and velocity.
Fracturing an existing well again to restore or increase production.
Permeability after exposure to a fluid divided by the original permeability.
The broad, deep part of a gravity or magnetic field.
A seaward shift of the shoreline as sea level falls or sediment builds out, leaving shallower sediments over deeper ones.
A surface cut by waves on the seafloor as sea level falls.
A standard measure of how volatile a crude oil or condensate is at 100 °F. Abbreviated RVP.
A quick estimate of impedance changes obtained by integrating the seismic trace.
Amplitudes that keep their ratios to each other but not absolute values.
A rock's permeability to one fluid when other fluids are also present, expressed as a fraction of the absolute permeability.
A polymer that reduces water flow more than oil flow. Abbreviated RPM.
Sea level measured against a local point, combining eustasy and local subsidence or uplift.
An oil-base mud allowed higher filtrate to drill faster.
A tilted zone that connects two overlapping normal faults.
A tool that lets the string disconnect from a stuck tool.
A spear that can be released from the fish if the fish won't come free.
Permanent magnetism a rock kept from when it formed.
Cement work done to repair a primary cement job or seal leaks.
Movement of hydrocarbons from one trap to another after the first trap changes.
Watching field equipment and wells from a distant location.
Monitoring and controlling field equipment from an onshore or central location instead of on site.
Studying the earth's surface from satellites or aircraft, for example to map geology and seeps.
A field device that collects sensor data and sends it to SCADA, often at remote wellsites. Abbreviated RTU.
A short interval logged twice to check the tool repeats its readings.
How closely two surveys over the same area match, key for 4D seismic.
Perforating a zone again to improve flow.
The velocity used to correct times from the floating datum to the final datum.
Mud kept in reserve pits for weighting up or replacing losses.
An earthen pit at a land wellsite used to hold waste mud and cuttings.
Quantities of petroleum expected to be recovered commercially from known accumulations, from a given date forward, under defined conditions.
Building a quantitative description of a reservoir: its shape, layering, rock and fluid properties and how they vary.
A part of a reservoir isolated by faults or barriers.
A long drawdown that measures the drainage volume of a well.
The pressure of the fluids in the reservoir. It falls as fluids are produced unless it is supported by an aquifer or injection.
A rock-quality measure equal to 0.0314 × √(k/φ), used in hydraulic flow unit analysis. Abbreviated RQI.
The chance that reservoir rock is absent or too poor.
A rock porous enough to store hydrocarbons and permeable enough to let them flow to a well.
Numerical modeling of fluid flow in a reservoir, used to forecast production and compare development options.
Increase in hydrogen sulfide in produced fluids, often from bacteria in water injection.
Totals and averages of net pay and properties for each zone.
The local anomaly left after removing the regional trend.
Oil or gas left in the flushed zone after invasion.
Curvature left on gathers after moveout correction, used to update the velocity model.
The oil saturation left behind in rock that has been swept by a displacing fluid, written S<sub>or</sub>.
A zone below an oil–water contact that holds oil at residual saturation, a target for CO<sub>2</sub> EOR. Abbreviated ROZ.
How much rock permeability stays reduced after polymer passes.
Small time corrections, found statistically from the data, that remain after field statics.
A graphite material that springs back after compression, used to seal fractures and strengthen the wellbore.
Pumping resin into the formation to consolidate sand or seal leaks.
Proppant with a resin coating that bonds grains together in the fracture to stop flowback.
How much a polymer solution reduces mobility compared with water.
A fracture that appears bright on resistivity images, usually because it is cemented.
Difference between vertical and horizontal resistivity, often caused by thin laminations.
A pad tool with many small electrodes that makes a resistivity picture of the borehole wall.
The ratio of true resistivity to wet resistivity, related to saturation. Symbol I.
A log of how strongly the formation resists electric current. Oil and gas do not conduct, so hydrocarbon-bearing rock reads higher than water-bearing rock.
Differences between deep and shallow resistivity curves, which show invasion and permeability.
An open data standard for exchanging reservoir models between software applications.
Acid made to react more slowly so it travels farther.
The average time liquid stays in a separator, which controls separation.
A small electric still that heats a measured mud sample to find its water, oil and solids content by volume.
Heating a mud sample to distill water and oil and find the volumes of liquids and solids.
A packer that can be released and pulled out of the well with the tubing.
Landward stepping-back of a shoreline as accommodation grows faster than sediment supply.
The formation of liquid when pressure drops in a gas-condensate reservoir, the opposite of what happens in most systems.
The permeability of a core after exposure to a fluid compared with before, a measure of how damaging the fluid is.
The lower limit on mixture stiffness, from averaging compliances by volume.
Repeated short-period reflections, such as within a water layer, that make the data ring.
A valve in a test string opened at the end of a test to circulate out produced fluids.
Pumping down the annulus and up the tubing or drillpipe, which brings returns up faster.
Pumping cement down the annulus and returning through the casing.
Combustion in which the burning front moves against the air flow.
A fault where the hanging wall has moved up relative to the footwall, caused by compression.
Circulate down the annulus and up the pipe to remove fluid or debris from the pipe.
A migration method that propagates waves backward in time through a velocity model, good for imaging steep dips and salt.
A survey with the source in the well and receivers at the surface.
A dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous forces that indicates whether flow is laminar or turbulent.
A plot of shear stress against shear rate for a fluid.
Properties that describe how a fluid flows, such as plastic viscosity, yield point and gel strength.
The study of how fluids deform and flow under stress. For mud it covers viscosity, yield stress and gel behavior at different shear rates.
An additive that changes low-shear viscosity and gel strength, especially in oil- and synthetic-base muds.
A common mnemonic for bulk density.
Husks of rice used as a flaky lost circulation material.
Natural gas with many heavier hydrocarbons.
A symmetric, zero-phase wavelet with one main peak and two side lobes, used widely in modeling.
A basin formed where the crust is stretched and pulled apart, bounded by normal faults.
The raised edge of a rift basin.
The working platform of the rig where the crew handles pipe and the driller controls the operation.
Moving a rig from one location to the next.
The time when a rig finishes work on a well and is released.
Assemble a rig or equipment ready to work.
A slurry that goes from fluid to set very quickly, which limits gas migration.
Well work done without a rig, using wireline, slickline, coiled tubing or pumping units.
A carbonate shelf with a reef or sand rim at its edge.
A piece of mud torn up by a current and deposited in sand.
Small ridges formed on sediment by flowing water or wind.
Extra mud weight so the well stays balanced if the riser is disconnected and its mud column is lost.
A system that holds a marine riser in tension.
Drilling top-hole sections offshore with returns to the seabed instead of a riser.
A quick lab method for estimating minimum miscibility pressure by watching a gas bubble rise through oil.
A resource estimate multiplied by its chance of success.
A delta built mainly by river input, often bird-foot shaped.
The root-mean-square amplitude in a window, often mapped to find bright spots.
The root-mean-square of interval velocities down to a reflector, approximately the velocity that best corrects normal moveout.
Noise in sonic logs from the tool scraping the borehole.
A three-parameter rheological model used for muds and cement slurries.
Minerals such as quartz, calcite or clay that grow between grains and bind them together, reducing porosity.
The fractional change in pore volume per unit change in pressure.
A number in Lucia's method describing carbonate pore geometry.
The study of how rock and fluid properties control seismic velocity, density and other measurements.
A crossplot showing where rocks of different lithology, porosity and fluid should fall, used to interpret elastic properties.
Grouping rocks into classes that share similar pore structure and flow behavior, so properties can be assigned consistently in a model.
A lab test that heats rock samples to measure their hydrocarbon content, generating potential and maturity (T<sub>max</sub>).
A cement plug that seals across the whole wellbore, casing and annulus included.
A tool for recovering parted sucker rods.
Pulling and running sucker rods to repair a rod pump well.
The sucker rods connecting a surface pumping unit to a downhole pump.
A bit with two or three rotating cones whose steel teeth or tungsten carbide inserts crush and gouge the rock.
A reamer with rollers that keeps hole gauge and reduces torque.
A fold formed in the hanging wall of a curved growth fault.
A thick, rope-like underflow from an overloaded hydrocyclone.
The fitting that attaches wire to the top of a toolstring.
Drilling by turning a bit on a string of pipe while circulating fluid.
A cutting shoe on washpipe used to wash over a fish.
A sidewall core drilled from the borehole wall, less damaged than a percussion sample.
A downhole tool that steers the bit while the entire drillstring keeps rotating, giving a smoother hole and better hole cleaning than sliding with a motor.
The turntable in the rig floor that rotates the drillstring on rigs without a top drive. It also holds the slips.
A jetting tool whose nozzles spin to clean the full pipe wall.
A concentric-cylinder instrument, often called a Fann viscometer, that reads dial deflection at fixed speeds such as 600, 300, 6 and 3 rpm.
A member of the rig floor crew who handles pipe and equipment. Also called a floorhand.
How smooth and rounded grain edges are, a sign of transport distance.
Standard core measurements of porosity, permeability, fluid saturations and grain density. Abbreviated RCA.
A share of production, or of its value, paid to the mineral owner or government, free of production costs.
True resistivity of the undisturbed formation beyond the invaded zone.
The step-by-step plan for running completion equipment.
A tool that carries a device downhole and releases it once it is set.
A thin disk that bursts at a set pressure to protect equipment.
Resistivity of the formation water.
Calculating apparent water resistivity in each zone; the lowest values suggest water-bearing zones.
Resistivity of the flushed zone near the borehole.
A well that builds angle, holds it, then drops back toward vertical.
A shear wave in which particles move at right angles to the direction of travel. It cannot travel through liquids or gases.
The speed of shear waves in a material. Symbol Vs.
Free hydrocarbons in a rock, released at low temperature in Rock-Eval pyrolysis.
Hydrocarbons released by cracking kerogen in Rock-Eval pyrolysis, the remaining potential.
Carbon dioxide released from kerogen in Rock-Eval pyrolysis.
A flat coastal salt plain in an arid climate where evaporites form within the sediment.
A standard bag of mud material, usually 100 lb for barite or 50 lb for many chemicals.
A blade at the hopper used to open bags of additives.
A connection that can be released easily to leave a stuck tool behind.
Steam-assisted gravity drainage: steam from an upper horizontal well heats bitumen that drains to a lower producer.
The path a seismic vessel follows while recording.
The amount of salt dissolved in water.
Working out formation water salinity from SP, resistivity or samples.
Grading the salinity of injected slugs so the surfactant passes through optimal conditions in the reservoir.
How well a chemical keeps working in salty water.
A basin with thick salt that controls structure and traps.
A sheet of salt that has spread sideways over younger sediment.
Salt from drilled salt or saltwater influx entering a fresh water-base mud, which flocculates the clay.
The salt in crude oil, often reported in pounds per thousand barrels.
Slow flow of salt into the wellbore that can squeeze casing or stick pipe.
A body of salt that has pierced upward through overlying layers.
Washing out of salt by undersaturated mud, enlarging the hole.
A column of salt that has risen through overlying rock, bending the layers around it and often forming traps on its flanks.
The steep side of a salt body, where traps often form against the salt.
Attapulgite clay, which builds viscosity in salt water.
A gentle swell of salt beneath unbroken overlying layers.
Deformation caused by the flow of buried salt, which forms domes, walls and traps.
A trap formed against or above a salt body.
A long ridge of salt that rose through overlying layers.
Influx of salt water from a formation into the well.
A thin remnant where a salt layer has flowed away, leaving the rocks above and below nearly touching.
Flow of salt away from an area, causing the layers above to sink.
Water holding as much salt as it can dissolve.
A pressure-rated bottle that collects reservoir fluid downhole and keeps it at pressure.
Heating and agitating a sample in the lab to bring it back to a single phase.
A pressure vessel used to store and ship fluid samples.
A written description of cuttings from each interval.
Moving a sample from one cylinder to another without changing its phase.
Checking a sample's opening pressure, bubble point and contamination to confirm it is representative.
A pressure-rated container for fluid samples.
The time between digital samples on a seismic trace, commonly 2 or 4 milliseconds.
A place where fluid samples are taken during a test.
The plan for which samples to take, where, how and how many.
Grains between 0.0625 and 2 mm. In mud testing, solids that won't pass a 200-mesh screen.
A bailer with a valve at the bottom used to pick up sand.
Removing sand that has filled the bottom of a well.
Treating the formation with resin to bind sand grains together.
The volume percent of particles larger than 74 µm (API sand) in a mud, measured with a sieve and graduated tube.
Washing mud through a 200-mesh screen to measure the volume of sand-size solids.
Methods that stop formation sand from entering the well and eroding or plugging equipment, including screens, gravel packs, frac packs and consolidation.
A sensor that detects sand in the flow, usually by sound.
Equipment in a well-test spread that removes sand from the flow before it reaches the choke.
Separating and disposing of sand produced with oil.
Estimating whether and when a well will produce sand.
Formation sand carried into the well with the produced fluids, which erodes equipment and fills the wellbore.
A laboratory test of how well a screen or gravel holds back a given formation sand.
A filter tube, such as wire-wrapped, premium mesh or expandable, placed across the reservoir to keep formation sand out of the well.
Fines or mud blocking screen openings, which cuts production.
The first compartment below the shale shaker, where coarse solids that pass the screens can settle out.
A sedimentary rock made of sand-sized grains, mostly quartz, bound by cement or clay. It is one of the main reservoir rock types.
The line on a neutron-density crossplot where clean, water-filled sandstone plots.
A pressure gauge using a sapphire sensing element.
Splitting crude into saturates, aromatics, resins and asphaltenes.
Gravity mapped from satellite measurements.
Using satellite images to watch sites, emissions or ground movement.
Oil at its bubblepoint pressure, holding as much dissolved gas as it can at that pressure.
A water-base mud saturated with sodium chloride, used to drill salt sections without dissolving them.
The water-saturation exponent n in the Archie equation, often taken as 2.
An equation that gives water saturation from height above free water and rock quality.
Repeating cased-hole logs over time to track changes in saturation.
The bubblepoint pressure of an oil or the dew point pressure of a gas condensate.
A rule for sizing gravel at about five to six times the median formation grain size.
A sub below the top drive that takes the wear of repeated connections.
Wood particles used as a fibrous lost circulation material.
Supervisory control and data acquisition: a system that collects data from remote field equipment and allows operators to control it from a central location.
Mineral deposits, such as calcium carbonate or barium sulfate, that build up in perforations, tubing and surface equipment and restrict flow.
A chemical, such as a chelating agent, that dissolves scale too hard for acid.
A chemical that prevents mineral scale from forming.
Pumping scale inhibitor into the formation so it slowly returns with produced water and prevents scale.
Taking out mineral scale from tubing or perforations by chemicals or milling.
How likely a water is to deposit scale under given conditions.
A thin spot machined in a gun carrier where each charge fires through.
A coarse first shaker that removes large cuttings and gumbo.
A microscope that images rock surfaces at high magnification. Abbreviated SEM.
Apparent energy loss caused by waves scattering off small features.
A metamorphic rock with platy minerals aligned in layers.
A biopolymer viscosifier that tolerates salt and temperature well, used in drilling fluids and polymer flooding.
How easily liquid passes through a screen, per API RP 13C.
Wear of a sand screen by high-velocity, sandy flow.
A quick test of polymer solution elasticity by timing flow through screens.
The number of openings per linear inch of a shaker screen.
A replaceable frame holding shaker screen cloth.
A sudden pressure rise during fracturing when proppant bridges and blocks the fracture or perforations, stopping the treatment.
An NMR permeability estimate from porosity and the log mean T2.
A low-permeability rock, such as shale or salt, that stops hydrocarbons from escaping a trap. Also called cap rock.
Elastomer seals on the bottom of the tubing that slide into a packer bore to seal while allowing some movement.
The height of hydrocarbon column a seal can hold before capillary leakage.
The chance that a seal is absent or leaks.
A fault that stops flow, seen in a test as a doubling of the semilog slope.
In a test near one sealing fault, the semilog slope doubles and the derivative steps up to twice its radial-flow level.
A nipple in which a pump or plug seats.
Bentonite or attapulgite mixed in seawater.
A water-base mud made with seawater, common offshore for top-hole sections.
The backup barrier if the primary fails, such as casing and BOP.
A surfactant that strengthens the emulsion and oil-wets solids in an invert mud.
An explosive that needs a strong shock to start, such as RDX or HMX in charges.
Movement of hydrocarbons through carrier beds toward a trap.
Porosity created after deposition, for example by dissolution, dolomitization or fracturing.
Adding energy to a reservoir by injecting water or gas to keep up pressure and displace oil.
A mill that cuts away a length of casing, often for sidetracks or abandonment.
Milling away a length of casing to expose the formation, for abandonment plugs or sidetracking.
How much a sediment has been sorted and weathered toward quartz.
A low area of the crust where thick sediment has accumulated over time. Oil and gas are found in sedimentary basins.
Rock formed from deposited sediment or chemical precipitation, such as sandstone, shale and limestone. Nearly all petroleum is found in it.
A feature formed during deposition, such as ripples, cross-beds or mud cracks.
A starting pick used by autotracking.
A slow, continuous loss of mud into permeable formations, usually under about 10 barrels per hour.
Data and reporting standards published by the Society of Exploration Geophysicists.
The field format standard for recorded seismic data.
The standard file format for exchanging seismic data, defined by the Society of Exploration Geophysicists.
Flow in which phases separate into layers, as in horizontal wells.
The fieldwork of recording seismic data: laying out sources and receivers and firing the survey.
The height of a seismic reflection. It depends on impedance contrast, tuning, attenuation and processing.
A seismic feature that departs from the background, such as an amplitude or velocity anomaly.
Loss of seismic energy, especially high frequencies, as waves travel through rock.
A quantity derived from seismic data, such as amplitude, frequency or coherence, that helps reveal geology or fluids.
Comparing attributes with well data to predict reservoir properties between wells.
A map of an attribute extracted along a horizon.
The range of frequencies in seismic data. Wider bandwidth gives sharper resolution.
A channel imaged in seismic, often by amplitude or edge attributes.
The look of a reflection, its amplitude, frequency, continuity and shape, used to correlate and interpret.
The team that lays out equipment and records a seismic survey.
A collection of seismic surveys and their metadata.
The reference level to which seismic times are corrected, such as mean sea level or a flat elevation.
Any alignment on seismic data that represents a single arrival, such as a reflection, refraction or multiple.
A group of reflections with distinct character, such as amplitude, continuity and geometry, interpreted as a type of deposit.
Grouping reflections by pattern to infer depositional settings.
The number of traces that sample the same subsurface point and are stacked together. Higher fold improves signal-to-noise.
Calculating the seismic response of a rock model.
Studying the shapes of buried landscapes seen in seismic slices.
A reflector that has been picked and mapped across a seismic survey, usually representing a geological surface.
How well seismic waves reach and return from a target, which controls image quality.
Noise from another seismic crew working nearby.
Creating virtual sources by cross-correlating recordings at different receivers, for example from ambient noise.
Mapping horizons, faults and amplitude features on seismic data to build a picture of the subsurface.
Programs used to view seismic and map horizons and faults.
The sequence of steps from loading seismic to final maps.
Converting seismic reflection data into a model of rock properties such as acoustic impedance.
A 2D survey line, or the vertical section recorded along it.
A processing step that moves dipping reflections to their true positions and collapses diffractions, giving a sharper image.
Seismic energy that has bounced more than once, for example between the sea surface and the seabed. It can be mistaken for a real reflector.
Positioning sources and receivers accurately during acquisition, mostly with GPS and acoustic networks.
The horizontal distance between a seismic source and a receiver.
The convention for whether an increase in acoustic impedance is shown as a peak or a trough on the seismic display.
Estimating pore pressure ahead of drilling from seismic interval velocities.
Turning raw field records into an interpretable image through steps such as deconvolution, velocity analysis, stacking and migration.
Energy returned toward the surface from a boundary where the acoustic impedance changes.
The bending of a seismic wave as it passes into a layer of different velocity. Refracted waves are used to study the near surface.
Processing old seismic data again with newer methods to get a better image.
Using seismic data to map reservoir properties such as porosity, thickness and fluid between wells.
The smallest separation between two features that seismic data can show. Vertically it is roughly one quarter of the dominant wavelength.
The thinnest layer whose top and base can be separated, about one quarter of a wavelength.
Seismic energy redirected in many directions by small heterogeneities.
A vertical display of seismic traces along a line.
A package of reflections bounded by unconformities.
A device that generates seismic energy, such as an air gun, vibrator or explosive charge.
Interpreting depositional sequences from the geometry of seismic reflections, such as onlap, downlap and truncation.
A long cable towed behind a survey vessel that holds the hydrophones for marine seismic.
A survey that sends sound waves into the ground and records the echoes from rock boundaries to image the subsurface.
Choosing source and receiver layout, spacing, offsets and fold to image a target at an acceptable cost.
Building a velocity model by inverting travel times measured along many ray paths.
The record of ground motion or pressure against time at one receiver position.
The range of possible depths, amplitudes or properties from seismic.
The speed at which seismic waves travel through rock. It is needed to convert time to depth and to image the data correctly.
A ship equipped to tow seismic sources and streamers.
Displaying seismic in 2D and 3D to aid interpretation.
A 3D block of seismic data that can be sliced in any direction.
The short pulse of seismic energy that is reflected from each boundary. A seismic trace is the sum of overlapping wavelets.
Recording checkshots during drilling with sensors in the BHA.
Adjusting seismic interpretation and attributes to agree with measured well data.
A sensitive instrument that records ground motion, used in earthquake and passive monitoring.
A system that fires gun sections one at a time on one run.
A switch system that fires several perforating guns one at a time on a single run.
A completion that lets zones be opened or shut individually, for example with sliding sleeves.
Measuring each layer's inflow at several rates with production logs. Abbreviated SIP.
A landing nipple that lets tools be set at chosen depths in a string of identical nipples.
Blocking high-permeability zones, for example with microbial growth or gels.
Acid that thickens as it spends, diverting fresh acid into less treated zones.
Cement that swells to reseal cracks when hydrocarbons contact it.
Measuring natural voltages in the ground.
A measure of how well traces agree along a trial moveout curve, used in velocity analysis.
A plot of pressure against log of time, where radial flow forms a straight line.
A floating rig supported on submerged pontoons and columns, which make it very stable in rough seas.
Combining data from several sensors for a better estimate.
The distance from a sensor to the bit.
The distance between two wells divided by their combined uncertainty, used in anti-collision.
A pressure vessel that separates the wellstream into gas and liquid, or into gas, oil and water.
The pressure and temperature in a separator when samples and rates are taken.
Gas from the separator divided by oil from the separator.
A PVT test that flashes oil through one or more separator stages to find the best separator conditions.
A fibrous clay viscosifier stable at high temperature and in salt water.
An unconformity, and the surface that continues from it, formed when relative sea level falls.
Interpreting sedimentary layers as packages bounded by surfaces linked to changes in sea level and sediment supply.
A geostatistical method that fills a grid with continuous properties such as porosity, honoring the data and the variogram while showing realistic variability.
A geostatistical method for distributing categories such as facies across a reservoir grid.
A petroleum agreement in which a contractor performs exploration and production for the state in return for a fee or a share of proceeds. It is the model used in the Philippines.
The tool used to run, set and pack a gravel pack assembly.
The area of rig floor where stands of pipe stand during trips.
A tool that sets packers or plugs mechanically, hydraulically or by explosive.
A mud pit in which solids are allowed to settle before the fluid moves on.
The speed at which a particle falls through a fluid.
A pattern with one well in the center of six others in a hexagon.
A tool that cuts pipe downhole.
The woven wire mesh panel on a shale shaker that separates cuttings from mud.
A fine-grained, laminated sedimentary rock of clay and silt. It acts as a seal or source rock, and in some plays as a reservoir.
A test that measures how much shale sticks to a steel bar rolled in mud.
The density of shale cuttings, which can track compaction and pressure.
A body of overpressured shale that has risen through overlying layers.
Shale breaking apart into fine particles in water-base mud.
Natural gas held in, and produced directly from, fine-grained, organic-rich shale, using horizontal wells and multistage fracturing.
The fraction of shale that has slid past a point on a fault, used to estimate whether the fault seals.
Reducing the reaction of shale with drilling fluid, chemically or by sealing.
A mud additive, such as potassium chloride, glycol or an amine, that reduces the swelling and dispersion of water-sensitive shale.
Light oil produced from shale or adjacent tight rocks with horizontal wells and fracturing. Also called tight oil. Not the same as oil shale.
The log values chosen to represent pure shale.
A vibrating screen that removes drilled cuttings from the mud returning from the well. It is the first and most important piece of solids-control equipment.
Screen openings plugged by near-size particles or sticky clay, which cuts shaker capacity.
The fraction of the rock that is shale, written V<sub>sh</sub>, often estimated from the gamma ray log.
Gas trapped at shallow depth that can flow uncontrollably before a BOP is installed.
Features near the seabed or surface, such as shallow gas, faults or unstable sediment, that threaten drilling.
A resistivity reading near the borehole, mostly in the invaded zone.
Overpressured water sand near the seabed that flows into the well.
Sandstone containing clay, whose conductivity makes the basic Archie equation overestimate water saturation.
An explosive charge with a cone-shaped metal liner. On detonation it forms a very high-speed jet that pierces casing, cement and rock.
Polymer molecules being broken by high shear, for example at the bit nozzles or pumps, which lowers viscosity.
The product of density and shear-wave velocity. Combined with acoustic impedance it helps separate rock and fluid effects.
Resistance of a material to shape change, which controls S-wave velocity.
A pin designed to break at a set force, releasing or activating a tool.
A BOP ram that cuts through pipe to seal the well in an emergency.
How quickly fluid layers move past one another, in reciprocal seconds.
The force per unit area that causes a fluid to flow.
A drop in apparent viscosity as shear rate increases. Mud should be thin at the bit and thicker in the slow-moving annulus.
A shear wave dividing into fast and slow waves in anisotropic rock, used to detect fracture orientation.
A pump that applies high shear to help polymers and clays hydrate.
The edge of the shelf where the seafloor steepens into the slope.
A large area of exposed old crystalline rock in a continent.
A slickline tool that engages a sliding sleeve to open or close it.
The sharp saturation jump at the leading edge of a waterflood in Buckley-Leverett theory.
Sudden pressure and force on tools and tubing when guns fire.
A sub that absorbs axial vibration in the drillstring.
The casing between the float shoe and float collar, which holds cement left inside.
The zone between low tide and the depth where waves stop moving sediment, often forming well-sorted sand bodies.
A multiple that arrives soon after its primary and changes the wavelet shape.
The near detector on a density or neutron tool, used to correct for mudcake.
The number of perforations per unit length of gun, usually in shots per foot (spf).
The depth of the explosive charge below the surface.
All the traces recorded from a single source firing, displayed side by side.
A drilled hole that holds an explosive charge for land seismic.
The distance or time between successive shots.
The location where a seismic source is fired.
A log reading affected by neighboring beds when a bed is thin.
Signs of hydrocarbons in cuttings, mud or gas while drilling.
Paper shreds used as a fibrous lost circulation material.
Reduction in oil volume as gas comes out of solution when pressure and temperature fall.
The fraction of separator oil volume that remains when the oil is brought to stock-tank conditions and more gas leaves it.
A simplified form of the Zoeppritz equations that expresses reflectivity as intercept plus gradient times sin²θ.
A tube on a screen that carries slurry past any bridges, so gravel can still reach the whole interval.
Close a well so it stops flowing.
The pressure read on the annulus at surface after the well is shut in on a kick. Abbreviated SICP.
The pressure on the drillpipe at surface once the well is shut in after a kick. Added to the mud hydrostatic pressure, it gives formation pressure and the kill mud weight. Abbreviated SIDPP.
A production logging run made with the well closed, to check crossflow and calibrate.
A temperature log run after a well has been shut in.
The pressure at the wellhead with the well closed. Abbreviated SIWHP.
A tubing section with an offset pocket that holds a gas-lift valve or other device, which can be replaced by slickline.
A towed acoustic system that maps the texture and objects on the seabed to the sides of its track.
Iron carbonate, a dense cement in some sandstones and shales.
Drilling a new hole that departs from an existing wellbore, to bypass a problem or reach a new target.
A small rock plug taken from the borehole wall, either shot in by a gun or cut with a rotary bit.
Measuring grain size distribution by passing sand through stacked screens.
A pulsed neutron log of capture cross section used to monitor saturation behind casing.
A drilling-data method that estimates pore pressure from normalized drilling rate.
An S-shaped clinoform formed when sea level rises during progradation.
The strength of the wanted signal relative to noise. Higher values give cleaner data. Abbreviated S/N.
A lump sum a company pays the government when a petroleum contract is signed.
Fine ground quartz added to cement to prevent strength loss above about 230 °F.
A water-base mud containing sodium or potassium silicate, which gels in shale pores and helps stabilize them.
Made of silicate grains such as quartz and feldspar.
A sedimentary rock made mostly of silt-sized grains, between sand and clay in size.
The period from about 444 to 419 million years ago.
A water-saturation equation that adds a shale-conductivity term to Archie's equation for shaly sands.
Fracturing two or more wells at the same time.
Gas chromatography that estimates a crude's boiling point distribution.
Inverting several angle stacks together to estimate P-impedance, S-impedance and density.
Firing two or more sources so close in time that their records overlap.
Injecting water and gas together instead of alternating them. Abbreviated SWAG.
A well completed to produce one zone through one tubing string.
A sample kept above its saturation pressure so it stays one phase.
A test that injects and back-produces a tracer from one well to measure residual oil saturation in place. Abbreviated SWCTT.
The curve a plane makes on an unrolled borehole image, used to measure dip.
Pipe bending into a snake-like wave under compression, before helical buckling.
Returning a well site to its natural state after abandonment.
A high-resolution survey of a planned well or platform location to check for seabed and shallow hazards.
Ground calcium carbonate in controlled particle sizes, used for bridging and weighting. Acid-soluble, so it can be cleaned up.
Ground salt in controlled sizes used as bridging material in saturated brines; it dissolves later in undersaturated water.
Limestone made of whole or broken organism skeletons.
A tank in which produced water stands long enough for oil to float to the top and be skimmed off.
A dimensionless number for the extra pressure drop near the wellbore. Positive skin means damage; negative skin means stimulation, such as a fracture.
The depth at which an electromagnetic field falls to about 37 percent of its surface value.
Collecting cuttings in skips offshore and sending them to shore for treatment.
A test that measures how much shale breaks down when tumbled in fluid.
A fine metamorphic rock that splits into thin sheets, formed from shale.
A polished, striated fault surface that shows the slip direction.
A single, smooth steel wire used to run, set and retrieve mechanical tools in a well. It carries no electrical signal.
A low-viscosity fracturing fluid made of water with a small amount of friction reducer, pumped at high rates.
Drilling with a bent motor without rotating the string, to change direction.
A tubing component with ports that can be opened or closed, usually by slickline, to let fluid flow between the annulus and the tubing.
A well drilled with smaller hole sizes than normal to save cost.
A lab test that displaces oil from a long, thin sand-packed tube at several pressures to find the minimum miscibility pressure.
Moving drill line through the blocks and cutting off the worn end to spread wear.
A telescoping joint that lets a test string lengthen and shorten.
The difference in velocity between two phases flowing together, such as oil rising faster than water.
How much slower cuttings rise than the mud carrying them.
Starting a vibroseis sweep before the previous one ends, to speed acquisition.
Wedges set in the rotary table that hold the drillstring while connections are made.
A liner with machined slots that holds back coarse sand while letting fluids in; a simple, low-cost sand control method.
Shale that falls into the borehole from the wall, causing tight hole, fill and stuck pipe.
A reduced pump rate, and the pressure it needs, recorded regularly so a kill can start at a known pressure. Abbreviated SCR.
The inverse of velocity, usually in microseconds per foot.
Processing that finds wave slowness from coherence across receivers. Abbreviated STC.
A small volume of heavier mud pumped down the drillpipe before a trip, so the pipe comes out dry.
A large vessel or set of pipe fingers at a pipeline's end that absorbs liquid slugs before processing.
A multiphase flow pattern of large gas bubbles alternating with liquid slugs, which causes pressure surges.
The volume of a chemical or solvent slug, usually as a fraction of pore volume.
Pump a heavy slug before tripping so the pipe pulls dry.
A block of sediment that slides downslope and is folded or deformed internally.
Grinding cuttings into a slurry so they can be injected.
The weight per volume of a cement slurry.
Settling of solids in a cement slurry, which makes the set cement uneven.
A frac stage pumping fluid that carries proppant.
The volume of slurry made from one sack of cement.
A field fitted with sensors, controls and software for integrated management.
Injection water with its ion makeup adjusted to improve oil recovery.
A swelling clay mineral group, including montmorillonite, that absorbs water and causes shale instability.
An AVO approximation that gives P- and S-velocity reflectivity, used for the fluid factor.
Burning test oil with air or water injection so it makes little smoke.
The rule linking the angles of incident and transmitted waves to the velocities on each side of a boundary.
Running pipe into or out of a well while it is under pressure, using hydraulic jacks to push the pipe against the well pressure.
The force needed to push pipe into a well against pressure.
Equipment that pushes pipe into a well under pressure.
The time a well stays shut in after steam injection in cyclic steaming.
Sodium carbonate, used to remove calcium from mud and make-up water.
A phosphate (SAPP) used to thin mud and treat cement contamination.
Bicarbonate of soda, used to treat cement contamination in water-base mud.
A single-salt brine reaching about 12.5 ppg, used where calcium must be avoided.
Soda ash, a common alkali for flooding and for treating calcium in mud.
Common salt, used in brines up to about 10 ppg and in saturated salt muds.
A formate salt making brines up to about 1.3 SG.
A phosphate thinner and calcium sequestrant for low-temperature water-base mud.
An alkali used in flooding that tolerates hard water better than carbonate.
A synthetic polymer used as a thinner at low molecular weight or for fluid-loss control at high molecular weight.
Water glass: the main additive in silicate mud, which forms a seal on shale.
An oxygen scavenger added to water-base mud and brines to reduce corrosion.
Slowly increasing air-gun output so marine animals can move away.
Folding or disruption of layers before they hardened.
Mixing drilling waste with binders so it becomes solid for disposal.
Calculating amounts of high- and low-gravity solids from retort and mud weight.
The volume percent of solids in mud.
Removing drilled solids from mud with shakers, hydrocyclones and centrifuges, so that density, viscosity and wear stay under control.
The fraction of drilled solids removed by the solids-control system.
Mud solids entering the formation.
A clear brine or polymer fluid without suspended solids, used to avoid plugging the reservoir.
Volume of oil or water dissolved in a microemulsion per volume of surfactant.
Calcium and magnesium that dissolve from barite, limited by the barite specification.
A drive mechanism in which gas coming out of solution in the oil expands and pushes oil to the wells. Recovery is usually low.
The volume of gas dissolved in oil at reservoir conditions, per barrel of stock-tank oil. Written R<sub>s</sub>.
Oil leaching from a cuttings sample into a solvent, which shows the oil is present and movable.
Injecting a solvent that mixes with oil to displace it.
Placing a solvent in a well and letting it sit to dissolve wax or asphaltene deposits.
A pill of solvent that dissolves oil-mud residue from pipe walls.
SAGD with a light hydrocarbon solvent added to the steam to lower viscosity further and reduce the steam-oil ratio.
The sensor section of a logging tool.
Difference in sonic velocity with direction, caused by stress or fractures.
The growing difference between sonic-log integrated time and checkshot time with depth, corrected before well ties.
A log of how long a sound wave takes to travel through the formation (interval transit time). It is used for porosity, mechanical properties and seismic ties.
Porosity calculated from sonic transit time.
The full recorded acoustic signal from a sonic tool.
How similar in size the grains of a sediment are. Well-sorted sand usually has higher porosity and permeability.
Crude oil with high sulfur content.
Natural gas containing significant hydrogen sulfide.
Equipment rated to resist cracking by hydrogen sulfide.
Several sources, such as air guns, fired together to shape and strengthen the pulse.
How deep a marine source is towed, which affects ghost notches and output.
A line of source points in a land 3D survey.
A rock rich in organic matter that has generated, or can generate, oil and gas when buried and heated enough.
The reaction rates that control how fast kerogen turns into oil and gas with temperature.
The shape of the pulse a seismic source emits, measured or modeled so processing can remove it.
A ship that tows only a source, used in multi-vessel surveys.
The compass direction from source to receiver, important in surveys designed to study anisotropy.
The SP reading in shale, used as the reference.
Formation water resistivity calculated from the static SP and mud filtrate resistivity.
Adjusting tubing length so the hanger lands correctly with seals in place.
A fluid pumped between mud and cement to keep them from mixing and to help clean the annulus.
A mechanical slickline jar with sliding links that delivers blows.
Clear, coarse calcite crystals that fill pores in limestone as cement.
A high-resolution marine seismic source that discharges an electrical spark in the water.
Inversion that assumes few, strong reflectors to estimate a blocky impedance.
Aliasing of steep events caused by receivers or traces spaced too far apart.
A fishing tool that enters the inside of a lost tubular and grips it from within.
Advanced core tests such as relative permeability, capillary pressure, wettability and electrical properties. Abbreviated SCAL.
The ratio of a substance's density to that of water (for liquids and solids) or air (for gases).
Splitting seismic data into frequency bands to reveal thin beds and channels that tune at particular frequencies.
A log that splits natural radioactivity into potassium, thorium and uranium.
A gamma ray log that separates the contributions of potassium, thorium and uranium, which helps identify clay types and radioactive sands.
Flattening the frequency spectrum of seismic data to widen its usable bandwidth.
Acid that has reacted and lost its strength.
Restoring amplitude lost as the wavefront spreads with distance.
A flow regime in which fluid converges in three dimensions, as toward a short perforated interval. The derivative has a −½ slope.
Deconvolution designed to compress the wavelet into a sharp spike, widening bandwidth.
A very dense brine added to raise the density of a lighter brine.
The lowest point of a trap. Once a trap is filled to this level, extra hydrocarbons spill out and migrate further.
The chart method a density tool uses to correct for mudcake using two detectors.
Relating spinner speed to fluid velocity using passes at different cable speeds.
Processing multipass spinner data to separate cable speed from fluid velocity.
A production logging tool with an impeller that turns faster as fluid velocity increases. It is used to measure flow profiles.
The change in spinner speed per change in fluid velocity.
The fluid velocity below which a spinner does not turn.
An instrument that measures very low interfacial tension from a drop's shape in a spinning tube.
A drill collar with spiral grooves that reduce contact and differential sticking.
An overshot grapple shaped like a coil spring.
A borehole with a corkscrew shape, which disturbs logs.
Charges arranged in a spiral around the gun.
Long, thin cavings that often mean the mud weight is too low.
A receiver layout with receivers on both sides of the source.
Coring with a sponge liner that traps fluids leaking from the core, to measure saturation.
A fluid drawn into rock by capillary forces without pressure.
A natural voltage measured between the mud and the formation. It is caused by the salinity contrast between mud filtrate and formation water and helps identify permeable beds. Abbreviated SP.
A small volume of special fluid placed across a stuck section of pipe to soak the filter cake and help free differentially stuck pipe.
A fan-shaped underflow from a hydrocyclone working properly.
To start drilling a new well. The spud date is when drilling begins.
A simple, cheap mud, often bentonite and water, used to drill the first hole section.
The start of drilling a new well.
The burst of filtrate that passes into the formation before a filter cake forms.
Forcing cement under pressure into perforations, channels behind casing or casing leaks to seal them.
Flow with steady rates and pressures, needed for valid test measurements.
A bottomhole assembly tool with blades that keeps the collars centered and helps control the hole's direction.
A drilling fluid of gas bubbles in liquid with a foaming agent, used for underbalanced and low-pressure drilling.
Adding together seismic traces that sample the same subsurface point, which strengthens the signal and cancels random noise.
How parasequences stack: progradational, aggradational or retrogradational.
The velocity that best flattens a reflection on a common-midpoint gather before stacking.
Cementing a long string in two or more stages using a stage tool.
The length of lateral treated in one fracturing stage.
A casing component with ports opened to cement the upper stage. Also called a DV tool.
Rows of injectors and producers offset by half a spacing.
Two, three or four joints of pipe screwed together and racked in the derrick during a trip.
A sand screen run without gravel, used in well-sorted, clean sands.
Reference conditions for reporting volumes, in US oilfield practice usually 60 °F and 14.696 psia.
A cubic foot of gas at standard conditions. Abbreviated scf.
A one-way valve in tubing that holds fluid in the string.
The gap between a logging tool and the borehole wall, which affects some measurements.
The vertical pipe on the rig floor that carries mud from the pumps up to the hose and top drive. Pump pressure is read here.
A low-cost polymer used for fluid-loss control in water-base and saturated-salt muds.
A time shift applied to land seismic traces to remove the effects of elevation and the near-surface weathered layer.
Fluid loss into the formation while the mud is not moving, as measured in the standard filter press tests.
The gel strength cement develops at rest as it begins to set.
Measuring pressure at several depths in a shut-in well to find fluid levels and densities.
Mud lost to the formation while not circulating.
A 3D grid that holds the reservoir's structure, layering and rock properties, built before any flow simulation.
An elastic modulus measured by loading a sample, usually lower than the dynamic one.
The density of mud measured at rest at surface.
The pressure in a pipe measured without the effect of flow velocity.
A test that checks whether discharged mud or cuttings leave an oil sheen on water.
The largest SP deflection possible in a thick clean bed, used to find water resistivity. Abbreviated SSP.
The ideal SP deflection in a thick, clean, water-bearing bed, used to calculate R<sub>w</sub>. Abbreviated SSP.
A reading taken with the tool held still at one depth.
Slips fixed to the snubbing unit that hold the pipe between strokes.
Flow in which pressure at every point doesn't change with time.
The distance at which pressure is assumed constant in steady-state flow.
When injected steam reaches a producer.
The steam-filled zone that grows above and around the injector in SAGD, where heated bitumen drains along its edges.
Vaporization of light oil components by steam, which helps recovery.
Foam made with steam to reduce steam override.
A boiler that makes steam for injection.
A heater that warms well fluids during a test to prevent hydrates and wax.
Injecting steam to heat heavy oil and lower its viscosity.
The mass fraction of steam that is vapor rather than hot liquid water. Higher quality carries more heat per pound.
Managing SAGD producers so steam doesn't flow straight into them.
The part of a reservoir heated to steam temperature.
A thermal method that uses a pair of horizontal wells: steam injected through the upper well heats the bitumen, which drains by gravity to the lower producer. Abbreviated SAGD.
The volume of steam (as cold-water equivalent) injected per volume of oil produced, the key efficiency measure of thermal projects. Abbreviated SOR.
Continuous steam injection into injectors to heat and drive oil to producers.
Weight bars in a slickline toolstring that help it fall and add impact. Also called sinker bars.
Lowering rate in steps to separate perforation friction from tortuosity.
Injecting at increasing rates in steps to find the pressure at which the formation fractures.
A biomarker derived from sterols, used for source and maturity.
Torsional vibration where the bit stops and then spins fast in cycles.
A polygon plot of major ions used to compare water samples.
Foam thickened with polymer or bentonite to carry larger cuttings.
A method that predicts waterflood performance in layered reservoirs.
The volume of rock around a well whose permeability has been effectively increased by the fracture network. Abbreviated SRV.
A tank at the lease where treated oil is stored at atmospheric pressure before it is sold.
Gas released from oil per barrel at stock-tank conditions.
Oil at standard surface conditions after gas has been separated. Measured in stock-tank barrels (STB).
A fast frequency-wavenumber migration for constant velocity.
A slow wave that travels along the borehole wall. It is sensitive to open fractures and permeability.
The right and duty of every worker to stop any task they believe is unsafe.
In a dual-porosity model, the fraction of total storage in the fractures. Written ω.
A pressure gauge that measures deflection with strain-sensitive wires.
A broad coastal plain of beach ridges.
A slice through a seismic volume that follows a geological surface proportionally between two horizons.
Phases flowing in separate layers in horizontal pipe.
A diagram showing the sequence of rock units in an area, with their thickness and age.
A surface used as the zero level when hanging well logs for correlation.
A trap formed by changes in rock type or by erosion, such as a sand that pinches out into shale, a reef or an unconformity.
The study of rock layers: their order, ages and how they correlate from place to place.
How deep a streamer is towed, which affects ghost notches and noise.
The sideways drift of a towed streamer caused by currents, which shifts receiver positions.
Noise in streamer data from swell, tugging and flow.
The crossline distance between neighboring streamers.
A marine seismic survey with hydrophone streamers towed behind a vessel.
Loss of cement strength at high temperature without silica.
Sealing small induced fractures near the wellbore with sized particles so the rock around them is stressed and can hold more pressure.
The difference in minimum horizontal stress between layers, which helps contain fracture height.
Firing a charge into a stressed rock sample to measure realistic penetration.
Small time adjustments to a synthetic to match it to seismic.
The compass direction of a horizontal line on a tilted rock surface.
A basin, such as a pull-apart, that forms along a strike-slip fault.
A fault where the blocks move sideways past each other.
Choosing pipe sizes, grades and weights for the expected loads.
A mill in the string used to ream out casing restrictions.
A detonating cord fired at a connection to help back off pipe.
A seal around coiled tubing or pipe that holds back well pressure while the pipe moves.
Moving pipe into or out of a well under pressure through closed BOPs.
Rams used to seal around pipe while it moves through them.
A device that counts mud pump strokes to measure volume pumped.
The speed of a mud pump. Abbreviated SPM.
A layered carbonate structure built by microbial mats.
A fold that dips toward a central low in all directions.
The faults and horizons that form the skeleton of a geological model.
Mapping faults and folds on seismic data to build the structural framework.
A 3D framework of the reservoir's main horizons and faults that a geological grid is built on.
Reversing deformation on a section or model to see its earlier shape.
A trap formed by deformation of the rocks, such as an anticline or a fault that seals.
A contour map of the depth or elevation of a rock surface, showing folds, faults and possible traps.
Smoothing seismic along local dip to reduce noise while keeping faults.
A condition in which the drillstring cannot be moved up or down, or rotated, because of hole collapse, packed cuttings, key seats or differential pressure.
A seal around a moving slickline or polished rod that holds well pressure.
A jagged surface formed by pressure dissolution in carbonates. Stylolites can act as barriers to flow.
A high-frequency acoustic system that images the top tens of meters below the seabed.
In SAGD, the difference between steam temperature and the temperature at the producer. Keeping it positive stops live steam from being produced.
Where one plate sinks beneath another, forming trenches and volcanic arcs.
A deep valley cut into the shelf and slope that carries sediment to deep water.
A fan-shaped deposit at the foot of a continental slope, built by turbidity currents.
Imaging rocks beneath salt bodies, which bend and scatter seismic waves and need depth migration and accurate velocities.
A valve assembly in the BOP that lets an offshore test string be shut in and disconnected quickly.
A Christmas tree installed on the seabed, controlled remotely from a platform or vessel.
The wellhead installed on the seafloor for floating-rig and subsea wells.
Gradual sinking of the earth's surface or of a basin, making room for sediment.
The frame that supports the rig floor and derrick above the wellhead.
A valve in the tubing, usually controlled from surface through a hydraulic line, that closes automatically if surface control is lost. Abbreviated SSSV.
A biopolymer viscosifier that thins sharply above a set temperature.
A downhole plunger pump driven by a string of rods that a beam pumping unit (pumpjack) at surface moves up and down.
A device on the pump suction that smooths flow into the pump.
The mud tank from which the pumps draw.
Adding sulfate to injection water in carbonates to make the rock more water-wet.
Bacteria that produce hydrogen sulfide and cause corrosion. Abbreviated SRB.
A compound of sulfur, such as hydrogen sulfide in mud.
Cracking of high-strength steel under stress in the presence of hydrogen sulfide.
A tannin modified to work at higher temperature and salt content.
Asphalt treated to disperse in water, used in water-base mud to stabilize shale.
A polyacrylamide with sulfonate groups that better tolerates heat and salt.
A synthetic thinner and dispersant for high-temperature water-base mud.
The amount of sulfur in crude oil, which sets whether it is sweet or sour.
A packer below the perforations that forms the bottom of a gravel pack.
A formation pressure reading that is too high because mud filtrate is still leaking in.
Carbon dioxide above about 88 °F and 1,070 psi, dense like a liquid but flowing like a gas.
The velocity a phase would have if it alone filled the whole pipe: its flow rate divided by the pipe area.
Adding together the pressure responses of individual rate changes, or of image wells, to model complex tests and boundaries.
The casing string that protects fresh-water aquifers and provides a foundation for the blowout preventer.
Friction loss in the standpipe, hose, swivel and kelly or top drive.
Sampling soil or seabed for hydrocarbons that have leaked from below.
Receivers at the surface that record microseismic events.
Sending downhole gauge data to surface during a test so it can be watched live.
Logging with data sent up the cable to surface in real time.
How strongly pore surfaces speed up NMR relaxation.
An automatic valve on the tree, usually the upper master or wing valve, that closes if a safety system trips. Abbreviated SSV.
Separator oil and gas samples taken at surface and recombined in the lab.
The energy at the surface of a liquid that makes it behave like a stretched skin; lowered by surfactants.
A valve assembly at the top of the test string that controls flow during a drillstem test or well test.
The pressure at the wellhead during a treatment.
A seismic wave that travels along the earth's surface, such as a Rayleigh or Love wave.
The equipment and crew used at surface to control, separate, measure and dispose of fluids during a well test.
Correcting amplitudes for source and receiver coupling differences.
Deconvolution that separates source, receiver and offset effects on the wavelet.
A data-driven method that predicts and removes multiples that bounced off the sea surface. Abbreviated SRME.
A surface-active agent that lowers tension between two fluids or a fluid and a solid.
Injecting surfactants that cut the oil–water interfacial tension sharply, so trapped oil droplets can move.
Loss of surfactant to rock by adsorption and trapping.
A batch of surfactant solution injected to mobilize residual oil.
A pill of surfactant that cleans oil-mud film from casing.
Alternating slugs of surfactant solution and gas to make foam in the reservoir. Abbreviated SAG.
A chemical flood with a surfactant slug to free trapped oil, followed by polymer for mobility control. Abbreviated SP flooding.
The extra bottomhole pressure created by running pipe into the hole. If too large it can fracture the formation.
A pressure-rated tank used in well testing to measure oil rate and shrinkage.
Another name for a proxy model.
Planning a seismic survey's geometry, fold and offsets to meet imaging goals.
A depth where inclination and azimuth are measured.
A well that is temporarily shut in with barriers in place, awaiting further work or decision.
Pressure in a well annulus that builds back after being bled off, a sign of a leak in a barrier.
