A rubber cup on a swab mandrel that lifts fluid up the tubing.
Gas drawn into the well by swabbing as pipe is pulled.
The wire used to run swab cups.
The drop in bottomhole pressure created by pulling pipe out of the hole. If too large it can let formation fluid in.
The valve at the top of a Christmas tree that gives vertical access to the well for wireline and coiled tubing.
Pulling a cup-fitted tool up the tubing on wireline to lift fluid and start a well flowing.
A strip of a 3D land survey recorded with one set of receiver lines.
A pill of high-viscosity or weighted mud pumped around to carry out cuttings the normal circulation leaves behind.
The fraction of the reservoir volume actually contacted by the injected fluid, made up of areal and vertical sweep.
The duration of a vibroseis sweep.
Crude oil with low sulfur content, usually below about 0.5%. Crude with more sulfur is called sour.
Natural gas with little or no hydrogen sulfide.
An area within a play where rock quality and production are better than average.
Removing hydrogen sulfide and carbon dioxide from gas.
An attribute equal to amplitude divided by the square root of frequency, which highlights clean sands in clastic sequences.
Envelope divided by the square root of instantaneous frequency, used to spot sands.
Low-frequency noise in marine data caused by waves.
A packer with an elastomer that swells in oil or water to seal the annulus, with no setting mechanism.
A PVT test that measures how much an oil expands as injection gas dissolves in it.
A device that hangs the drillstring and lets it rotate while mud flows in from the hose. A top drive includes this function.
Potassium chloride mineral found in evaporites.
Bitumen blended with synthetic crude.
A downward, trough-shaped fold with the youngest rocks in its core.
Deposited while rifting was active, so the layers thicken toward the faults.
Light crude produced by upgrading bitumen. Abbreviated SCO.
A manufactured base fluid such as olefin or ester used in synthetic-base mud.
A seismic trace calculated from sonic and density logs, used to tie well depths to seismic reflections.
An invert-emulsion mud that uses synthetic liquids such as olefins or esters instead of diesel or mineral oil. It performs like oil-base mud with lower toxicity.
A group of linked depositional systems formed during one part of a relative sea-level cycle.
The NMR recovery time of magnetization along the magnetic field.
A 2D NMR display that separates fluids by their two relaxation times.
The NMR relaxation time used to separate bound fluid (below) from free fluid (above), often 33 ms in sandstone.
The spread of NMR transverse relaxation times measured in a rock. Longer times correspond to larger pores.
The NMR decay time of magnetization across the magnetic field.
Flat cavings that come off along bedding planes.
A float at the far end of a streamer that carries GPS and lights.
The last, denser slurry pumped to cover the shoe and lower annulus.
A contract clause requiring the buyer to pay for a minimum quantity whether or not it takes delivery.
A by-product of pulping pine whose fatty acids make oil-mud emulsifiers.
A straight, constant-angle section of a directional well.
Measuring a tank's dimensions to build a table converting liquid level to volume.
A plant extract used as a thinner in water-base mud.
A fishing tool that screws into the inside of a lost tubular to grip it.
Coiled tubing with wall thickness that changes along its length.
A mill shaped like a cone, used to dress or open tight spots.
The point or zone a well is planned to reach.
A transform that maps data into intercept time and ray parameter, used to separate events and remove noise.
A roller cone bit with tungsten carbide inserts, for harder rock.
Tubing-conveyed perforating: guns run on tubing or drillpipe, allowing long intervals and underbalance.
Reversal of movement on faults, for example a basin compressed after extension, which can form anticlines.
Diagenesis after uplift back toward the surface.
A departure from the expected temperature profile, often at fluid entries or leaks.
A factor that corrects measured volume to a standard temperature.
Tubing length change caused by temperature change.
A record of temperature down the well. Changes from the geothermal trend show where fluids enter or leave, and where there are leaks.
The highest temperature at which an additive or fluid is designed to work.
Mud density adjusted for the effect of downhole temperature and pressure.
A bed deposited by a storm, often with a sharp base and hummocky layering.
Securing a well with plugs so it can be safely left and re-entered later.
A barrier meant to be removed later, such as a retrievable plug.
Drilling from a platform with support from a nearby tender vessel.
A triangle plot of three-component mixtures, used to show phase behavior and miscibility.
A gravity correction for the effect of nearby hills and valleys.
Recovery carried out after secondary recovery, usually by an EOR method, to produce some of the oil left behind.
A burner on a boom that burns oil produced during an offshore well test.
How long the flow and shut-in periods of a test last.
A manifold that routes one well at a time to the test separator.
A heat exchanger in a well test spread that warms fluids to prevent hydrates and help separation.
The report of a test's analysis and conclusions.
The flowline from the test header to the test separator.
What a well test is meant to find, such as productivity, pressure or boundaries.
A packer in a test string that isolates the zone being tested.
A summary of a well test's rates, pressures, samples and results.
Planning and controls that keep people and equipment safe during a test.
A separator used to measure one well at a time, so its individual rates can be determined.
The planned order of flow and shut-in periods in a test.
The full layout of surface test equipment on location.
The pipe and tools run into a well for a drillstem test, including packers, valves, gauges and samplers.
A jar in a test string used to free the packer if it sticks.
The set of surface equipment and crew for a well test.
Opening and closing the downhole tester valve, often by annulus pressure.
The downhole valve in a test string that opens and closes the well to flow.
A phosphate thinner used in freshwater mud at low temperature. Abbreviated TSPP.
A maturity scale based on the color of spores and pollen.
The rate at which thermal neutrons are absorbed, measured by pulsed neutron tools. Abbreviated TDT.
Breakdown of mud polymers at high temperature, which reduces their viscosity and fluid-loss control.
Heating oily cuttings to vaporize and recover the oil, leaving clean solids.
The fraction of injected heat that stays in the target reservoir.
How much mud volume grows as it heats.
Increase in oil volume when heated, which helps push oil out.
How far heat has transformed the organic matter in a source rock, from immature through the oil window to the gas window.
A neutron slowed to the energy of its surroundings. Many neutron tools count these to estimate porosity.
Recovery methods that heat the reservoir, such as steam injection and in-situ combustion, to cut oil viscosity.
How well an additive or mud keeps its properties at high temperature.
Slow sinking of a basin as stretched lithosphere cools.
Gas formed by heating organic matter deep in the earth.
How long a cement slurry stays pumpable at downhole temperature and pressure.
A high-permeability layer that takes most of the injected fluid.
A bed thinner than the tool's or seismic resolution.
A slice of rock ground to about 30 microns so it can be studied under a microscope.
Interpreting beds thinner than a tool's resolution, often with high-resolution or image logs.
A chemical that lowers mud viscosity and gel strength.
A depositional sequence lasting roughly 0.5 to 3 million years.
The ability of a fluid to build a gel structure when left still and to thin again when it is stirred or pumped.
A method that uses porosity and shale volume to tell whether shale is laminated, structural or dispersed in a sand.
The parameters ε, δ and γ that describe weak elastic anisotropy in layered rock.
Oil, water and gas flowing together.
A separator that splits the wellstream into gas, oil and free water, each leaving through its own outlet.
A trap closed by dip on three sides and by a fault on the fourth.
Describes tools or operations run inside the production tubing, so the tubing does not have to be pulled.
A plug small enough to pass through tubing that expands to seal the larger casing below.
A gravel pack installed through existing tubing.
Work done inside the tubing without pulling it.
Fishing done inside tubing with small tools.
A zone of stacked thrust faults and folds at the front of a mountain range.
A low-angle reverse fault that can push older rocks over younger ones.
A gravity correction for the pull of the sun and moon.
Small regular pressure changes in a reservoir caused by earth tides.
A broad, gently sloping coastal area flooded and drained by tides, made of mud and sand.
A delta whose shape is controlled by tides, with elongate sand bars.
A line on a phase diagram joining compositions of two phases in equilibrium.
A casing string run from a liner top back to surface to give the well a full-length casing.
Gas in sandstone or carbonate with very low permeability, typically below 0.1 mD, that needs fracturing to flow at economic rates.
A section where pipe drags or sticks, or a well whose data are kept confidential.
Oil produced from very low-permeability rock using horizontal wells and fracturing.
A fluid contact that is not horizontal, often from water flow or production.
The time between drilling a depth and logging it, which affects invasion.
Lining up time axes of data and type curve to find wellbore storage.
Migration done in time with smoothly varying velocities. It is faster than depth migration but less accurate in complex geology.
A change in travel time between surveys caused by velocity or thickness changes.
A horizontal section through a 3D seismic volume at a constant time.
The rate of change of 4D time shift with time, related to velocity and compaction.
A map of horizon two-way time.
A plot relating two-way time to depth at a well, from a checkshot or VSP.
A table linking seismic time to depth at a well.
The difference between two seismic surveys taken at different times.
Measurements recorded with timestamps at regular intervals, such as pressures and rates from sensors.
A maturity measure that combines how long and how hot a rock has been.
An empirical equation estimating permeability from porosity and irreducible water saturation.
Deliberately letting proppant bridge at the fracture tip so continued pumping widens the fracture, as in frac packs.
The temperature of maximum hydrocarbon release in Rock-Eval pyrolysis, an indicator of thermal maturity.
A model that represents mixing of solvent and oil in simulation with a mixing parameter.
The far end of a horizontal well's lateral.
A pressure-activated sleeve at the toe of a well, opened to start the first fracturing stage without perforating.
A combustion process using a vertical injector and horizontal producer. Abbreviated THAI.
Statics computed from a near-surface velocity model built by first-break tomography.
A device at the top of the lubricator that grabs the toolstring if the wire breaks.
The direction a steering tool or bent motor is pointing around the hole.
The thick, threaded connector at each end of a joint of drillpipe.
A logging tool getting stuck in the well.
Several logging tools connected and run in one trip.
A device that stops tools from falling down the well if the line parts at the surface.
A short safety meeting held at the worksite before a job starts.
The rig supervisor responsible for the crew and equipment on a drilling rig.
A motor hung from the derrick that rotates the drillstring directly and lets the crew drill with full stands of pipe.
The highest point of cement in an annulus. Abbreviated TOC.
The depth of the top of a fish.
A solid wiper plug pumped behind cement to separate it from displacement fluid.
Layers ending upward against an overlying surface, where sediment bypassed or was eroded.
A bar chart that ranks how much each uncertain input changes the result, with the biggest effect at the top.
The friction forces that resist rotating and moving the drillstring. They limit how far and how deep a well can be drilled.
Lowering rotational friction, for example with lubricants or beads.
The constant a in the Archie equation, often taken as 1 (or 0.62 to 0.81 in some sandstone forms).
The amount of base needed to neutralize the acids in crude oil. Abbreviated TAN.
The combined compressibility of rock and fluids, weighted by saturation. Written c<sub>t</sub>.
The final depth reached by a well. Abbreviated TD.
The total amount of dissolved salts and other matter in water, in mg/L. Abbreviated TDS.
The combined cross-sectional area of all the bit nozzles, used in bit hydraulics calculations. Abbreviated TFA.
The combined hydrocarbon gas detected in the returning mud by the mud logger, a quick indicator of shows.
The total calcium and magnesium content of water or mud filtrate, measured by titration.
Losing all returns, so no mud comes back to surface.
The strength of the measured magnetic field. Abbreviated TMI.
The weight percent of organic carbon in a rock, a basic measure of how rich a source rock is. Abbreviated TOC.
The measured amount of oil in a sample such as soil or cuttings. Abbreviated TPH.
All pore space in a rock, whether connected or not and including clay-bound water.
The sum of all skin components measured by a test.
A test of how harmful a fluid is to marine organisms, required for offshore discharge.
Scaling traces so their average amplitudes match.
Removing or fixing bad traces during processing.
A record of animal activity, such as a burrow or track, preserved in rock.
The data block at the start of each trace with its location, offset and other information.
Creating missing seismic traces from their neighbors.
A powered tool that drags wireline tools along horizontal wells.
A rule set that slows or stops injection when induced seismicity passes set magnitudes.
A pump that moves liquids between tanks or to a pipeline.
An area that links offset fault segments and passes displacement between them.
A strike-slip fault that links offset plate boundaries.
The fraction of a source rock's original potential that has turned into hydrocarbons.
A landward shift of the shoreline as sea level rises relative to the land, which leaves deeper-water sediments over shallower ones.
The first major flooding surface over a lowstand, at the base of the transgressive systems tract.
Deposits laid down while the shoreline moves landward. Abbreviated TST.
An EM method that measures the decay of induced currents after a current is switched off. Abbreviated TEM.
Flow in which pressure is still changing as the disturbance spreads.
A test that measures the changing pressure response to a change in rate.
The time a slurry takes to go from 100 to 500 lbf/100 ft² static gel strength.
The interval above the free water level where water saturation falls gradually from 100% toward irreducible because of capillary pressure.
A seismic survey across shallow water, beaches and marshes.
Flow between laminar and turbulent.
Strike-slip movement combined with compression.
Strike-slip movement combined with extension.
An arrangement of reservoir rock and seal that stops hydrocarbons from migrating further and lets them accumulate.
The chance that a trap is not present as mapped.
A telescoping tubing joint that lets the string lengthen or shorten slightly during operations.
The moving set of sheaves that hangs from the drilling line and carries the hook or top drive.
A plot showing nearby wells around the planned path, used for anti-collision.
Slips on the moving part of a snubbing unit that grip the pipe.
The time a seismic wave takes to travel from source to receiver along a path.
High-pressure pipe from the pumps to the wellhead during a treatment.
How much of an additive is added per unit of mud or time.
The cap on top of the Christmas tree that seals the vertical bore and allows a lubricator to be attached.
The period from about 252 to 201 million years ago.
An induction tool with coils in three directions that measures horizontal and vertical resistivity.
The combined axial, radial and hoop stresses in pipe.
A roller cone bit with three cones.
Pull the drillstring out of the hole and run it back in.
A gas peak in the returns after a trip, from swabbing and fluid seeping in while the pumps were off.
Extra mud weight above the minimum needed, to offset swab pressure when pulling pipe.
A small, accurately calibrated tank used to measure the mud needed to keep the hole full while pipe is tripped.
A mud pump with three pistons, the standard type on modern rigs.
Pulling the drillstring out of the hole (tripping out) or running it back in (tripping in), for example to change the bit.
How fast pipe is pulled or run, limited to control surge and swab.
Amplitudes processed so they keep their relative strength.
A distillation that separates crude into cuts by boiling range. Abbreviated TBP.
The temperature at which salt crystals form in a clear brine as it cools. Brines must stay above it. Abbreviated TCT.
The maximum dip of a surface, measured perpendicular to strike.
The resistivity of the undisturbed formation beyond the zone invaded by mud filtrate, written R<sub>t</sub>.
The thickness of a bed measured perpendicular to the bedding. Abbreviated TST.
The vertical distance from a reference level to a point in the well. Hydrostatic pressure depends on this depth, not on the measured length. Abbreviated TVD.
The vertical thickness of a bed, corrected for well deviation and dip. Abbreviated TVT.
Layers cut off at an erosional surface.
Tilted transverse isotropy: anisotropy whose symmetry axis is tilted, as in dipping shales near salt.
A wave traveling in the borehole fluid, a source of noise in VSPs.
A device that holds tubing in place, often in rod pump wells.
Pulling and replacing the tubing string.
The threaded collar that joins two tubing joints.
A tool that cuts tubing downhole by chemical, jet or mechanical means.
Sizing tubing and choosing its grade so it handles the loads and flow rate.
The strength rating of tubing steel, such as J-55, L-80 or P-110.
The device in the wellhead that supports the weight of the tubing and seals the tubing–casing annulus.
The wellhead spool that holds the tubing hanger and seals the tubing–casing annulus.
The pressure at the top of the tubing at surface. Abbreviated THP or FTHP when flowing.
Checking pulled tubing for wall loss, pitting and cracks before it is reused.
A hole or failed connection in the tubing string.
Lengthening or shortening of tubing with temperature and pressure changes.
A curve showing bottomhole pressure needed to lift fluids at various rates through tubing.
A small charge that makes a hole in tubing, for example to circulate between tubing and annulus.
A tool that makes holes in tubing to allow circulation.
The pipe in a completed well through which fluids are produced or injected.
A tapered tool driven down tubing to straighten slightly collapsed sections.
Equipment that pressure tests tubing as it is run.
Perforating guns run on tubing or drillpipe rather than wireline, allowing long intervals and large underbalance in one run. Abbreviated TCP.
A subsurface safety valve built into the tubing string, recovered only by pulling the tubing. Abbreviated TRSV.
A completion that produces through small casing without separate tubing, used to cut costs.
Rock formed from volcanic ash.
An air-gun array whose gun sizes are chosen so their bubble pulses cancel.
The bed thickness, about a quarter wavelength, at which reflections from the top and base interfere most strongly.
A sediment layer deposited by a turbidity current, an underwater flow of sediment-laden water. Turbidites form many deepwater reservoirs.
A sheet-like sand body deposited at the end of a deepwater channel.
Cloudiness of a fluid caused by suspended particles.
A dense, sediment-laden flow that rushes down an underwater slope and deposits a turbidite.
A flowmeter whose rotor spins at a speed proportional to the flow rate.
A downhole motor with turbine blades driven by mud flow, turning the bit at high speed.
A turbine that cools gas deeply by expanding it while recovering work, used for high NGL recovery.
Chaotic, mixing flow at high velocity, with higher friction pressure.
The rate of change of well azimuth, usually in degrees per 100 ft.
An anticline formed between two salt withdrawal basins.
A pressure function that accounts for oil and gas flowing together near the well.
A cement job with bottom and top plugs.
The time a seismic wave takes to travel down to a reflector and back up to the receivers. Seismic sections are normally displayed in two-way time.
A family of dimensionless pressure responses for a reservoir model, matched to field data to estimate reservoir parameters.
Overlaying test data on type curves to find permeability, skin and storage.
A representative well log chosen to define the formations and markers of an area.
The reference exposure or well where a rock unit was first described.
An average production profile used to plan and value wells in a play.
Flow caused by different fluid densities in the drillpipe and annulus, which continues after the pumps stop until pressures balance.
The total oil expected to be recovered from a reservoir over its life.
Interfacial tension near 0.001 mN/m, low enough to free trapped oil.
A lab instrument that tracks cement strength development by sound speed. Abbreviated UCA.
A rotating ultrasonic tool that maps cement bonding all around the casing.
A flowmeter that measures velocity from the travel time of sound pulses through the fluid.
A tool that maps the borehole wall with a rotating ultrasonic transducer.
Studying the range of possible outcomes from uncertain inputs.
Estimating the range of possible outcomes, such as volumes in place or recovery, and how likely each is.
The axial stress at which a rock sample fails with no confining pressure. Abbreviated UCS.
A buried surface of erosion or non-deposition that separates rocks of very different ages.
A trap formed where a reservoir is cut off by an unconformity and sealed above it.
Loose sand with little or no cement, prone to sand production.
Oil or gas that cannot be produced economically without special techniques, such as massive hydraulic fracturing or steam.
Drilling with bottomhole pressure deliberately kept below formation pressure, so the reservoir flows while it is being drilled.
A fluid light enough that well pressure stays below formation pressure.
Perforating with wellbore pressure below reservoir pressure. The sudden inflow surges debris out of the tunnels and cleans them.
A trap that holds less hydrocarbon than its closure could.
The heavy, solids-rich discharge of a hydrocyclone or centrifuge.
A tool whose cutters open below a restriction to enlarge the hole beneath it.
Oil above its bubblepoint pressure, so it holds all the gas it could dissolve with none free.
Salt mud deliberately kept below saturation to wash slightly and offset salt creep.
Placing sources and receivers on opposite sides of an obstruction, such as a platform, to record data beneath it.
A fracture model in which fluid enters evenly along its length.
The ratio of D40 to D90 grain sizes, showing how well sorted a sand is.
A 45-degree line on a log-log plot that shows wellbore storage or pseudosteady state.
Combining leases that share one reservoir so it is developed as a single unit, with costs and production shared.
Mud with no added weighting material, getting its density only from water, salts and drilled solids.
A logging run pulling the tool up the well.
The part of a VSP traveling upward, mainly reflections.
A plant that converts bitumen into lighter synthetic crude.
Processing heavy oil or bitumen to make it lighter and less viscous, for example by coking or hydrocracking, to produce synthetic crude.
Measuring travel times from a shot at the bottom of a hole to surface receivers to find the velocity of the near surface.
Raising of the earth's crust, which can expose rocks to erosion and alter traps.
The part of a completion from the reservoir to surface: tubing, safety valve, gas-lift mandrels, gauges and the tubing hanger.
Converting fine-scale rock properties into averaged values for the larger grid blocks used in flow simulation.
The exploration and production part of the oil and gas industry: finding, drilling and producing hydrocarbons.
The pressure before a choke, valve or meter.
A vibroseis sweep that starts at low frequency and rises.
Calculating a potential field as if measured higher, which smooths shallow effects.
A wettability test using areas under centrifuge capillary pressure curves.
Universal Transverse Mercator: a projection that divides the earth into 60 zones.
A box with ultraviolet light used to check cuttings for oil fluorescence.
The opening in the derrick where pipe is brought onto the rig floor.
A degasser that uses a vacuum to pull gas bubbles from mud.
Double-wall tubing with a vacuum between walls to cut heat loss.
The parts in a mud pump fluid end that open and close to control flow.
Injecting grease into gate valves to keep them sealing and moving freely.
A plot of hydrogen/carbon against oxygen/carbon ratios used to classify kerogen.
Vapor extraction: like SAGD, but a vaporized solvent instead of steam dilutes the heavy oil so it drains to the producer.
A process like SAGD that uses solvent vapor instead of steam. Abbreviated VAPEX.
A compressor package that collects gas vapors from tanks instead of venting or flaring them. Abbreviated VRU.
A miscible process in which lean gas picks up intermediate components from the oil until it becomes miscible.
A seismic display with peaks shaded black and troughs left blank.
A seismic display that shows amplitudes as colors or gray shades.
A display of the full acoustic waveform from a cement bond tool, used to judge bonding to the casing and formation. Abbreviated VDL.
A cementation exponent that changes with depth or rock type.
A streamer towed deeper toward its far end to broaden the frequency band.
An attribute that measures how different neighboring traces are, highlighting faults and edges.
A function that describes how different two samples are expected to be as the distance between them grows. It is the basis of kriging and stochastic simulation.
Finding the velocities that best flatten reflections on gathers, usually by scanning semblance.
A zone of unusual velocity that distorts seismic times.
Change of velocity with frequency.
A model of seismic velocity across a survey area.
The rate at which velocity increases with depth.
A layer with lower velocity than the layer above, often a sign of overpressure or gas.
Creating the velocity model used for depth migration and depth conversion, with tomography, well data and interpretation.
Choosing stacking velocities from velocity analysis displays.
The factor converting spinner-measured velocity to average velocity across the pipe.
An apparent upward bending of reflectors beneath fast rock such as salt or a reef, a time effect that depth conversion removes.
A downward bulge in seismic events beneath a slow zone such as gas.
A display of semblance against time and velocity used to pick stacking velocities.
A smaller tubing, often coiled tubing, installed in a gas well to raise gas velocity and stop liquid loading.
A narrowing in the hopper line that creates suction to draw in dry materials.
A flowmeter that measures flow from the pressure drop through a smooth constriction.
A centrifugal dryer that spins oil from cuttings.
Permeability across the bedding. Symbol kv.
Resistivity measured across the bedding. Symbol Rv.
The thinnest bed a logging tool can measure correctly.
The horizontal distance along a chosen direction, plotted against depth in well plans.
A survey with receivers placed in a well and the source at surface. It gives accurate time–depth data and an image close to the well. Abbreviated VSP.
The fraction of the reservoir's vertical cross-section that the injected fluid has contacted, reduced by layering and gravity.
Fluid density measured from the vibration frequency of a fork.
A truck that shakes the ground with a controlled sweep as a land seismic source.
A land seismic source in which a truck-mounted plate vibrates the ground with a controlled sweep of frequencies.
Cross-correlating a recorded vibroseis signal with the sweep to compress it into a short pulse.
The controlled signal a vibrator emits, rising or falling in frequency over several seconds.
Estimating well rates from pressure and temperature data with models instead of meters.
Mild thermal cracking that lowers the viscosity of heavy oil.
Having both viscous and elastic behavior, as some polymer fluids do.
A polymer-free fracturing or acid fluid thickened by surfactant micelles.
Checking a viscometer with standard calibration fluids.
A rig-site test that measures barite sag in a viscometer cup fitted with a sloped shoe. Abbreviated VSST.
Any additive that raises mud viscosity, such as bentonite, xanthan gum or organophilic clay.
Lowering oil viscosity, for example by heat or dissolved gas, so it flows more easily.
An unstable displacement in which a less viscous injected fluid pushes through the oil in finger-like channels, bypassing much of it.
A thick spacer that pushes mud ahead of it during a displacement.
Displaying data as images or 3D views to help understanding.
The percentage of light reflected by vitrinite (woody organic particles) under a microscope, used to measure thermal maturity. Written R<sub>o</sub>.
An empirical inflow relationship for wells below the bubblepoint: q/q<sub>max</sub> = 1 − 0.2(p<sub>wf</sub>/p̄<sub>r</sub>) − 0.8(p<sub>wf</sub>/p̄<sub>r</sub>)².
The reservoir volume of fluids withdrawn by production.
The reservoir volume of fluids injected divided by the reservoir volume produced. A value of 1 holds reservoir pressure steady.
The upper limit on mixture stiffness, from averaging moduli by volume.
The average of the Voigt and Reuss bounds, used to estimate mineral mixture moduli.
A chain of volcanoes above a subduction zone.
Rock made of volcanic fragments that have been transported and deposited.
Parts of a component per hundred parts of total volume.
A well-control method used when circulation is impossible: gas is allowed to rise while mud is bled off to hold bottomhole pressure constant.
Pe times electron density, which adds linearly by volume in mixtures. Symbol U.
The product of areal and vertical sweep: the fraction of the reservoir volume contacted by the injected fluid.
An equivalent stress used to check combined loads against pipe yield strength.
A meter that measures flow by counting vortices shed behind a bluff body.
The ratio of P-wave to S-wave velocity, which helps distinguish lithology and gas.
Vertical transverse isotropy: rock whose properties are the same in all horizontal directions but differ vertically, typical of shale.
A cavity in rock, larger than the surrounding pores, typically formed by dissolution in carbonates.
Large irregular pores, called vugs, formed by dissolution in carbonates.
A mud-supported carbonate with more than 10% grains.
Change in relative permeability between water and gas cycles in WAG injection.
The ratio of water volume to gas volume injected in a water-alternating-gas scheme.
A one-circulation kill method. Kill-weight mud is mixed first, then pumped while the influx is circulated out. Also called the engineer's method.
The time allowed for cement to set before drilling resumes. Abbreviated WOC.
A VSP with sources in a circle around the well, used to study anisotropy.
A vertical seismic profile with the source moved to many offsets from the well, used for AVO and anisotropy studies.
Ground nut shells used as a granular lost circulation material.
The return of temperature toward geothermal after injection stops, used to find where fluid went.
A small pipe run inside the screen during gravel packing that returns carrier fluid to surface.
An enlarged section of borehole, or a hole cut through pipe by fluid flowing through a leak.
Errors in pad-type logs caused by an enlarged hole.
Running a large-diameter pipe with a cutting shoe over a stuck fish to free it.
A measure of how freely water in a fluid can move to another material. Matching the mud's water activity to the shale's limits shale hydration.
An instrument, usually a hygrometer, that measures the water activity of oil-mud or shale.
Measuring ions and properties of produced or formation water.
Water trapped near the wellbore by capillary forces, which reduces gas or oil relative permeability.
Lower gas permeability caused by water trapped near the wellbore.
The first arrival of injected or aquifer water at a producing well, after which water cut rises.
A spray of water that shields equipment from burner heat.
The fraction or percentage of water in the total liquid produced.
Measuring the fraction of water in the liquid produced.
An instrument that measures the water fraction in a liquid stream.
A drive mechanism in which water from an aquifer moves into the reservoir as fluids are produced, keeping pressure up.
A depth where water flows into the well.
Work on injectors and producers to keep a waterflood running.
An influx of water into the well, such as shallow water flow offshore.
A pulsed neutron measurement that detects water moving behind or inside casing.
Separating, treating and disposing of produced water.
The fraction of pipe area filled by water.
Pumping water into a formation, either to dispose of produced water or to maintain reservoir pressure.
Facilities that treat and pump water into injection wells.
Another name for fluid loss: filtrate passing from mud into the formation.
The salt concentration, usually calcium chloride, of the brine droplets in an invert-emulsion mud. It is set to stop water moving into shale.
A sample of formation water taken for analysis.
The fraction of the pore volume filled with water, written S<sub>w</sub>. Hydrocarbon saturation is 1 − S<sub>w</sub>.
Treatments such as gels, cement or mechanical plugs that reduce unwanted water production.
Finding which zone or channel is producing unwanted water.
Injecting slugs of water and gas in turn. The water reduces gas channeling and improves sweep. Abbreviated WAG.
A drilling fluid whose continuous phase is fresh water, seawater or brine. It is the most common and lowest-cost type of mud.
Pilot tests that add a contaminant, such as cement or salt, to a mud sample to plan treatments.
Invasion of water-base mud filtrate into a formation, which lowers resistivity close to the borehole in oil zones.
A multiple that bounces between the sea surface and the seabed.
The amount of mix water per amount of cement, which controls density and strength.
Mud diluted by an influx of formation water.
Water produced per volume of gas.
An emulsion with water droplets in continuous oil, the basis of invert muds.
Water produced per unit of oil produced. Abbreviated WOR.
The shallowest depth where water is proven in a well. Abbreviated WUT.
Solids coated with water in an invert-emulsion mud, which clump, settle and destabilize the emulsion.
The layout of injectors and producers in a waterflood.
Injecting water into a reservoir to maintain pressure and push oil toward the producing wells. It is the most common secondary recovery method.
The equation describing how waves travel, the basis of modern migration and modeling.
A delta whose shape is controlled by waves, with smooth sandy shorelines.
Migration that solves the wave equation to move energy to its true position.
The whole pattern of seismic waves moving through the earth at a moment in time.
Splitting recorded data into upgoing and downgoing or P and S parts.
A surface joining all points that a wave has reached at the same time.
The distance between successive peaks of a wave: velocity divided by frequency.
Estimating the seismic wavelet from the data, often using a well tie, for inversion and modeling.
The phase of the seismic wavelet, ideally zero for interpretation.
The temperature at which wax crystals first form as crude oil cools. Abbreviated WAT.
Scraping paraffin from tubing walls with a slickline cutting tool.
A shaly-sand saturation model that accounts for clay conductivity through the cation exchange capacity.
A deliberately weaker link at the cable head that breaks first if the tools stick.
The loose, low-velocity layer near the surface, which delays and distorts land seismic signals.
A model of a thinning layer used to study tuning.
A reservoir bounded by two faults that meet at an angle.
A land source that drops or drives a heavy mass onto the ground.
The rig gauge that shows hook load, from which the driller works out weight on bit.
The downward force on the bit, supplied by part of the drill collars' weight. Abbreviated WOB.
Mud with added weighting material to raise its density.
A dense, finely ground solid, such as barite, hematite or calcium carbonate, added to mud to raise its density.
Raising mud density by adding weighting material, for example before drilling into a high-pressure zone.
A biopolymer viscosifier with good temperature and salt stability.
A tangent drawn to the fractional-flow curve that gives the shock-front saturation and average saturation behind the front.
An envelope of one or more elements, such as cement, casing, packers and valves, that prevents unintended flow from the well.
Flowing a new or treated well to remove completion fluids, solids and acid before testing.
The record of how a well was completed.
The equipment, procedures and training used to keep formation fluids from entering the well and to remove an influx safely.
Matching rock layers from well to well using logs, cores and fossils.
Transfer of a well between drilling, completion and production teams with its records.
Applying technical and operational measures so a well keeps its fluids contained through its whole life.
A log run to check casing, tubing and cement condition.
Any operation carried out on a producing or injecting well to diagnose problems, maintain it or improve its output.
Pumping fluid heavy enough to stop a well flowing before intervention.
A continuous record against depth of rock and fluid properties, measured by tools run in the well.
A database that stores logs and their metadata for many wells.
The two parallel horizontal wells used in SAGD: a steam injector a few meters above a producer.
The designed path of a well from surface to target.
The rate a well could produce with no restrictions, used for planning and allocation.
Another name for recompletion.
Routine maintenance on producing wells, such as rod and pump changes and cleanouts.
The distance or area allotted between wells in a field. It balances recovery against drilling cost.
Regularly checking well data to spot problems early.
Temporarily securing a well with barriers while it is not in use.
A barge carrying surface test equipment for testing in shallow water.
Planning rates, durations and gauges so a test answers its questions.
Downhole and surface equipment used to flow and measure a well.
Analyzing pressure and rate data to find permeability, skin, boundaries and reservoir pressure.
Temporary surface equipment, such as choke manifold, heater, separator and burner, used to flow and measure a well.
Modeling expected test responses to plan or interpret a test.
Matching a well's synthetic seismogram or VSP to seismic data so horizons are linked to the right rock layers.
How well a synthetic seismogram matches the seismic at a well.
A pick of where a horizon is met in a well.
Fluid lost into fractures when circulating and returned when pumps stop, which can be mistaken for a kick. Also called breathing.
Removing fill, scale or debris from a well, often by circulating through coiled tubing with a jetting nozzle.
Scraping, brushing and circulating to clean casing before completion.
Replacing drilling mud with clean completion brine, using spacers and scrapers so no solids are left behind.
Choosing the method, equipment and risks for well work.
The rapid pressure change in the well right after guns fire.
Keeping the borehole wall from collapsing, swelling or fracturing, through mud weight, mud chemistry and drilling practices.
The early-time effect of fluid compressing or expanding in the wellbore, which hides the reservoir's response at the start of a test.
The volume of fluid the wellbore releases per unit pressure drop. Symbol C.
Techniques that raise the pressure a formation can take before losses, for example sealing small fractures with sized particles.
Surface equipment that suspends the casing and tubing strings, seals the annuli between them and provides a base for the BOP or tree.
Greasing, testing and repairing wellhead and tree valves.
The maximum working pressure of wellhead equipment.
Taking off the wellhead after a well is plugged.
The geologist at the rig who examines cuttings, picks formation tops and monitors the well.
In-situ combustion with water injected alongside air to carry heat forward.
A shoe with no cement left in it after over-displacement.
A gas ratio showing the share of heavier gases, used to tell oil from gas zones.
Whether the rock surface prefers to be in contact with water or with oil when both are present. It strongly affects flow and recovery.
A change in whether rock prefers oil or water, caused by surfactants, mud additives or injected fluids.
A number describing whether rock prefers water or oil.
A surfactant that makes solids wet by a chosen liquid.
A chart that plots stratigraphic units against time rather than depth, showing gaps and deposition through time.
A wedge set in a well to deflect the bit or mill sideways to start a sidetrack.
Lateral vibration where the bit or BHA spins off-center around the hole.
A full-diameter core cut while drilling.
Loss of mud, solids included, into fractures or caverns.
A marine or land survey recording many source-receiver azimuths, giving better illumination below salt and complex structure. Abbreviated WAZ.
A display of each seismic trace as a line.
An exploration well drilled in an area where no oil or gas has yet been discovered.
Cutting an opening in casing, guided by a whipstock, to drill a sidetrack.
The valve on the side outlet of a Christmas tree that routes flow to the flowline.
The pore throat radius at 35 percent mercury saturation, estimated from porosity and permeability.
A classification (types I, II and III) of oil–water–surfactant mixtures. Type III, with a middle microemulsion phase, gives the lowest interfacial tension.
A rubber plug pumped ahead of or behind the cement to keep it apart from mud and wipe the casing clean.
A short trip to clean and condition the hole.
The pull at which a wire or cable breaks.
A sand screen made of a keystone-shaped wire wound around a perforated base pipe.
Sending downhole test data to surface by acoustic or electromagnetic signals instead of cables.
Cable used to lower tools into a well. Electric line contains conductors that power logging tools and send data to surface.
A small blowout preventer with rams that close on the wireline during intervention.
Depth measured by the length of cable run into the well.
A bevelled fitting at the bottom of tubing that guides tools back into it.
Using a wireline tool to measure pressures and sample fluids at chosen depths.
A jar run on slickline or braided line to deliver blows.
A log recorded by tools lowered on wireline.
Running logging tools on an electric cable after a section has been drilled, to record formation properties.
Perforating with guns run and fired on electric wireline, which gives fast runs and precise depth control.
A plug set in a landing nipple by slickline to isolate the tubing below.
A powered tool that drives wireline tools along highly deviated or horizontal wells.
A truck carrying the winch, cable and recording unit for land logging.
The truck or skid with a winch, cable and control cabin used to run tools into a well on wireline or slickline.
A BOP on the wellhead that seals around wire.
A subsurface safety valve set in a landing nipple and run or pulled on slickline. Abbreviated WRSV.
Wellsite Information Transfer Standard Markup Language: an open XML standard for exchanging drilling and well data between companies and software.
Heating value divided by the square root of gas gravity, used to judge interchangeability of fuels.
An equation for the bulk modulus of a fluid mixture or suspension.
A share of ownership in a lease or license that carries the right to produce and the obligation to pay that share of the costs.
Major repair or modification of an existing well, often requiring the production tubing to be pulled.
The fluid in a well during workover, chosen to control pressure without damaging the formation.
The written plan for a workover.
A smaller, often mobile, rig used to pull and run tubing and do repair work on existing wells.
A high-permeability channel created in an unconsolidated heavy-oil reservoir when sand is produced in CHOPS.
Channels formed in unconsolidated sand by producing heavy oil with sand.
West Texas Intermediate: a US light crude used as a benchmark price.
A relation that estimates porosity from sonic transit time, assuming time is averaged between matrix and fluid.
A lab method that identifies minerals by how they scatter X-rays. Abbreviated XRD.
A method that measures elements in rock from the X-rays they emit. Abbreviated XRF.
A biopolymer viscosifier that gives water-base mud strong shear-thinning behavior and good low-shear suspension.
A rock physics model for shaly sands using pore shapes to predict velocities.
An aromatic solvent used to dissolve asphaltenes and paraffins.
In the Bingham-plastic model, the 300-rpm reading minus the plastic viscosity, in lbf/100 ft². It reflects attractive forces between particles and helps the mud carry cuttings.
Another name for the Herschel-Bulkley model.
The stress needed to start a fluid flowing. Estimated at the rig from low-speed viscometer readings.
The ratio of stress to strain for rock stretched or compressed in one direction, a measure of stiffness.
An operation in which no mud or cuttings are released into the environment; all are shipped or reinjected.
A symmetric wavelet with its peak at the reflector time, preferred for interpretation.
A seismic section as if source and receiver were at the same point, which a stack approximates.
A vertical seismic profile with the source next to the well, used for time-depth data and well ties.
A gun with all charges pointing one way, used for oriented perforating.
The electric charge at a particle's surface that controls whether particles stay dispersed.
A land survey layout with source points laid out in a zigzag between receiver lines.
A salt used for the heaviest clear brines, above about 15 ppg. It is corrosive and hazardous to handle.
A hydrogen sulfide scavenger that reacts with sulfides to form insoluble zinc sulfide.
A heavy salt sometimes blended into zinc brines.
A zinc compound used as a hydrogen sulfide scavenger, mainly in oil-base mud.
Fracturing two neighboring horizontal wells by alternating stages between them, so one well is treated while the other is being prepared.
A manifold that switches frac flow between wells on a pad.
A very durable mineral used for dating rocks and tracing sediment sources.
A crosslinker for high-temperature fracturing gels.
The exact equations giving reflection and transmission amplitudes at a boundary for any angle.
Splitting a well's production among zones.
Preventing fluids from moving between formations along the wellbore, mainly by cement and packers.
Dividing a reservoir into layers or zones.
Shutting off one zone, often with a plug, packer or cement.
